prisma-calibration/technical-reference/s.title: Spline model fitting (v1)
prisma-calibration/technical-reference/s.content:
In one sentence: “Color Model v1” is the server’s label for the legacy-spline model — a per-filament monotone PCHIP transmission profile built from processed-sample measurements by fit_spline_profile (calibration.fitting.fitting, fitting.py:1137), predicted and stacked by predict/compose (calibration.fitting.composition), and installed as Calibration’s current v1 fit through one staged all-or-nothing fitter reached by both the unified workflow and /api/profiles/fit-all — while the notebook-era batch_fit.py / fitter_core.py / strip_loader.py / export.py chain sits off the live path.

This page maps the code of the v1 fitter: the modules, the data flow from sample to profile, how a stacked appearance is predicted, and how its two public callers converge on one internal current-fit boundary. The older code names this boundary “publication”; it does not create or change a Generator library. It deliberately does not re-derive the physics — why PCHIP, what an optical-density transmission curve is, or what pair corrections compensate for. For the model form and math — including the empirical two-filament pair corrections — read Color Model v1. For where a v1 fit sits in the operator workflow, see Model workflow, publication, and review and The Modeling page.
Related: calibration.fitting.fitting · calibration.fitting.legacy_spline_fit_job · calibration.fitting.composition · calibration.fitting.color_math · calibration.fitting.fitter_core · calibration.fitting.batch_fit · calibration.fitting.strip_loader · calibration.fitting.export
”Color Model v1” is the legacy-spline model
The UI and the persistence layer call this the legacy-spline model. The server’s three current-fit kinds are gated by _MODEL_KINDS = {"camera_transform", "legacy_spline", "photo_stack_v2"} (sqlite_data_access.py:49); a v1 fit is recorded under model_kind="legacy_spline" (server.py:789). Wherever the interface says “Color Model v1,” the code says legacy_spline. Everything on this page produces or consumes that artifact set: per-filament profile JSONs plus a single pair_corrections.json.
The live core is calibration.fitting.fitting (fitting.py). Its own header states it “Ports the logic from batch_fit_spline.py and model_spline.py into a single module” with UI-driven parameters (fitting.py:1-13). It is the module the live fit paths actually call; the modules it was ported from still exist (see the last section) but are not on the production path.
The spline profile — build, predict, serialize
A v1 profile is a plain dict: knots_mm (thicknesses, first knot 0.0) plus per-channel T_r/T_g/T_b transmission arrays, tagged model: 'spline' (fitting.py:1375-1390). The primitives that operate on it:

build_spline (fitting.py:133) constructs three PchipInterpolators (one per channel), asserting the first knot is at d=0 and clipping T to [0,1].
predict (fitting.py:149) evaluates a profile at thickness d, returning a linear-RGB T triple; below d=0 it returns ones, and beyond the last knot it hands off to _extrapolate (fitting.py:171), a log-linear extension. The why of that extrapolation belongs to Color Model v1.
to_srgb (fitting.py:197) gamma-encodes linear T for display; profile_from_dict (fitting.py:202) pre-builds and caches the interpolators; profile_to_save_dict (fitting.py:208) strips the non-serializable _splines object and staleness flags before JSON write.
save_profile / load_profile (fitting.py:965, :975) write/read {profiles_dir}/{fid}.json. Loading routes through _load_fresh_profile_path (fitting.py:218), which treats any profile carrying a stale/stale_reason/stale_at flag as missing (_profile_is_stale, fitting.py:214) — a stale profile is never silently used.

OKLab conversion (linear_to_oklab, fitting.py:115) and deltaE_ok (fitting.py:123) live here too and back the fit-quality diagnostics.
From sample to strip dict — the adapters
The fitter’s internal unit is a strip dict (thicknesses, per-swatch linear transmission, optional fixed_layers). Adapters convert a live Sample into that shape:

_legacy_spline_geometry (fitting.py:247) reads a sample’s canonical physical stack (via physical_stack_for_swatch, calibration.fitting.physical_stack) and returns the one variable filament plus any fixed base layers below it — or None for richer geometries the legacy spline deliberately refuses to reinterpret (is_legacy_spline_supported_stack).
_sample_to_strip_dict (fitting.py:273) is the legacy adapter reading color from Sample.measurements. _sample_to_strip_dict_from_sidecar (fitting.py:325) is its production twin, pulling measured transmission and I0 from the per-sample extraction_result sidecar while keeping geometry and filament assignments from the live sample; a measurement-bearing sample with an absent or malformed sidecar raises SidecarAdapterError (fitting.py:319) rather than falling back.
The active source is a module switch _MEASURED_SOURCE = "sidecar" (fitting.py:399); _strip_dict_for (fitting.py:402) dispatches on it, and use_measured_source (fitting.py:409) is a context manager for oracle/rollback/test runs. Production reads the sidecar.

_load_strips_from_samples (fitting.py:455) and _load_all_strips_from_samples (fitting.py:482) walk store.list_samples(), keep only processed samples with measurements and a strip definition, and bucket the resulting strip dicts by variable filament. The fit paths pass this pre-built strips_by_filament cache down so the whole corpus is loaded once per run.
The four data sources and the fit
For each filament, four loaders extract (d, T_rgb) points, each targeting a different strip geometry:

load_single_fil_data (fitting.py:701) — solo strips (“thick”), skipping colored-base and white-base strips.
load_thin_strip_data (fitting.py:741) — white-base + overlay strips (“thin”), peeling the base by local d=0 normalization (_d0_normalize_strip, fitting.py:627).
load_fixed_role_data (fitting.py:799) — Role-B cross-cal, where the filament is the fixed base and a d=0 swatch is a direct profile-independent measurement of it.
load_crosscal_data (fitting.py:862) — Role-A cross-cal (filament is the variable overlay on a colored base), T0-weighted; diagnostic-only for fitting.

fit_spline_profile (fitting.py:1137) is the core. It merges the caller’s exclusions with the hardwired EXCLUDED_EXPERIMENTS (fitting.py:80, still pinning exp-135 pending its per-sample migration) and the always-on registry-driven samples_excluded_by_filament set (fitting.py:1190). It then combines sources by priority (thick baseline, thin fills gaps and wins below thin_wins_below; combine_datasets, fitting.py:984), drops outlier knots against a log-linear neighbor trend (_drop_outlier_knots_with_removed, fitting.py:1064), prepends the d=0/T=1 anchor, enforces per-channel monotone non-increase (fitting.py:1337-1341), applies a T_FLOOR of 0.003 (fitting.py:95, :1345), and truncates a trailing noise floor. It returns (profile_dict, diagnostics_dict) — (None, diagnostics) on failure with an error key. get_fit_data_points (fitting.py:1531) and compute_delta_e (fitting.py:1398) expose the same data for the review charts.
Predicting stacked appearance and pair corrections
calibration.fitting.composition (composition.py) predicts what a stack of layers looks like. compose (composition.py:43) multiplies each layer’s predict(profile, d) per channel, then — if a corrections table is supplied and there are ≥2 layers — applies an interpolated per-pair factor keyed overlay_fid|base@d (_interpolate_correction, composition.py:28). predict_two_layer (composition.py:80) is the direct overlay-plus-base convenience path using calibration.fitting.color_math’s interp_single (color_math.py:10). calibration.fitting.color_math is a pure-math leaf (no intra-project imports) that is genuinely live — imported by both composition.py and the server. compute_sample_predictions (fitting.py:1594) drives compose over every processed sample of a filament to build the predicted-vs-measured review payload.
The pair corrections themselves are computed on the live path by compute_and_save_pair_corrections (fitting.py:1861): it builds a registry with _build_pair_corrections_registry (fitting.py:1769), then calls into calibration.fitting.fitter_core for compute_pair_corrections (fitter_core.py:258) and save_pair_corrections (fitter_core.py:367), writing pair_corrections.json beside the profiles. This is the one live thread through the notebook-origin fitter_core — its correction math is reused, but its strip-file fitting is not. When a full model library is explicitly published, Generator reads the copied correction file from its selected immutable library at LUT build time; what the corrections model is covered by Color Model v1’s pair-corrections section.
The two entry points share one staged publisher
Both live entry points now converge on run_legacy_spline_fit_all and its staged all-or-nothing publication path:


Unified workflow → calibration.fitting.legacy_spline_fit_job. run_legacy_spline_fit_all (legacy_spline_fit_job.py:305) creates a private .legacy-spline-fit-<uuid> workspace for SQLite publication (:315-:329). The implementation fits profiles and pair corrections there, then calls publish_staged_legacy_spline_fit only when the complete set succeeded (:266-:301). Despite the “legacy” name this module is live and is called by the unified model-fit workflow.


Direct /fit-all routes → calibration.server. The synchronous and asynchronous endpoints call _run_profile_fit_all, whose entire implementation is a wrapper around _run_legacy_spline_fit_all(..., publish=True) (server.py:6379-:6395). The direct API is therefore a second entry into the same fitter and publication transaction, not a separately maintained fitting implementation.


publish_staged_legacy_spline_fit swaps the staged profiles and pair corrections into the live paths before publishing SQLite. If database publication fails, it restores the previous files; if that rollback is itself incomplete, it raises a distinct error and preserves surviving .rollback-* copies for manual recovery (model_publication.py:218-:288). Successful publication records the new artifact set, deletes the prior fit row and children, and removes the temporary rollback copies.
Notebook-origin modules off the live path
fitting.py was ported from an earlier strip-file pipeline that still ships but is not what the live fit runs:

calibration.fitting.batch_fit (batch_fit.py) is the original batch_fit_spline.py: it reads pre-materialized strip files from STRIPS_DIR (batch_fit.py:54), prints progress, and has a __main__ main() (batch_fit.py:841). Its fit_spline_profile (batch_fit.py:727) is the direct ancestor of fitting.fit_spline_profile. It has no intra-project imports and is imported only by fitter_core (fitter_core.py:23); on the live pair-correction path it is loaded as a side effect but its fitting functions are never invoked. Strip files are themselves legacy — the live fitter reads sample JSONs directly.
calibration.fitting.fitter_core (fitter_core.py) wraps batch_fit for the notebook fitter (fit_profile, fitter_core.py:386; load_all_data, :63). Only its pair-correction helpers (compute_pair_corrections, save_pair_corrections) are live-reachable, pulled in lazily by fitting.compute_and_save_pair_corrections; the rest is notebook/CLI surface. It is imported by calibration.fitting.export.
calibration.fitting.strip_loader (strip_loader.py) builds a filament→strips registry by scanning strip-file JSONs (load_strip_registry, strip_loader.py:67); self-described as extracted from 01_fitter.ipynb/02_composer.ipynb. Imported only by export.
calibration.fitting.export (export.py, originally fitter_json_export.py) turns fitter results into REST-serializable dicts (export_transmission_curve, export.py:99; export_filament_summary, :363), replacing the notebook’s matplotlib output. Its Architecture node lists no importers — it is not wired into the live server graph.

The heavy numerical photo-stack model referenced by the v2 pages lives in the shared lib.photo_stack_model.*, not here; this page’s modules are strictly the v1 legacy-spline path.

prisma-calibration/technical-reference/t.title: The camera transform fitter
prisma-calibration/technical-reference/t.content:
In one sentence: run_camera_transform_build_job (calibration.fitting.camera_transform.job) builds a corpus of (transmission → embedded-JPEG appearance) pairs, validates with deterministic five-fold sample-grouped cross-validation, refits on all clean evidence, bakes the numeric inverse into a 3D LUT, and writes a staged generation that the shared publication boundary coordinates with SQLite before retiring the old generation.

This page is the code-level map of the module cluster under calibration/fitting/camera_transform/: how a Camera Transform artifact is built. The model form it fits — the root-polynomial feature map, the per-channel monotone PCHIP curves, F (fitted transmission → appearance) and its numeric inverse G baked as a LUT — is derived in The Camera Transform; this page links it rather than re-deriving it. The distinction between the transmission the corpus reads and the appearance it targets is Transmission vs Appearance. The shared model runtime that both the fitter and the generator import is lib.camera_transform. How this build job is dispatched alongside the other model fits, and how its output is published, is Model workflow, publication, and review.
Here, the older internal “publication” names mean coordinated replacement of Calibration’s current working Camera Transform. They do not create or update a Generator library; that requires the separate user-facing Publish Models action after all three working fits are current.
Related: calibration.fitting.camera_transform.job · calibration.fitting.camera_transform.corpus · calibration.fitting.camera_transform.fit · calibration.fitting.camera_transform.lut · calibration.fitting.camera_transform.export · calibration.fitting.camera_transform.fingerprint · calibration.fitting.camera_transform.parity · lib.camera_transform
The build job — five phases, two gates
run_camera_transform_build_job (job.py:52) is the single entry point. It is called by both the unified workflow and the server’s standalone Camera Transform job: its Imported by list is calibration.fitting.model_fit_workflow and calibration.server. It takes a store, an optional output_dir (default store.root / "camera_transform", job.py:61), and a use_fit_exclusions flag (default False, job.py:58); it emits progress through an optional callback (_emit, job.py:30) with total = 5 phases (job.py:60).
The phases run in fixed order:

Corpus. build_camera_transform_corpus_from_extraction_results builds the (T, appearance) corpus from stored sidecars (see below). Alongside it, build_camera_transform_fit_fingerprint computes the robust fit-input fingerprint. An empty corpus raises RuntimeError; fewer than five eligible samples cannot support the validation policy; a corpus below MIN_USABLE_SWATCHES = 200 does not fail — it appends a “coverage is thin” warning and continues.
Fit (job.py:89-90). fit_camera_transform(corpus.rows) (job.py:90) returns a CameraTransformFitResult.
Validate. The pooled out-of-fold mean dE76 is read from fit.metrics["validation"]["dE76_CIELAB"]["mean"]; if it exceeds MAX_VALIDATION_MEAN_DE76 = 6.0, the job raises RuntimeError and — crucially — the existing artifact is not modified. Nothing is written until this gate passes.
Bake (job.py:103-104). bake_inverse_lut(fit.params) (job.py:104) produces the inverse LUT.
Export (job.py:134-:141). write_camera_transform_artifact writes the payload, LUT, and manifest into a complete generation directory. Its activate=publish argument controls whether the writer also advances CURRENT; both production webapp callers pass publish=False and publish through publish_camera_transform_fit afterward (model_fit_workflow.py:542-:549; server :7614-:7621).

Between bake and export the job assembles the payload and manifest. The manifest carries the corpus summary, pooled and per-fold out-of-fold CIELAB/OKLab metrics, final-fit training diagnostics, hygiene drop counts, the source_data_fingerprint, the params_sha256 identity hash, and the quality-gate thresholds and warnings. The return value reports status "warning" or "ok" and echoes the summary and manifest.
Stable identity hash across identical re-fits
_previous_params_sha256_if_same (job.py:36) is a small but deliberate detail: before hashing the new payload it loads the existing artifact, and if the freshly fit params array is bit-for-bit equal to the stored one it reuses the prior params_sha256 (job.py:38-49, used at :107). So a rebuild that lands on identical parameters keeps its identity hash stable rather than minting a new one from an unrelated payload field.
The corpus — transmission paired with embedded-JPEG appearance
calibration.fitting.camera_transform.corpus builds the training table. Each row pairs a swatch’s transmission (T_R/T_G/T_B, the linear measured values) with its appearance (jpeg_r/g/b, median byte RGB from Canon’s embedded CR2 JPEG). The appearance target is the embedded JPEG render specifically — the module docstring is emphatic that it never falls back to the libraw visual render, thumbnails, or measurement medians, because those use per-image auto-brightening and different tone/hue rendering (corpus.py:1-16). This transmission-vs-appearance split is the whole point of the Camera Transform; see Transmission vs Appearance.
There are two builders, and only one is on the live path:

build_camera_transform_corpus_from_extraction_results (corpus.py:660) is the live builder. It reads appearance from stored extraction_result sidecars rather than re-extracting embedded JPEGs at fit time. Membership, row order, fit_state, excluded_swatches, and variable_fid are read from the live Sample.measurements.swatches; the sidecar is a keyed side-table supplying only the stored appearance. It fails loud via StoredCorpusError when a measurement-bearing sample is missing or has a malformed sidecar, or when an included swatch lacks stored appearance — never a silent skip.
build_camera_transform_corpus (corpus.py:529) is the older fit-time re-extraction path — it opens each CR2, locates the strip in the JPEG frame, and samples swatch boxes directly. It is aliased build_camera_transform_corpus_legacy_extract and is kept callable only for the parity oracle and tests; the job comment records it was retired from the fit path once a full-library parity oracle passed exact (job.py:63-70). Its geometry helpers still live here — _locate_strip, _compute_swatch_boxes, _box_median — and the fit-time and stored paths share _build_corpus_summary (corpus.py:635) so their summaries stay identical.

Both builders return a frozen CameraTransformCorpus (corpus.py:52): the rows DataFrame, a summary dict, the skipped_samples list, and a source_fingerprint. Orientation is resolved by _orient_colors (corpus.py:406), which correlates each swatch’s stored G_linear transmission against the JPEG luminance (signed Spearman) and flips the swatch order if the reversed correlation is stronger; the resulting order_correlation is a per-sample extraction-quality guard, not a transmission-vs-thickness check (corpus.py:10-15, :410-417).
The corpus module is imported well beyond the fitter — calibration.maintenance, calibration.maintenance_reextract, calibration.processing.extraction_result, and calibration.processing.extraction_visuals all reuse its extraction helpers for sidecar production and review visuals (see its Imported by list).
The fit — filter, cross-validate, refit
calibration.fitting.camera_transform.fit holds fit_camera_transform (fit.py:338) and the numerical machinery around it. It runs three stages on the corpus rows:

Filter. load_and_filter (fit.py:120) applies five hygiene rules — drop fit_state == "excluded", drop whole samples whose order_correlation is below 0.8, drop physically suspicious bright/opaque rows, drop NaNs, and mark (but keep) JPEG-clipped rows so they are censored from the loss (JPEG_CLIP_THRESHOLD = 250, fit.py:47, :153-155). It returns the cleaned frame plus a drop_counts dict that becomes the manifest’s hygiene_drop_counts.
Assign validation folds. assign_validation_folds scores each sample from its measured transmission, sorts samples by score and id, and assigns each consecutive block across five folds using a seeded SHA-256 ordering. Every swatch from one sample stays in the same fold. No name-derived filament category participates.
Cross-validate and refit. Five temporary fits each train on four folds and predict the fifth, producing exactly one out-of-fold prediction per clean row. The pooled dE76/OKLab metrics drive the publication gate. After validation, a sixth fit trains on all clean rows and supplies the published parameter vector. als_fit provides an alternating-least-squares warm start, then joint_polish refines with scipy.optimize.least_squares.

fit_camera_transform returns a frozen CameraTransformFitResult carrying the final params, the cleaned frame, out-of-fold predictions, the sample-to-fold assignment, validation/final-fit metrics, and hygiene counts. The parameter layout, feature map, and monotone-curve construction are the model form — see The Camera Transform and lib.camera_transform.
The LUT bake — numeric inverse on a grid
calibration.fitting.camera_transform.lut is one function. bake_inverse_lut (lut.py:13) samples a grid_size = 33 cube over [0,1]³ appearance space, calls invert_forward from lib.camera_transform to solve back to transmission at each grid point, clips to [0,1], and returns a (33, 33, 33, 3) float32 array. This is the baked G — the numeric inverse of the fitted forward model — that the generator interpolates at solve time. Why the inverse must be baked numerically rather than solved in closed form belongs to The Camera Transform.
Staged export and coordinated publication
calibration.fitting.camera_transform.export writes complete generation directories so a reader never sees half-written files. write_camera_transform_artifact (export.py:175) validates the payload and LUT first (:188-:189), then:

Writes camera_transform.json, inverse_lut_33.npz, and manifest.json into a unique temporary generation, computes the two data-file hashes into the manifest, and fsyncs all three files (:194-:220).
Renames that temporary directory to gen-<timestamp>-<uuid> (_unique_generation_name, :87; rename :221), making the staged generation complete but not necessarily current.
If activate=True, activate_camera_transform_generation writes and atomically replaces CURRENT, then finalize_camera_transform_generation removes legacy flat files and garbage-collects old generations with keep=1 (:223-:228; helpers :137, :169). This direct activation mode remains available, but production fitting uses activate=False.

Any failure while writing removes the unfinished temporary directory and re-raises (:229-:238), so a failed staged build leaves CURRENT untouched. build_payload (export.py:54) is the sibling that stamps the schema, model version, architecture string, and parameter layout into the JSON.
Production activation is owned by publish_camera_transform_fit (model_publication.py:172). It advances CURRENT, publishes the new generation as the replaceable SQLite camera_transform fit, and only then finalizes keep-1 garbage collection (:189-:215). If SQLite publication fails, it restores the previous pointer and discards the staged generation (:210-:213). This is a coordinated pointer/database replacement with compensation, not one cross-filesystem/SQLite transaction.
The fingerprint — what actually reached the optimizer
calibration.fitting.camera_transform.fingerprint answers “does this need rebuilding?” more robustly than a sample count. build_camera_transform_fit_fingerprint re-runs load_and_filter and assign_validation_folds, then hashes the rows that reach validation/final fitting plus the deterministic fold assignment. It produces fit_input_hash, raw_corpus_hash, validation_hash, and diagnostic_hash under CT_FINGERPRINT_SCHEMA_VERSION = 3, with floats canonicalized to 17 significant digits. The fit policy records five-fold validation followed by a final all-data fit; it contains no filament-name classification metadata. The job stores the whole fingerprint as the manifest’s source_data_fingerprint; robust_fit_input_hash reads it back for rebuild decisions.
Parity — a migration oracle, not steady state
calibration.fitting.camera_transform.parity is read-only and transitional. It captures a legacy (or stored) corpus plus hygiene and validation-fold assignment into a deterministic snapshot, so the parity oracle can prove the extraction-path switch preserves membership, row order, skips, folds, and per-row values. It is a verification harness invoked from tests/tooling, not part of the live build path.

prisma-calibration/technical-reference/t.title: The extraction pipeline
prisma-calibration/technical-reference/t.content:
In one sentence: a lightbox photograph becomes a committed per-swatch ExtractionResult by the headless process_sample (calibration.processing.processor, processor.py:284), which detects the strip, deskews it, divides out a registered flatfield blank, samples a median color per swatch, and hands the measurements to the commit_extraction_result transaction (calibration.processing.extraction_result, extraction_result.py:248) that writes the sidecar into the store — while extract_strip_manual (calibration.processing.manual, manual.py:369) is the 4-corner fallback for strips that fail auto-detection.

This page is the code-level map of the path from a raw photo to a stored extraction. For the phenomena — what flatfield division and median extraction physically mean — see Extraction. For the operator’s view — which buttons run this and what the review states mean — see Processing and extraction and Assigning images.
Related: calibration.processing.processor · calibration.processing.extraction · calibration.processing.manual · calibration.processing.extraction_result · calibration.processing.blank_registry · calibration.processing.artifact_sinks · calibration.processing.extraction_visuals · calibration.processing.backfill · Extraction · Processing and extraction
Production orchestration and shared image math
The image math (loading, detection, deskew, flatfield, boundaries, median color) lives as free functions in extraction.py (calibration.processing.extraction) — a module of stateless helpers with no intra-project imports (see its Architecture node). Orchestration belongs to the production callers:

process_sample (processor.py:284) — the headless production pipeline. It has no UI, takes a Sample plus resolved image/blank paths, and is the one the web server and maintenance re-extract paths call (see Imported by on calibration.processing.processor: server, maintenance, maintenance_reextract). commit=True is the durable path; commit=False is used for previews/thumbnail regeneration and must not mutate the sample or delete a valid sidecar. This is the path this page describes.
extract_strip_manual (manual.py) owns the operator-selected four-corner fallback and commits through the same extraction-result transaction.
maintenance_reextract stages re-extraction candidates for review before applying accepted replacements.

The old notebook-era process_one/Tkinter path has been removed. It had no repository caller or supported CLI entry point and wrote unconsumed per-swatch crops, segmentation JSON, and debug PNGs outside the webapp artifact contract.
Stage 0 — configuration: SwatchConfig
Every stage reads geometry from a SwatchConfig dataclass (extraction.py:33). It carries the physical strip geometry that must match the printed design — num_swatches (default 8), border_mm, step_w_mm, step_h_mm — plus lightbox dimensions, the open_side edge, and the sample_fraction (default 0.50, the central fraction of each swatch cell that is sampled). __post_init__ (extraction.py:62) derives the total strip width/height and border fractions. process_sample builds it per-sample via _build_swatch_config (processor.py:125), which reads the sample’s strip_definition through SwatchConfig.from_experiment (extraction.py:71) and falls back to class defaults for any field a legacy sample lacks. For the geometry contract behind these numbers, see Geometry and strip definition.
Stage 1 — load the image (preview first, then full RAW)
process_sample is deliberately two-pass on resolution to keep detection cheap:

Preview load for detection. load_preview_jpeg (extraction.py:154) pulls the camera’s embedded JPEG at up to 2000 px for the fast detection/deskew pass (processor.py:322). If there is no embedded preview it falls back to a full RAW decode (processor.py:325-327).
Full RAW load for measurement. Once the strip is located, load_raw_both (extraction.py:116) decodes the CR2 twice via rawpy: a visual 8-bit sRGB-ish render (RAWPY_PARAMS_VISUAL, camera white balance, auto-bright) and a linear 16-bit render with gamma=(1,1) and no_auto_bright (RAWPY_PARAMS_LINEAR, extraction.py:92-97). The linear array — normalized to [0,1] — is what the transmission math consumes; the visual array drives detection and the display hex. Stored per-image rotations are applied via _apply_rotations (processor.py:80) plus the sample’s open-side orientation count from _open_side_to_rotation_count (processor.py:88).

Stage 2 — find the strip: find_strip_contour
find_strip_contour (extraction.py:299) first crops to the lightbox with find_lightbox_region (extraction.py:252), then runs a multi-strategy cascade, stopping at the first success (extraction.py:307-314):

Flatfield ratio (per-channel division reveals a strip of any color),
Flatfield absolute difference,
Otsu BINARY_INV (strip darker than lightbox),
Otsu BINARY (strip brighter),
Canny edges (brightness-agnostic),
Saturation/chroma (translucent tinted filaments),
Physical-dimensions fallback (synthesize the expected rectangle from geometry).

Candidate hulls are scored against the expected strip area fraction and aspect ratio (_best_hull, extraction.py:370; area bounds extraction.py:366-368). When a blank is available it is threaded in as flatfield_bgr so strategies 1–2 can background-subtract (processor.py:342). If every strategy fails, process_sample returns a failed_detection result and — only on a committing run — stamps the sample failed and deletes any stale sidecar (processor.py:344-361). A non-committing preview reports the failure without changing durable sample or sidecar state.
Stage 3 — deskew
deskew_strip (extraction.py:511) fits a cv2.minAreaRect, rotates the whole frame to level the strip, and crops to the rotated bounding box plus a fixed DESKEW_PAD_PX (6 px) margin, forcing a landscape crop. deskew_strip_linear (extraction.py:543) applies the same rotation/crop geometry to the float32 linear array so visual and linear stay pixel-aligned. process_sample re-detects the contour on the full-resolution visual before the measurement deskew (processor.py:412), falling back to a scaled preview contour if that re-detection fails (processor.py:417-422). It then flips the strip 180° if the brighter (thinner-swatch, higher-transmission) end is on the right, enforcing thin-on-left (processor.py:439-443).
Stage 4 — flatfield correction: register, then divide
The blank is the per-pixel reference illumination I0. Two steps:

Register the blank onto the strip frame. register_flatfield (extraction.py:802) detects the lightbox border in both images and warps the blank through a border homography; if detection fails it warns and falls back to a bare cv2.resize (extraction.py:819-822). The registered blank is deskewed with the same contour as the strip (processor.py:452).
Divide. apply_flatfield (extraction.py:883) computes per-pixel transmission strip_linear / max(blank, 1e-6) clipped to [0,1] (extraction.py:886). This is the multiplicative inverse of the illumination — the physical meaning is in Extraction.

There is a strict variant, register_flatfield_strict (extraction.py:842), which raises FlatfieldRegistrationError (extraction.py:838) instead of resizing when the lightbox cannot be located — a physically-correct-or-fail contract used by the manual path (the bare resize stretches the blank without aligning the lightbox and is wrong; annotation [@theo 2026-06-17], extraction.py:851). Automatic register_flatfield is intentionally left with the lenient fallback.
Stage 5 — swatch boundaries and median color

Extent. detect_swatch_extent (extraction.py:903) computes the inner swatch rectangle geometrically from border_mm/step_w_mm/step_h_mm and the measured pixel scale — it does not hunt for edges. The bottom is inset 5% of step_h to dodge the open-edge over-extrusion artifact (extraction.py:934). The deskew_pad_px argument must match the padding actually present (auto strips carry DESKEW_PAD_PX; manual perspective strips carry 0).
Dividers. find_swatch_boundaries (extraction.py:945) returns num_swatches + 1 x-offsets. As of the current code it uses pure equal spacing from the known swatch width; the gradient-snapping branch is disabled below the early return (extraction.py:965-966) because geometry-first margins proved more reliable than signal snapping.
Sampling boxes. swatch_sampling_boxes_from_boundaries (calibration.processing.extraction_visuals, extraction_visuals.py:13) turns those boundaries into the exact half-open crop box per swatch, shrinking each cell by sample_fraction on every side.
Median. For each swatch, median_color_bgr (extraction.py:998) takes the per-channel median of the visual patch (→ the display hex/RGB via rgb_to_hex, extraction.py:1004), and the linear transmission is the per-channel median of the flatfield-corrected patch, rounded to 6 places into a SwatchMeasurement (processor.py:522-536). The blank’s own median over the inner crop is stored as I0_linear for traceability (processor.py:539-544).

The per-swatch measurements plus I0_linear, blank_image, and source_image are packed into a legacy Measurements object (processor.py:546).
The manual fallback — extract_strip_manual
When auto-detection fails (typically near-transparent filaments that blend into the lightbox), the operator clicks the strip’s four corners and calibration.processing.manual takes over. extract_strip_manual (manual.py:369) scales the preview-space corners into raw coordinates (_scale_corners, manual.py:161; rotation-aware scale via _preview_scale_for_rotation, manual.py:189), rectifies the quad with a perspective warp (_perspective_extract, manual.py:103, expecting tl,tr,br,bl order), then runs the same flatfield-and-extract math as the automatic path — but through register_flatfield_strict, so a manual strip either gets a properly registered blank or fails explicitly rather than silently diverging (manual.py:23-24, module docstring). Manual extraction does not use the brightness heuristic to reorder the strip; the operator’s corner order and open-side are authoritative (manual.py:22-24). Commit runs through the shared _commit_manual producer (manual.py:206), which requires image promotion before building the sidecar (manual.py:229-235).
The commit — what “commit” actually writes
Accepting or committing a successful extraction runs the canonical transaction commit_extraction_result (extraction_result.py:248), the IO half of the producer. process_sample calls it inside its commit=True branch (processor.py:597), after promoting the source image into managed storage so the sample is Camera-Transform-eligible and cr2_source resolves against the post-promotion location (processor.py:589, _resolve_cr2 processor.py:229). Manual extraction uses the same producer (manual.py:329-340). The transaction is (extraction_result.py:283-308):

Set sample fields — processing_status (processed or flagged), flag_reason, measurements, and review_accepted = False.
Snapshot any prior sidecar bytes (store.snapshot_extraction_result, extraction_result.py:290).
Build the canonical sidecar via build_extraction_result (extraction_result.py:162).
Save the sidecar — store.save_extraction_result(sample_id, result.model_dump()) (extraction_result.py:306).
Save the sample (extraction_result.py:308).

On any exception in build/save this is an aborted commit, not a committed failure: the in-memory measurements/review_accepted are cleared, the prior sidecar bytes are restored exactly (or the new one deleted if there was none), and the exception re-raises without saving a failed sample (extraction_result.py:309-315) — so the durable sample and durable sidecar stay paired. process_sample catches that re-raise and returns a rolled-back failure (processor.py:627-638). A failure outside that protected commit block reaches the outer handler, which saves processing_status="failed" and deletes the sidecar (processor.py:680-690).
Be precise about the store. process_sample takes a store: DataStore, but the live backend is the SQLite store — save_extraction_result persists the sidecar as a row keyed by sample_id, not a loose JSON file, on a production install. (The JSON DataStore is the non-production path; see Data access and persistence.) And commit is not acceptance: the freshly built ExtractionResult carries review_state="pending_review" and the sample’s review_accepted is False (extraction_result.py:237, :287). Commit writes a pending-review sidecar; operator acceptance is a separate downstream state change.
What the built sidecar contains
build_extraction_result (extraction_result.py:162) is a pure projection of the legacy Measurements into the canonical ExtractionResult shape (extraction_result.py:231): an extraction_result_id, the sample_id/geometry_id, the method ("automatic"/"manual"), method_provenance and evidence_binding (caller-built), and ExtractionMeasurements where each swatch is projected by _project_swatch (extraction_result.py:124) into transmission + display + appearance buckets. All swatches are stored, including excluded ones — exclusion is a downstream fit-control concern (extraction_result.py:11-12).
Appearance is the one impure step (extraction_result.py:187-219): the builder calls _extract_appearance (extraction_result.py:83), which delegates to the Camera Transform corpus’s embedded-JPEG extractor _embedded_jpeg_extraction (calibration.fitting.camera_transform.corpus, imported function-locally at extraction_result.py:99). A failure here is recorded in diagnostics.appearance_error and leaves appearance=None — an appearance failure never fails the transmission extraction (extraction_result.py:213-219). For the camera-transform side of this, see The Camera Transform.
Registering a blank — blank_registry
Before any of the above can use a flatfield, a photo of the empty lightbox is registered as a blank. The public /api/blanks/register route branches on the backend (server.py:6904-6930): SQLite calls SQLiteDataStore.register_blank_from_image (sqlite_data_access.py:5823), which requires the image to already be an onboarded managed asset, inserts the registered_blanks relation in a write transaction, and reuses the managed asset path; it does not copy a second file into blanks/. The legacy JSON branch calls register_blank_image (blank_registry.py:49), which verifies the image, best-effort reads DateTimeOriginal (:24), copies it into blanks/{blank_id}{suffix}, and rolls that copy back if registration fails (:88-:111). Both paths reject duplicate registration. How a sample points at its blank is in Assigning images.
Visual artifacts — durable accepted views and transient review views
The pipeline’s visual artifact destination is normally an ExtractionArtifactSink (calibration.processing.artifact_sinks). LiveThumbnailSink writes bounded JPEGs under {store.root}/thumbnails/{sample_id}/; SampleArtifactDirectorySink writes staged candidate artifacts into a caller-selected directory for maintenance re-extraction. Both validate the sample id, artifact kind, and filesystem boundary before writing. write_thumbnail_image encodes to a same-directory temporary JPEG, requires cv2.imwrite to report success and produce a non-empty file, and promotes it with rollback-capable os.replace publication instead of writing directly over the live path. Accepted samples retain only source.jpg and strip.jpg. Blank, appearance, and transmission-ROI views are review-time artifacts: re-extraction writes them inside the current candidate set, and applying or superseding that set removes them instead of promoting them into the accepted thumbnail tree. The processor retains a direct write_thumbnail_image fallback when no sink is supplied; production automatic/manual calls create a LiveThumbnailSink by default, while re-extraction passes the staged sink explicitly. Overlay geometry is shared in calibration.processing.extraction_visuals, so the sampled boxes drawn on a review ROI are the boxes the median sampler used.
The backfill migration (transitional, not steady-state)
backfill.py (calibration.processing.backfill) is a one-shot migration, not part of the live extraction path — it is not imported by any other calibration module (see its Architecture node). It exists to populate extraction_result sidecars for legacy samples that already carry Sample.measurements but predate the sidecar format, so the historical corpus has appearance buckets before the Camera Transform starts reading stored appearance. It writes sidecars only — it never re-extracts transmission and never mutates Sample.measurements (backfill.py:5-8). run_backfill (backfill.py:144) drives a read-only classify pass (classify_backfill_sample, backfill.py:45) and acts only on the HAS_MEASUREMENTS_NO_SIDECAR class (BACKFILL_ELIGIBLE, backfill.py:42); malformed or incomplete sidecars are reported, never silently repaired. Once the corpus is migrated it has no steady-state role.

prisma-calibration/technical-reference/t.title: The maintenance backend
prisma-calibration/technical-reference/t.content:
In one sentence: every standard maintenance chore is one frozen MaintenanceOperation (calibration.maintenance, maintenance.py:310) in a single OPERATIONS registry, run through a uniform preflight → execute → JSON report lifecycle where each operation declares a structured frontend-refresh impact; the heaviest operation, Re-extract Sample Images, is registered as preflight-only and uses a separate staged, non-destructive backend (calibration.maintenance_reextract) that builds a candidate set the operator reviews sample-by-sample before anything overwrites accepted data.

This page maps the framework: how an operation is defined and registered, the lifecycle that runs it, the refresh impact it reports, and the staged re-extraction candidate store. It deliberately does not explain what each operation means or when to run it — for that, see Maintenance Operations (the mechanism, per operation) and Running maintenance (the operator surface). The one-operation-at-a-time run lock lives in the server, not here (see Web API and job orchestration); the Fit Models operation delegates to the model workflow (Model workflow, publication, and review); and re-extraction commits write through the stores in Data access and persistence.
Related: calibration.maintenance · calibration.maintenance_reextract · Maintenance Operations · Running maintenance · Web API and job orchestration
An operation is a frozen dataclass in one registry
MaintenanceOperation (maintenance.py:310) is a frozen dataclass — the whole definition of one chore. Its fields:

Identity and display — operation_id, name, category (e.g. "Audit", "Images", "System Maintenance", "Geometry Artifacts", "Calibration Models"), description.
Risk and modes — risk_class (e.g. "read_only", "cleanup", "writes_derived_files", "writes_user_output", "changes_semantic_data"), a tuple of allowed modes and a default_mode, and a writes flag.
Concurrency metadata — resource_claims describes everything the operation reads or writes (for example "sqlite_semantic_state", "preview_cache", and "geometry_artifacts"). conflict_resources is the smaller, enforced set of ordinary-writer categories that must remain stable while the operation is queued or running. Both are exposed by public_dict; the server uses the latter at its shared maintenance resource gate.
Cancellation metadata — cancellation_policy is either "safe_points" or "not_supported"; the derived cancellable boolean is exposed to the frontend. Public job state also includes dynamic cancel_available, which becomes false after the request is accepted or the job reaches a terminal state.
Availability — enabled plus an unavailable_reason string for operations that are registered but not runnable.
Behavior — two callables, preflight and execute (maintenance.py:323-324), each Callable[..., dict] | None.

public_dict serializes everything except the two callables — that dict is what the API hands the frontend. All operations live in one module-level OPERATIONS: dict[str, MaintenanceOperation]; list_operations returns their public dicts and get_operation looks one up by id (raising KeyError on an unknown id). The registry spans audits, image/artifact rebuilds, a read-only SQLite integrity check, geometry export, model fitting, and re-extraction.
The two resource lists intentionally differ. A filesystem audit may read SQLite to discover ownership without needing to freeze every unrelated database-backed edit, while an integrity operation can require a stable database snapshot by declaring the enforced sqlite_write conflict. Image custody/preview, extraction evidence/sample visuals, geometry state, and model evidence/artifacts have their own conflict categories. Ordinary browsing remains available, except that source and blank preview GET routes acquire a preview_cache writer lease when they may generate a missing JPEG on demand.
The preflight → execute → report lifecycle
Two module functions drive every operation uniformly:

preflight_operation (maintenance.py:353) resolves the mode (defaulting to default_mode), rejects a mode not in operation.modes with ValueError, and short-circuits a disabled operation into a synthetic blocked result carrying its unavailable_reason (:364-380). Otherwise it calls operation.preflight(store, mode, scope). Preflight is read-only: it computes the target set and any blockers so the operator can confirm before writes happen.
execute_operation (maintenance.py:386) re-validates mode and enablement, then introspects the execute function’s signature with inspect.signature and passes through only the optional kwargs it accepts — preflight, confirmation, job_id — alongside the always-present progress_cb and should_cancel (:406-421). This is how one caller drives execute functions with different signatures. After the operation returns its report dict, it writes it to disk via report_path_for + _atomic_write_json and stamps report_path onto the returned payload (:423-425).

Reports are canonical JSON. _report (maintenance.py:232) builds the "prisma-maintenance-report-v1" schema: operation_id, mode, scope, status, timestamps, a summary dict, findings, changed_paths, blocked, warnings, errors, and the ui_refresh impact (:249-264). Findings are built by _finding (:201) with a severity/category/target/message shape and tallied by _count_findings (:218). Reports land in reports_dir(store) = <project>/output/maintenance/reports/, named {timestamp}_{operation_id}_{job_id[:12]}.json (report_path_for, :98); the same maintenance root holds a .tmp scratch dir (temp_dir, :90) and a quarantine dir (:94). startup_scan_interrupted_temp (:3008) reports leftover temp entries from an interrupted run so the server can surface them at boot.
Quarantine Orphaned Artifacts has a deliberately narrow destructive boundary. It can move only direct preview JPEGs whose exact filenames are not expected by a current image/blank record, strictly named interrupted publication files directly inside a sample-thumbnail directory, direct sample-thumbnail directories with no matching sample, direct managed geometry-artifact directories with no matching geometry, and 64-hex fingerprint directories that are direct children of a live geometry but are not its recomputed current fingerprint. Preview ownership is computed once after the operation has reserved preview_cache; this avoids re-listing every image and blank for every orphan while keeping ownership stable through the run. Geometry fingerprints and live-row ownership are still revalidated per target, so a fingerprint that becomes current is skipped. Source photographs, blank source files, SQLite, models, backups, RAW archives, public geometry exports, and reports are not eligible. Quarantine is only a seven-day filesystem safety buffer: prune_quarantine_runs deletes expired Prisma-named runs during startup/activity housekeeping, while malformed entries and anything containing a filesystem link are skipped and reported.
Source preview cache stems come from a SHA-256 digest of stable image_asset_id (source_preview_cache_stem in processing/extraction.py), with the rotation suffix added afterward. The filename fallback exists for the legacy backend. Consequently, same-stem files with different extensions and filenames containing cache-like __rN text cannot share a SQLite source-preview key. Older filename-derived JPEGs have no current owner: the missing-preview audit requests regeneration under the current key and the orphan audit can quarantine the old cache files.
Preview publication is pair-safe within a running process. generate_preview_jpeg encodes and verifies both same-directory staged JPEGs before publish_staged_files replaces either live file. The publisher copies existing targets to rollback siblings, promotes with os.replace, and restores already-promoted targets if a later promotion fails; a rollback failure preserves and reports its recovery copy. Rebuild Extraction Images Only similarly stages all requested source.jpg/strip.jpg replacements for one sample and promotes that sample’s set together. Cancellation or one renderer failure removes the staged set and leaves that sample’s previous live images unchanged. A process crash can leave a strictly named stage/rollback JPEG; preview-root leftovers are ordinary orphan previews, while thumbnail-root leftovers have their own narrow quarantine category.
Progress and cancellation are cooperative only for operations registered with the "safe_points" policy: execute functions call _progress (:184) to emit phase/current/total updates and _cancelled (:197) to poll the should_cancel check, returning a status of "cancelled" when interrupted. The job API changes accepted requests to "cancelling", preserves its resource reservation, and reports terminal cancellation only after the executor returns. Repeated requests while cancelling are idempotent; unsupported and terminal requests receive HTTP 409. Library Integrity, SQLite Integrity, and Fit Models are registered as "not_supported" and run to completion once started.
The frontend-refresh impact
Every operation reports what the UI must invalidate after it runs, so the frontend re-fetches exactly what changed instead of a blanket reload. The vocabulary is fixed by ui_refresh_none (maintenance.py:128), the canonical empty impact:

a kind of "none", "targeted", or "full";
four coarse booleans — reload_app_data, reload_import_data, rerender_workspace, rerender_open_drawers;
four fine-grained invalidation sets — invalidate_preview_cache (by filename / blank id), invalidate_sample_thumbnails (by sample id / kind), invalidate_geometry_artifacts (by geometry id), and invalidate_model_artifacts (by filament id / model type), each with an all flag; plus a display message.

An audit reports ui_refresh_none — it changed nothing. A write operation reports a targeted impact naming exactly what it touched: for example _execute_rebuild_image_previews reports kind: "targeted" with reload_import_data, rerender_workspace, rerender_open_drawers, and the rebuilt filenames/blank ids in invalidate_preview_cache (maintenance.py:1093-1104). merge_ui_refresh (:155) combines impacts when an operation aggregates sub-steps — booleans OR together, the list-valued invalidation sets union (deduped by _merge_unique, :143), and kind escalates toward full.
Two operations that delegate outward
Most operations implement their own preflight/execute in maintenance.py. Two hand off:

Fit Models (refit_calibration_models, maintenance.py:2974) is the maintenance entry to the whole calibration-model pipeline. Its executor _execute_refit_calibration_models (:2793) converts scope to options with options_from_scope and calls execute_model_fit_workflow (from calibration.fitting.model_fit_workflow), then wraps that workflow’s status/findings/ui_refresh back into a maintenance report (:2806-2832). The physics and publication of that fit belong to Model workflow, publication, and review.
Re-extract Sample Images (maintenance.py:2993) is registered with only a preflight (_preflight_reextract_sample_images_operation, no execute). Its multi-phase generate/review/apply lifecycle is too large for the single-shot execute contract and lives entirely in maintenance_reextract.py, orchestrated by the server (see Web API and job orchestration).

Staged re-extraction — a non-destructive candidate store
calibration.maintenance_reextract (maintenance_reextract.py, “Staged candidate storage and sample-image re-extraction workflows”) re-runs image extraction for already-accepted samples without touching live data until the operator explicitly commits. The whole design is a stage-then-review-then-apply cycle keyed on a candidate set.
Scope options
_normalize_scope (maintenance_reextract.py:355) defines three independent scope axes, and _mode_supported (:387) is the gate on their combinations:

domain_mode — "complete", "transmission_only", or "appearance_only": which parts of the extraction result get regenerated.
segmentation_mode — "existing_coordinates" (replay extraction at the sample’s stored swatch coordinates) or "redetect_from_scratch" (re-run detection; only valid with complete).
sample_scope — {"kind": "all_accepted"} or {"kind": "sample_ids", ...} for an explicit list.

The candidate store
Staged artifacts live under reextract_root(store) = <store.root>/maintenance/reextract_sample_images/, one directory per id-validated rext_<32 hex> candidate set. create_candidate_set writes a ReextractManifest containing schema version, scope (workflow_options), plan_digest, per-status counts, sample ids, and generation/apply report ids. Each ReextractCandidatePayload records its status, source/blank fingerprints, the current extraction_result_id it was staged against, the replacement result when applicable, and staged source/blank/strip/transmission/appearance JPEGs. Statuses include ready_changed, ready_unchanged, manual_required, failed, blocked, stale, applied, and rejected_in_candidate_set. Creating a new set supersedes older sets; prune_candidate_sets retains at most the newest recoverable set for seven days and removes older validly named sets. Candidate paths and cleanup refuse linked ancestors and linked contents.
Generation is a family of functions: preflight_reextract_sample_images (:1009) plans the target rows and blockers; generate_reextract_candidates (:2286) is the main producer; generate_appearance_existing_coordinate_candidates (:1631) is the appearance-only path; generate_manual_candidate (:2143) handles operator-guided re-detection; retry_candidate (:2785) re-runs a single failed one.
Per-sample save/skip review
A candidate carries a separate ReextractReviewPayload (:496) holding the operator’s decision — one of pending, save, skip (STAGED_REVIEW_DECISIONS, :102). update_candidate_review (:2665) sets one sample’s decision and update_candidate_reviews_bulk (:2701) sets many; both refuse to mark a candidate save/skip unless its status is a ready one (READY_CANDIDATE_STATUSES, :101). A candidate with nothing to change defaults to pending; a non-ready one defaults to skip (_default_review_decision, :536).
Non-destructive commit — save vs discard
apply_reextract_candidates (:3348) is the only step that writes to live data, and it is deliberately paranoid:

Appearance-only sets delegate to apply_appearance_candidates (:3097); the transmission/complete path requires the SQLite backend (:3373).
It applies only the sample ids the operator marked save (_saved_sample_ids_from_reviews, :3376); everything else is skipped.
For each saved sample it re-verifies staleness before writing — the current accepted extraction still exists and its extraction_result_id still matches what the candidate was staged against, the source/blank files still match (_candidate_sources_still_match), and the stored semantic digest is unchanged. Any mismatch flips the candidate to stale and skips it rather than overwriting drifted data (:3449-3492).
Only a surviving ready_changed candidate calls store.replace_accepted_extraction_result (:3537), which swaps the accepted extraction and returns the dependent model fits it just marked stale (stale_model_fit_ids); a ready_unchanged candidate rewrites live visual artifacts only. The candidate is then stamped applied (:3576).
Appearance-only apply can persist changed decoder provenance while remaining applied_unchanged: SQLiteDataStore.update_extraction_result_appearance distinguishes any persisted metadata change from model_inputs_changed. Decoder-version metadata alone does not alter Camera Transform’s corpus and therefore does not stale the current fit.

Because staging, review, and apply are separate steps, an operator can generate a whole set, inspect each sample, and discard it entirely with delete_candidate_set (:2918) — the accepted corpus is never modified unless apply runs and a candidate clears every freshness check. The commit itself flows through the SQLite store (see Data access and persistence); the run lock that keeps only one maintenance job (this or any other) in flight at a time is held in the server (Web API and job orchestration).

prisma-calibration/technical-reference/u.title: Assigning images
prisma-calibration/technical-reference/u.content:
In one sentence: on Images → Assign Images, a three-pane workspace connects the raw lightbox photos you shot outside the app to your samples — you import the photos, register the empty-lightbox blanks that flatfield correction needs, then attach an image (and a matching blank) to each sample so it is ready to extract.

Extraction can’t run until a sample knows two things: which photo is its printed strip, and which photo is the empty-lightbox reference. This screen is where you supply both. A blank is a photograph of the lit lightbox with no strip on it; during extraction the strip photo is divided by the blank to cancel the lightbox’s spatial unevenness — that division is the flatfield correction. See Extraction for how the blank is actually used.
Reach this screen from the Images tab, Assign Images subtab. The three panes read left to right: Registered Blanks, Image Inbox, and Assign Images and Blanks.
Related: Driving the calibration app · Processing and extraction · Samples and geometries · Extraction

The three panes
Image Inbox (center)
This is where raw photos enter the app and where you pick the one to assign.

Import from Inbox pulls newly-dropped photos into managed custody. New files land here first; nothing else on this screen can see a photo until it has been imported.
Open Inbox Folder opens the exact Calibration/Inbox folder used by this running app, so a user does not have to guess which installation receives a file.
Clean Up Unused moves eligible source files to Calibration/Inbox/Removed Images in the packaged Suite, removes their managed copies and custody rows, and leaves assigned sample images or blanks referenced by samples alone.
CSV Bulk Assignment opens the bulk-assignment dialog (below).

The grid groups thumbnails into collapsible Unassigned, Assigned, and Ignored sections. Each active thumbnail carries two controls: a rotate button (Rotate thumbnail 90 degrees clockwise), for photos the camera saved sideways, and an ignore button (the ×) that moves a photo you don’t want into the Ignored section. Rotation is persisted as a per-image 90-degree override; the server removes only stale exact cache variants owned by that image (and its registered-blank cache namespace, when applicable), preserving any filename currently expected by another record. The extraction pipeline reads the override for both detection and measurement. Rotation is rejected when the image is tied to a processed, failed, or flagged sample. For rotatable assignments, the server/store clears the sample’s open-side orientation and returns an assigned sample to unassigned, so rotation is an assignment reset for the affected evidence.
Below the grid, Selected Image names the thumbnail you’ve clicked, with two footer actions:

← Register as Blank turns the selected photo into a flatfield reference (it moves to the Registered Blanks pane).
Assign Image to Sample → attaches the selected photo to the sample selected in the right pane as its strip image.

Registered Blanks (left)
The catalog of empty-lightbox references. To add one, either select a photo in the inbox and click ← Register as Blank, or drag a thumbnail onto this pane’s drop zone (Drop image to register blank, shown compactly as Drop to Register). Registration assigns an id and records capture time from EXIF when available. SQLite reuses the managed image asset and inserts the registered_blanks relation; only the legacy JSON path copies a second file into blank storage.
Selected Blank names the blank you’ve clicked; Assign Blank to Sample → attaches it to the sample selected in the right pane.
Register one blank per lightbox session and reuse it across every sample shot in that session — the blank only has to match the lighting, not the strip.
Assign Images and Blanks (right)
The sample list, showing what each sample has so far. Selecting a row here sets the target for the two → assign buttons in the other panes; Selected Sample echoes your choice. Each sample’s assigned image and blank appear as slots with an Unassign (×) control to detach either one.
Changing a sample’s image or blank invalidates any earlier processing for that sample — the app clears stale results so the sample re-extracts against the new inputs rather than showing measurements from the old photo.

The assignment loop
For one sample by hand:

Import from Inbox to bring your session’s photos in.
Register the session’s empty-lightbox shot: select it, ← Register as Blank (do this once per session).
Select a sample in the right pane.
Select its strip photo in the inbox, Assign Image to Sample →.
Select the session blank in the left pane, Assign Blank to Sample →.

Repeat 3–5 for each sample. When every intended sample has both an image and a blank, move to Processing and extraction.

CSV Bulk Assignment (the bulk path)
For many samples at once, CSV Bulk Assignment assigns images and blanks from a spreadsheet instead of clicking each one. Place every referenced sample and blank image in the Calibration Inbox first, click Import from Inbox, and then open the bulk dialog. The flow is template → validate → commit.
Download CSV Template gives you a header-only file with four columns:

























ColumnWhat goes in itSample IDThe sample’s id (exp-123), or just the number 123 when that number is unambiguous.Sample ImageThe strip photo’s filename (extension optional).Blank ImageA registered blank’s id, or a photo filename — an unregistered photo here is registered as a blank during commit.OrientationWhich way the strip’s open side faces: U, D, L, or R (T is accepted as up, B as down).
Choose CSV loads your filled-in file; Validate CSV checks it without changing anything and returns a preview: a per-row table plus counts of rows ready, blocked, blanks to register, and warnings. Extra columns are ignored with a warning. A row is blocked (and skipped) when its sample or image can’t be found, an image is ambiguous, a photo is missing or ignored, an image is already assigned to another sample, or the sample isn’t eligible.
CSV assignment only touches fresh samples: a row is rejected if the sample already has an image, a blank, an orientation, a non-unassigned status, or existing extraction results. This makes bulk import a safe first-fill, not a way to overwrite work you’ve already done.
The commit button reads Import Assignments when every row is clean, or Import Valid Rows when some are blocked (only the ready rows commit). If any ready row names a photo that isn’t a registered blank yet, you’re asked to confirm registering those blanks before the import proceeds. Blank registration and all ready sample assignments then commit as one SQLite transaction: a failure leaves neither partial assignments nor a newly registered-but-unused blank. On success the app reports how many assignments landed and how many blanks it registered.

prisma-calibration/technical-reference/u.title: Backup and restore
prisma-calibration/technical-reference/u.content:
In one sentence: the topbar Backup / Restore dialog is where you snapshot the workbook to a ZIP you can move off-machine — a small Essential Data Only database backup or a full All Data and Artifacts package (raw source images optional) — restore either after the app validates and previews it, and separately archive bulky raw camera files out of the active library to reclaim space and pull them back later.

This page covers making backups and restoring them, plus the raw-image archive workflow that lives in the same dialog. It is a manual, operator-initiated screen; the app also keeps its own automatic database snapshots behind the scenes (see Automatic restore points below), which are a different thing and are not managed here.
Related: Driving the calibration app · Running maintenance · Managing filaments

Opening the dialog
The topbar Backup / Restore button opens a single dialog titled Backup / Restore with four stacked panels: Create Backup, Restore From Backup, Archive RAW Images, and Restore Archived Images. Everything below maps to one of those panels.
Backup, restore, and archive all share one lock, so only one of them runs at a time; starting a second while one is live returns a “Backup or restore is already running” error. They are also blocked while a Maintenance job is running (see Running maintenance). Each operation is start-then-report: you kick it off, a progress panel opens, and the dialog refreshes when it finishes.

Create Backup
Under Create Backup, pick a backup type, then click Create Backup. Two choices:
Essential Data Only
A small package of just the Prisma database — the semantic state: filaments, geometries, samples, image assignments, extracted measurements, and model-fit records. It does not include source images, model artifact files, or generated STEP/STL exports. Restoring it replaces only the database and leaves your existing files and exports untouched; those files are not guaranteed to match an independently restored database. Use it for a quick, portable snapshot of the workbook’s knowledge, not as a self-contained model-and-image archive.
All Data and Artifacts
The full working state: the database plus durable managed assets and the geometry STEP/STL exports. It includes the accepted source.jpg/strip.jpg sample visuals and every model artifact referenced by the retained SQLite fits. It deliberately omits regenerable preview-cache JPEGs, interrupted thumbnail transaction files, manual-review images, staged re-extraction candidate sets, generator cache files, logs, and other temporary work. Those are neither restore invariants nor reasons for backup creation to fail.
When All Data and Artifacts is selected, an Include raw image files checkbox appears. Leave it on to fold the camera raw source files (.cr2, .cr3, .dng, and similar) into the ZIP for a truly complete backup. Turn it off to keep everything except those bulky raw originals — the package still carries the database, extracted data, artifacts, and geometry exports, just without the multi-gigabyte source photos. The checkbox only shows for this option; Essential Data Only never contains images.
The backup is written as a timestamped .zip in the app’s backup folder. If Windows temporarily prevents the completed ZIP from being renamed into that folder, Prisma leaves the validated package in the backup .tmp workspace and retries promotion during later startup/activity housekeeping; invalid abandoned temp entries expire after 24 hours. Retrieve completed packages and move them somewhere safe — the dialog is the record that one was made, not a permanent package-management system.

Restore From Backup
Under Restore From Backup, point the Backup File control at a Prisma backup .zip (type or select its path), then click Restore Backup.
A full All Data and Artifacts backup is also the supported way to move an existing Calibration library into a fresh Suite release: create the backup in the old copy, keep the ZIP outside both Prisma folders, start the new blank copy once, and restore the ZIP through this dialog. Do not copy Calibration/Workspace by hand or point two Prisma copies at one working directory. After restore, verify the sample/image counts and Modeling status before retiring the old copy.
Restore never applies a package blind. It first validates and previews the ZIP — checking it is a well-formed Prisma package with an intact database — and shows you a summary of what the package is and exactly what restoring it will replace. Only then does it ask you to type a confirmation phrase (the exact wording depends on the package: an All Data and Artifacts package warns it “will replace all existing data,” an Essential Data Only package warns it “will replace the current database”). The Restore Backup action stays disabled until the typed phrase matches. Before overwriting anything, the app also takes an automatic emergency safety copy of the current database, so a restore is reversible if it goes wrong.
What a restore replaces depends on which package you are restoring:

Essential Data Only → replaces the database only; your current images and exports stay as they are.
All Data and Artifacts, with raw images → replaces the database, assets, and exports, and brings in the package’s raw images too.
All Data and Artifacts, without raw images → replaces the database, assets, and exports, but keeps your current raw source images in place (the package has none to supply).

When the restore finishes, the app refreshes automatically and the restored data is live. Restore refuses to operate when the configured asset tree, STEP export tree, or a contained directory is a symlink/junction/reparse point; it will fail before moving the current library aside. This is a safety boundary against accidentally restoring through a disposable worktree link into another library.
During replacement, Prisma temporarily moves the displaced state into a restore_previous_* rollback directory. It restores that state if validation or the post-restore smoke check fails. After success, cleanup handles Windows read-only files before removing that directory. If some other filesystem problem still prevents removal, the restore remains successful but reports a restore_previous_cleanup_failed warning with the residual path so the disposable copy can be removed manually after verifying the restored library.

Archive RAW Images
Raw camera files are the largest thing in the library and, once extracted, are rarely needed day to day. The Archive RAW Images panel lets you move them out of the active library without losing them. It has two steps, deliberately separated so you never delete originals you have not safely stored first.
Create RAW Image Archive
Create RAW Image Archive packages the current raw source images into a standalone raw-image archive ZIP. It only copies — nothing is deleted or moved out of the active library. Do this first, verify the archive, and move it somewhere safe.
Remove Archived Images From Active Library
This is the destructive step. Point its Archive or Backup File control at the archive you just made (a raw-image archive, or an All Data and Artifacts backup that includes raw images), and the app validates it and previews which active-library source files it covers. Because it deletes local raw files, it is confirmation-gated: you must type the phrase Remove archived images from active library before the Remove Archived Images From Active Library action enables. It only removes files that the archive actually contains, so nothing unmatched is touched. Run this only after the archive is stored somewhere safe.

Restore Archived Images
Restore Archived Images is the inverse: point its Archive or Backup File control at a raw-image archive ZIP (or an all-data backup that includes raw images) and click Restore Archived Images. The app validates the archive, previews how many images are missing from the active library, and restores only the missing compatible source images — it will not overwrite or duplicate images you already have. Use it to pull raw originals back into the library after you archived and removed them.

Automatic restore points (not this dialog)
Separately from anything on this screen, the app keeps its own internal SQLite restore points — automatic, database-only snapshots taken on startup and pruned over time. They carry no raw images, no artifacts, and no ZIP packaging; their sole job is to preserve a recent known-good database for corruption recovery. Applying one first preserves the displaced database under output/restore-points/recovery/; those emergency copies are not selectable restore points and use the same default 12-copy/30-day retention bounds. Restore points are not the same as the user backups you create here and are not managed from this dialog. Treat the Create Backup packages as your real, portable backups; treat restore points as an automatic safety net underneath them. The mechanism behind both lives in Maintenance Operations.
