prisma-calibration/technical-reference/u.title: Driving the calibration app
prisma-calibration/technical-reference/u.content:
In one sentence: the calibration app is a single-user FastAPI logbook that walks a filament from a printed strip to a fitted color model — you register filaments and geometries, create samples, assign each sample its lightbox photos, extract per-swatch colors, curate which measurements the models trust, fit Calibration’s current models, and explicitly publish an immutable Generator library — with every heavy job guarded so conflicting writers cannot overlap.

This page serves two readers: the operator driving the app end to end, and the developer who needs the backend’s shape — how the app is wired, which backend stores the data, and why a second job returns a “busy” error. For the phenomena behind each step (what a measurement is, how the models work) see the How It Works section; for the code-level map see the Technical Reference.
Related: Managing filaments · Samples and geometries · Assigning images · Processing and extraction · The Modeling page · Maintenance operations

Starting the packaged app
The Windows Suite starts this server through Prisma Calibration.exe (Prisma/calibration_launcher.py). The launcher fixes the app root to the folder containing the executable, creates and probes Calibration’s portable folders, takes an exclusive lock on Calibration/Workspace, creates a blank SQLite database only when that Workspace is genuinely blank, applies the SQLite/database/asset environment contract, reserves a loopback port (normally 8016), and opens the browser. Starting a second instance reuses the lock owner’s healthy local URL instead of creating a second writer.
server.py builds one FastAPI instance titled “Unified Calibration Workbook” (server.py:200) and — as the last mount, so it doesn’t shadow the API — serves the single-page frontend from calibration/app/ with html=True, so / resolves to index.html (server.py:8897). All JSON routes live under /api/...; everything else is the static frontend (app.js, api.js, style.css).
Which store the data lives in
The backend is chosen explicitly at launch and never falls back silently. server.py reads PRISMA_CALIBRATION_BACKEND and requires json or sqlite (server.py:305-321). The packaged launcher always supplies SQLite, Calibration/Workspace/calibration.sqlite3, Calibration/Workspace/Assets, and the portable app root through runtime_layout.calibration_environment. The older JSON file store and local pointer-file compatibility remain for migration tools, tests, and source maintenance; they are not packaged-runtime fallbacks.

The workflow, end to end
The five tabs are the workflow in order. A sample flows left to right, but the library tabs (Filaments, Geometries) are set up once and reused across many samples.
1 — Register the building blocks
Before a sample can exist, its parts must be in the library:

Filaments tab → + New Filament opens the create drawer: color name, manufacturer, material, hex color, and the policy checkboxes (White-cap eligible, Special role: Transparent, Special role: Black, Exclude from model fits and new generation). See Managing filaments.
Geometries tab → + New Sample Geometry opens the step builder, where you lay out the strip’s variable and fixed layers. Related geometries can be grouped with Manage Bundles. See Samples and geometries.

2 — Create samples
A sample is a strip geometry filled with specific filaments. On the Logbook tab, + New Samples opens the bulk create drawer: pick a single geometry or a bundle, assign a filament to each layer role (in Multi mode you batch across several filaments to spawn many samples at once), and create. The sample now exists in the logbook awaiting photographs. See Samples and geometries.
3 — Assign photographs
The physical strips are 3D-printed and photographed on a lightbox outside the app. On Images → Assign Images, a three-pane workspace connects those raw photos to samples:

Image Inbox — Import from Inbox pulls in new photos; select one and Assign Image to Sample →.
Registered Blanks — a blank is an empty-lightbox photo used for flatfield correction. Register one, then Assign Blank to Sample →.
Assign Images and Blanks — the sample list showing what each sample has so far.

For many samples at once, CSV Bulk Assignment bulk-assigns images and blanks from a spreadsheet. See Assigning images.
4 — Extract the colors
On Images → Processing Queue, samples with images assigned appear under Ready to Process. Process All (N) runs strip detection, deskew, flatfield correction, and per-swatch color extraction across the batch. Samples that fail auto-detection land in Failed or Flagged for Manual Processing, where Manual Process opens a modal to click the strip’s four corners by hand. See Processing and extraction.
5 — Accept the results
Extraction results appear in Post-Processing Review (the right side of the Processing Queue). You Accept or Reject each — accepting commits the extraction as the sample’s trusted measurement. Only accepted extractions feed the models.
6 — Curate the evidence
The Modeling tab is where you decide what the models learn. Its Overview subtab summarizes evidence and flags problems (stale models, samples missing extraction). Samples lists every sample with an Exclude / Include toggle; Filaments shows per-filament coverage and health. Excluding a sample (or an individual swatch) keeps a suspect measurement out of the fit without deleting it. See The Modeling page.
7 — Fit the working models
Fit Models (on the Modeling tab, or as the Fit Models maintenance operation) runs the unified fit for Calibration’s three current working models — Color Model v1 (the legacy spline), Color Model v2 (the photo-stack model), and the Camera Transform — from the currently included evidence. Each family’s replacement is atomic, but the three-stage workflow is not one all-or-nothing transaction: a family completed before a later failure may already be current. Generator cannot see this mutable working state. The mechanics of each model live in Color Model v1, Color Model v2, and The Camera Transform.
8 — Publish a Generator library
The topbar Publish Models action first reads /api/models/publication/readiness, which requires exactly one current, intact fit for each model family plus a valid public filament catalog. Publish to Generator calls /api/models/publication/install and installs a new inactive immutable library in the sibling Generator tree. Export Library Package calls /api/models/publication/export and writes the equivalent transfer ZIP to Calibration/Output/Published Models. Neither path activates the library, changes Calibration’s lifecycle, or mutates any older published library.

How the app is wired (developer view)
One process, one user
The app holds its live state in a single Python process. There is no per-user or per-browser isolation: two tabs pointed at the same server share one backend and one set of jobs. This is a workbench tool, not a multi-tenant service.
One heavy job at a time
Every expensive operation takes a module-level lock and refuses to start on top of another with an HTTP 409. The server declares a family of these locks near the top of server.py (server.py:205-241) — among them the maintenance run lock (_maintenance_run_lock), the model-fit run lock (_model_fit_run_lock), the extraction writer lock (_extraction_writer_lock), and locks for backups, restores, and image imports. When a job is running, a conflicting request comes back as a 409 with a message naming the blocker (e.g. server.py:2036, :2423, :2054). So you cannot, for example, fit models while a re-extraction is writing, or start a backup mid-maintenance.
The practical consequence: the UI’s long operations are start-then-report. A click kicks off a background job; the frontend polls for progress; a second attempt while one is live is rejected rather than queued.
Restarting
Restarting the server drops in-flight job state, but the data itself is durable — it lives in the configured store (SQLite database plus the materialized asset root), not in memory. Accepted extractions, filaments, geometries, samples, and current working models all survive a restart. Published Generator libraries are separate copies in Generator’s store.

prisma-calibration/technical-reference/u.title: Managing filaments
prisma-calibration/technical-reference/u.content:
In one sentence: the Filaments tab is the library of every filament the workbook knows about — you add each one once, giving it a name, manufacturer, material, and color, and set four policy flags that decide whether it can serve as a white cap, whether it carries a special role, and whether the color models and the generator are allowed to use it at all.

A filament must exist in this library before any sample can reference it. This page covers adding a filament and reading or changing its policy; the layer-by-layer strip that filaments get poured into lives on the Samples and geometries page.
Related: Driving the calibration app · Samples and geometries · The Modeling page · Color Model v1 · Color Model v2 · The Camera Transform

The Filaments table
The Filaments tab is a sortable table, one row per filament, with a summary line above it (e.g. “N filaments, M profiled”). Columns:

Filament — the color name, with its color chip.
Manufacturer.
ID — the slug (see below).
Samples — how many samples reference this filament.
Processed — how many of those have extracted measurements.
Profile — whether a fitted spline profile exists for it.

The toolbar has one button, + New Filament, which opens the create drawer. Clicking any row opens that filament’s view drawer.

Adding a filament
+ New Filament opens a drawer headed New Filament with a Create button. Fill in:

Filament — the color name, placeholder e.g. Basic Cyan.
Manufacturer — placeholder e.g. Bambu. As you type, previously-used manufacturers autocomplete from the library.
Material — placeholder e.g. PLA; defaults to unknown.
Hex Color — a color picker swatch and a hex text field, kept in sync. Must be #RRGGBB.
The Policy checkboxes and Notes (below).

A Generated ID field previews the slug live as you type the manufacturer and color name. The slug is {manufacturer}-{color_name}, lowercased, with every run of non-alphanumeric characters collapsed to a single hyphen — so “Bambu” + “Basic Cyan” becomes bambu-basic-cyan. If that ID already exists in the library the drawer warns you and blocks the save; manufacturer, color name, and a valid hex are all required. The ID is permanent once created — there is no rename.

The policy checkboxes
Four checkboxes under Policy set how the rest of the system may use this filament. They are the load-bearing part of this screen.
White-cap eligible
Marks the filament as a candidate for the white cap — the diffusing white layer a lithophane is printed against. When the color models are fit, every filament with this flag on is collected into the set of “model whites” that the fits and the generator treat as valid cap materials. Turn it on for your white and near-white diffusers; leave it off for colored filaments.
Special role: Transparent / Special role: Black
Two independent tags that record a filament’s special optical role — a fully clear/transparent filament, or a true black. They are stored on the filament record as descriptive metadata; a filament can carry either, both, or neither. They do not exclude the filament from anything on their own — that is what the exclude flag below does.
Exclude from model fits and new generation
The consequential one, and the reason it is styled as a warning. When checked, the filament is dropped from all three production fits — Color Model v1 (the legacy spline), Color Model v2 (the photo-stack model), and The Camera Transform — and it is withheld from new generation solves, so the generator will not place it in a lithophane.
Two things are worth being precise about:

It drops the sample, not just the swatch. Exclusion is evaluated per sample. A sample is removed from a fit whenever the excluded filament appears in it in any role — whether it is the variable filament being characterized or one of the fixed backing layers underneath. One excluded backing filament therefore quietly removes every sample printed on top of it from the evidence.
It is always on, and permanent to the filament. This is a standing property of the filament, not a per-run toggle. It is not the same as the per-sample Exclude / Include control on The Modeling page (which sidelines one suspect measurement); this flag removes the filament wholesale, everywhere, until you uncheck it.

Use it for a filament you have retired, mis-measured, or never intend to print with — it keeps that filament’s data from polluting the models without your having to delete it or hunt down every sample by hand.

Notes and read-only fields

Notes — a free-text textarea for anything you want to remember about the filament.
Used By N Samples — read-only; lists the samples that reference this filament (click through to open them).
ID — read-only; the slug, shown for reference.


Viewing and editing
Clicking a row opens the view drawer: name and chip, manufacturer, material, color (hex and RGB), a Policy summary (White Cap, Special Roles, Model Fit, Generation), notes, the used-by list, and the ID.
Edit (top of the view drawer) switches the same drawer into edit mode, exposing the fields and policy checkboxes with three buttons:

Save — commits the changes and returns to the view.
Discard — abandons the edits.
Delete — removes the filament, but only if nothing depends on it. A filament that is referenced by any sample, has a saved profile, or has processed strip data cannot be deleted; the app tells you so rather than deleting. Retiring such a filament is what Exclude from model fits and new generation is for.

Editing lets you change the manufacturer, color name, material, hex, policy flags, and notes. It does not change the ID — the slug is fixed at creation.

Color note: the Hex Color you set here is a display-referred label for the UI, not a measurement. The actual optical behavior of the filament comes from its extracted samples, in a different color domain entirely — see Transmission vs Appearance.

prisma-calibration/technical-reference/u.title: Processing and extraction
prisma-calibration/technical-reference/u.content:
In one sentence: on Images → Processing Queue you run extraction on every sample that has its photos, rescue the ones automatic detection can’t handle with the Manual Processing corner-picker, then Accept the results that look right — and only an accepted extraction becomes the trusted measurement the models are allowed to learn from.

This page is the operator’s reference for the Processing Queue screen: which button does what, when a sample lands in Failed versus Flagged for Manual Processing, and how the Manual Processing modal recovers a strip the automatic pipeline missed. It does not re-derive how detection, deskew, flatfield, and median extraction work — that mechanism lives in Extraction. Everything here is about driving the queue.
Related: Driving the calibration app · Assigning images · Extraction · The Modeling page

Getting here
Open the Images tab and switch to the Processing Queue subtab (the sibling of Assign Images). A sample only shows up here once it has an assigned photo and blank — assigning those is the previous step, covered in Assigning images.
The screen is split into two panes. The left pane, Pre-Processing Queue, is the work still to be done: samples waiting to be extracted, and the ones that failed or were flagged. The right pane, Post-Processing Review, is the finished extractions waiting for your yes-or-no. Work flows left to right: extract on the left, judge on the right.

The left pane — Pre-Processing Queue
The left pane groups samples into three collapsible sections by their state.
Ready to Process
Samples that have an image and a blank assigned but have not been extracted yet. Each card shows the strip layout, the source photo, the blank, and the open-side arrow, plus per-card actions:

Process — extract this one sample now.
Flag — mark it for manual handling without extracting first; it moves to Flagged for Manual Processing.
Reassign — unassign the photo and send the sample back to Assign Images (used when the wrong photo was attached).

The section’s batch action is Process All (N), where N is the number of ready samples. It runs the full automatic pipeline — strip detection, deskew, flatfield correction, and per-swatch median extraction — across the whole batch, one sample at a time, showing a live progress bar with running counts of processed, flagged, and failed. The underlying mechanism is described in Extraction.
Failed
A sample lands here when a committing automatic run could not finish. In practice that means detection found no strip outline in any of its strategies, or the blank/flatfield image couldn’t be resolved, or something threw partway through. A failed committing run leaves no partial measurements and removes any earlier sidecar; a preview run (commit:false) reports the failure without changing durable sample or sidecar state (Extraction calls the commit path “all or nothing”).
Flagged for Manual Processing
A sample is here because you pressed Flag on it, or because a low-confidence automatic run marked it for review. These samples are not broken measurements — they are ones you’ve decided the automatic path shouldn’t be trusted on.
Cards in Failed and Flagged for Manual Processing carry these actions:

Manual Process — open the corner-picker modal for this sample (see below).
Unflag — clear the flag; a sample with a usable prior result reverts to processed, otherwise it returns to the ready/assigned state.
Reassign — same as above: detach the photo and go back to Assign Images.

Each of these two sections has its own batch action, Manual Process All (N), which opens the modal as a queue that walks the whole section’s samples one after another.

One extraction job runs at a time. Extraction takes a server-side writer lock, so starting Process All (or a manual extract) while another extraction — or a model fit — is already running is refused with a “busy” error rather than queued. This is the same single-job discipline described in Driving the calibration app.


The right pane — Post-Processing Review
Every finished extraction appears here under Processed before it counts for anything. A committed extraction is not automatically trusted — it sits in review with acceptance withheld until you act on it.
Each review card shows the sample, the extracted strip image side by side with a mock strip built from the measured swatch colors, and two actions:

Accept — commit this extraction as the sample’s trusted measurement. This is the gate that matters: only accepted extractions feed the models. An accepted sample drops out of the review pane and becomes evidence the Modeling step can include in a fit.
Reject — throw the result away and send the sample back to the ready queue for another pass. Rejecting clears the measurements and returns the sample to Ready to Process.

The section header carries the bulk pair Accept All and Reject All, which apply the same action to every card currently in review.
Accepting is reversible in the sense that you can later exclude a sample or an individual swatch from fits on the Modeling tab without deleting it — accept here just means “this measurement is real”; the decision about whether it should train the model is made later.

Manual Processing (the corner-picker)
When automatic detection can’t find the strip — most often with highly translucent filaments that blend into the lightbox — you place the strip’s corners by hand. Manual Process (or Manual Process All) opens the Manual Processing modal, whose header names the sample being worked on.
The modal shows the source photo on a canvas with the instruction:

Click corners of the strip in order: TL, TR, BR, BL.

Click the four corners in that order — top-left, top-right, bottom-right, bottom-left. Placed corners can be dragged to fine-tune them. The controls are:

Extract & Process — run the manual pipeline on your four corners and show a preview of the result (the extracted strip). This is a preview only: it does not yet commit anything or change the sample’s state.
Reset Corners — clear all four corners and start placing them again.
Cancel — abort an in-progress run.

Once the preview appears you get two more buttons:

Accept — finalize this manual extraction. It re-runs the extraction to commit the result, marks the sample processed, and clears the flag. In a batch (Manual Process All) Accept advances to the next sample in the queue; on the last sample, or a single-sample run, it closes the modal.
Retry — discard the preview and re-place the corners.

The manual path fixes the strip’s direction from your clicked corner order plus the sample’s recorded open-side orientation, so it does not use the brightness heuristic the automatic path relies on. From the flatfield division onward the measurement is identical to the automatic one — the only difference is how the strip was located. See Extraction for the full manual-vs-automatic comparison.
A manually accepted sample lands in the same Post-Processing Review pane as an automatic one — it still has to be part of an accepted measurement to reach the models. (In practice pressing Accept in the manual modal already commits it as processed; it then appears in the review pane for the final acceptance, tying back to the Modeling step.)

The short version

Process All on the left to extract the ready batch.
Anything that lands in Failed or Flagged for Manual Processing → Manual Process, click the four corners, Extract & Process, Accept.
On the right, Accept the good results and Reject the bad ones.
Accepted samples are now trusted measurements — continue to The Modeling page to choose what the fit learns from them.

prisma-calibration/technical-reference/u.title: Running maintenance
prisma-calibration/technical-reference/u.content:
In one sentence: the topbar Maintenance button opens a dialog of named housekeeping operations — audits, image and geometry rebuilds, database health checks, and the model fit — each of which you run through the same preflight → run → report cadence, one at a time, with a running Maintenance Activity Log; the one exception is Re-extract Sample Images, a staged review workflow that never overwrites your accepted data until you explicitly save.

This page is the operator’s how-to for the Maintenance dialog: what each control does and in what order you click it. For what each operation does mechanically — what an audit inspects, what a rebuild regenerates, why the fit is safe to re-run — see Maintenance Operations and don’t re-derive it here.
Related: Maintenance Operations · Processing and extraction · The Modeling page · Backup and restore · Driving the calibration app

Opening the dialog
The topbar Maintenance button opens the Maintenance dialog. Operations are laid out as selectable cards, grouped under category caps and spread across up to three columns. Each card shows the operation’s name, a one-line description, and a small meta tag telling you whether it is Read-only or writes something. Clicking a card selects it; the Selected Operation panel on the right then shows a Start Workflow button.
The dialog header carries one extra button, Activity Log, covered below.
The operations, by group
The groupings and exact names come straight from the operation registry:

Audit — Audit Library Integrity, Audit Missing Artifacts, Audit Orphaned Artifacts, Audit Source Image Custody. All read-only; they report problems without changing anything.
Images — Rebuild Image Previews, Rebuild Extraction Images Only, Re-extract Sample Images.
Calibration Models — Fit Models.
Geometry Artifacts — Regenerate STEPs/STLs, Export Geometry Files.
System Maintenance — SQLite Integrity Check, Quarantine Orphaned Artifacts.

An operation that is currently unavailable appears grayed out with a reason line in its detail panel, and its Start Workflow button is disabled.
Two of these overlap actions you can reach elsewhere:

Fit Models here runs the exact same unified fit you can launch from The Modeling page — Color Model v1, Color Model v2, and the Camera Transform, from the currently-included evidence.
Export Geometry Files writes the same user-facing STEP/STL exports that the Geometries tab’s export action produces.


Running a standard operation
Every operation except Re-extract Sample Images runs through one workflow dialog with the same three beats.

Start Workflow opens the operation’s dialog, headed with the operation name. It restates the description and, where relevant, exposes options:

Operations with more than one mode show a Mode picker — for the rebuilds and exports this is Missing Only (act only on what’s absent or repairable) versus Force Rebuild / Force Export (rewrite everything in scope). A help line explains the difference.
Export Geometry Files adds an Export Options block: Only Geometries Used By Samples or All Geometries, plus STEP / STL file-type checkboxes.
Fit Models adds a Fit Options block with a Force Camera Transform checkbox.


Run Preflight inspects the current state and reports what the operation would do — a summary, any warnings, and any blockers — without touching data. If preflight blocks the operation, the run button stays disabled.
The run button (labeled by what it does: Run Audit, Run Maintenance, Export Files, or Fit Models) executes the job. Progress streams into the dialog. Safe-point operations offer Cancel and remain visibly Cancelling… until the worker actually stops; operations labeled Runs to completion never offer Cancel. A Result section then shows the outcome, summary, any warnings, and the path to the saved report. Export Geometry Files in its overwrite mode also asks you to type a confirmation phrase before the run button unlocks.

That preflight-first-then-run rhythm is deliberate: nothing that writes data does so until you have seen the preflight and clicked the run button.
Only one at a time
Maintenance operations are not queued. Only one maintenance job may run at any moment: if you try to start a second while one is live, the server rejects it with a 409 whose message names the job already running (for example, Maintenance job 'a1b2c3' is already running.). Backup, restore, or RAW-archive work in progress blocks maintenance the same way, and vice versa — see Backup and restore. In practice you start a job, watch it finish in its dialog, and only then start the next.

The Activity Log
The Activity Log button (dialog header) opens Maintenance Activity Log, a history of past reports. It is a four-column table: Name, Type, Status, File Name. Each completed operation writes one report row here; the newest sits on top.
The footer’s Clear Log button deletes those saved report files. It asks first (a Clear Activity Log confirmation), and it is narrow in scope: clearing the log removes only the maintenance report JSON files — it does not touch backups, RAW archives, source images, generated artifacts, quarantine files, SQLite data, or any sample records.

Re-extract Sample Images
Re-extract Sample Images is not a one-shot job — it is a staged review workflow, and the important thing to understand is that it is non-destructive: it re-runs extraction into a temporary candidate set and leaves your accepted measurements untouched until you explicitly save. You review every candidate and decide, sample by sample, whether to keep it.
Start Workflow on this card opens its own dialog with three scope controls:

Data — Complete, Transmission Only, or Appearance Only. This chooses which color data gets recomputed. (See Transmission vs Appearance for what those two halves are.)
Coordinates — Use Accepted Coordinates (reuse the strip corners already accepted for each sample) or Re-detect Strip (find the strip from scratch). Choosing Re-detect Strip forces Data back to Complete and disables the partial options — a full re-detect has to redo everything.
Samples — All Accepted (every accepted, processed sample) or Selected Samples, which reveals an id textarea. Type or paste sample ids separated by commas or spaces, e.g. exp-055, exp-056.

From there:

Run Preflight counts the targets and splits them into automated, manual, and blocked, and warns you which samples will need manual corners.
Extract Images runs the re-extraction into a fresh candidate set. Nothing accepted has changed yet.
Samples that couldn’t auto-detect surface in a manual step first: open each one, place Manual Corners by hand, then Review Results.
The Review Extracted Images dialog lists every candidate with a before/after strip comparison (Extracted Transmission and Extracted Appearance). For each reviewable sample, toggle Save or Skip; a failed candidate offers Retry, and a re-detect candidate offers Manual Corners. You must decide Save or Skip on every pending sample before you can commit.
Commit with Save Results (which shows the final Save / Skip / Failed / Blocked counts) or throw the whole candidate set away with Discard Results. Only Save Results writes the kept candidates over the accepted measurements.

Like other heavy jobs, re-extraction takes the maintenance run lock: a second re-extraction, or a maintenance job while one is running, comes back as a 409.

prisma-calibration/technical-reference/u.title: Samples and geometries
prisma-calibration/technical-reference/u.content:
In one sentence: the Geometries tab is where you design the printable strip shapes — variable and fixed layer roles, exported as STEP/STL for the printer — and group them into bundles; the Logbook tab is where you fill a geometry with real filaments to create the samples you will later photograph and measure.

This page covers two screens and the drawers they open. A sample geometry is a strip design: which layers it has and how thick each swatch is, with the material left unspecified. A sample is that geometry filled with specific filaments — one per layer role. A bundle is a named group of related geometries printed together, with their shared filament slots mapped once so you can create many samples in a single pass. For the anatomy and math behind a geometry — the staircase, the spine, the structural fingerprint — see Sample Geometry; this page stays on what you click and why.
Related: Sample Geometry · Driving the calibration app · Assigning images · Managing filaments

The Geometries tab
The table lists every sample geometry in the library, one row each, with columns Strip (a mini strip diagram), Alias, Bundle, # Layers, Used by (how many samples reference it), and Last modified. The summary above the table reads N sample geometries. The toolbar has three buttons:

+ New Sample Geometry — opens the step builder drawer to design a new strip.
Manage Bundles — opens the bundle management drawer (toggles: click again to close).
Export Geometry Files — writes user-facing STEP/STL files for all geometries into the public output folder (see Managed artifacts vs. exports).

Clicking a row opens its detail drawer. The drawer header carries Export and Edit; the body shows the geometry’s Alias, ID, Bundle chips, Last Modified, a Used By sample list, and the Exported Files and Managed Artifacts sections. Each stored file path has a Copy Path button that copies the absolute path to the clipboard.

Edit switches the drawer to edit mode, where the header shows Save, Discard, and Delete. Only the alias, bundle membership, and notes are editable — a geometry’s shape is immutable once created (Sample Geometry). Delete opens the Delete Sample Geometry confirmation; deletion is refused if any sample or bundle still references the geometry.
Export (drawer header) opens the geometry export dialog for that one geometry.


Building a geometry (the step builder drawer)
+ New Sample Geometry opens the New Sample Geometry drawer. Its header has two commit buttons: Create (save the geometry into the library) and Create + Export (save, then immediately open the export dialog).
You lay out the strip as a stack of layer role cards, ordered bottom to top:

Each card is either Variable or Fixed. Exactly one role must be Variable — its per-swatch thickness values are typed into the swatch input grid, and this is the staircase that sweeps the thickness axis. A Fixed role takes a single thickness that applies across the whole strip.
Drag a card by its handle to reorder the stack.
+ Add Layer Role appends a new fixed role; the small remove control on a card deletes it.


The builder has an older, non-structured layout still present in the code, where the variable row shows + Add Fixed Layer and per-fixed-layer Remove buttons. On the structured backend you see the role-card layout with + Add Layer Role instead.

A live strip preview updates as you edit, and the spine total thickness auto-fills from the tallest swatch stack unless you override it. Roles are slots, not materials — the geometry never names a filament; that happens when you create samples.

Managed artifacts vs. exports
There are two distinct sets of files, and the distinction matters:

Managed artifacts are the app’s internal, canonical STEP/STL files, generated and owned by the backend and tracked against the geometry’s structural fingerprint. The drawer’s Managed Artifacts section reports how many exist.
Exports are user-facing copies written into Calibration/Output/Steps for you to hand to the slicer. The drawer’s Exported Files section records the latest export paths.

Both Create + Export and the row-level Export open the Export Sample Geometry dialog. It has a name field plus Export STEP, Export STLs, and Cancel. STEP produces one model with a labeled solid body per layer role; STLs produce one file per role, named so the slicer shows which body is which layer. If an export of the same name already exists in the output folder, a Replace Existing Export? dialog appears listing the conflicting paths, with Overwrite and Cancel. While either export request is active, the parent dialog stays open with its controls disabled; Escape, outside-click, and a second Export action cannot detach the UI from the request.
The toolbar’s Export Geometry Files button is different: it runs an export across all geometries at once as a maintenance workflow, rather than exporting a single geometry.

Bundles (Manage Bundles drawer)
Manage Bundles opens the Manage Bundles drawer: a bundle list on the left, the selected bundle’s detail on the right.

Create a bundle by typing a name into the new-bundle row and clicking Create.
Select a bundle to edit it. Its header shows Rename (which reveals an inline field with Save / Cancel) and Delete.
Under Bundle Geometries, Add Geometries… adds member geometries; each member row has a remove control.
Under Bundle Filament Mapping, Edit Mapping opens the mapping editor, where you define the bundle’s shared filament slots and map each geometry’s layer roles onto them. A bundle must be fully mapped before it can drive bulk sample creation; if you save an incomplete mapping, a Save Incomplete Mapping dialog offers Save Anyway or Cancel. The bundle’s list entry shows a mapping-status pill.

A mapped bundle lets you assign a filament once per shared slot and spawn a sample for every member geometry in one action.

Creating samples (the Logbook tab)
On the Logbook tab, + New Samples opens the New Samples drawer. Its header has one commit button, Create. The drawer is a form on the left and a live Sample Preview strip diagram on the right.

Select Geometry Source — a toggle between Single Geometry and Geometry Bundle, plus a picker for choosing the specific geometry or bundle.
Selected Geometry Preview — shows the chosen strip so you can confirm it before assigning materials.
Filament slots — one row per assignable role (or per shared bundle slot). Each row has a Single / Multi toggle:

Single assigns one filament to that role.
Multi (batch) picks several filaments for one role at once; the app then spawns a separate sample for each — one strip design, many filaments under test. Only one role can be in Multi mode at a time.


Notes — an optional free-text note applied to every sample created in the batch.
Sample Summary — a running count and record preview of what Create will produce.

Because roles are just slots, one geometry serves any number of filaments — the geometry decides the shape, the sample decides the material. Newly created samples land in the logbook with no photos yet, ready for Assigning images.
A note on editing an existing sample: changing which geometry or filaments a sample uses is a provenance change. If the sample already has extraction results, the change invalidates them — the app clears the measurements and marks any dependent filament profiles stale, because the old measurement no longer describes the new material stack.

prisma-calibration/technical-reference/u.title: The Modeling page
prisma-calibration/technical-reference/u.content:
In one sentence: the Modeling tab is where you curate which measurements the color models are allowed to learn from — sidelining a suspect sample or swatch without deleting it — and then press Fit Models to rebuild Calibration’s three current working models (Color Model v1, Color Model v2, and the Camera Transform) from the evidence that is currently included.

This is the last stop before you can publish a complete library for Generator. Everything upstream produced measurements; this page decides which of them count, checks Calibration’s working models for staleness, and triggers the fit. It does not re-explain how each model works — for that, follow the links to Color Model v1, Color Model v2, and The Camera Transform.
Related: Driving the calibration app · Processing and extraction · Managing filaments · Running maintenance · Color Model v1 · Color Model v2 · The Camera Transform

What “evidence” means here
Only accepted extractions are evidence. A sample that has been photographed and processed but whose result you have not accepted in Post-Processing Review does not feed any model — it shows up here under Needs Extraction. Accepting an extraction is done on the Processing Queue; see Processing and extraction. This page assumes that step is behind you and lets you decide which of the accepted measurements the fit should trust.
Two levers coexist, and they are not the same:

Per-run curation (this page). The Exclude / Include toggle and the per-swatch controls sideline one measurement for the next fit. Reversible with one click, scoped to a sample or a swatch.
Permanent per-filament exclusion. The Exclude from model fits and new generation flag on Managing filaments drops a filament wholesale from every fit and from generation, and stays on until you uncheck it. Use that for a retired or mis-measured filament; use this page for a single bad strip.


The header — model status and Fit Models
The Modeling tab header carries a status line with one chip per working model — Color Model v1, Color Model v2, and Camera Transform — each showing whether that model is current, stale, or missing, and the primary Fit Models button.

Current — Calibration’s working model is up to date with the included evidence.
Stale — the working model no longer matches its contributing evidence: you have changed included evidence or another relevant fit input since it was built. A Fit Models needed banner appears above the subtabs when anything is stale or missing.
Missing — no current working model artifact exists yet.

Fit Models opens the Fit Models workflow (the same job as the Fit Models maintenance operation — see Running maintenance and Maintenance Operations). It runs the unified fit end to end: it rebuilds the legacy spline profiles (Color Model v1), the photo-stack model (Color Model v2), and — when needed — the Camera Transform, all from the currently-included evidence, replacing Calibration’s prior current fit for each family. It does not change Generator. Only one heavy job runs at a time, so if a re-extraction, backup, or another fit is in flight the button reports the conflict rather than starting (see Driving the calibration app).
When all three status chips are current, use the separate topbar Publish Models action to validate and copy that exact generation into an immutable library. Publish to Generator installs it inactive; Export Library Package writes a transferable ZIP. Generator continues using its previously selected library until you explicitly activate the new one through Models → Activate and Restart Prisma.
Three subtabs sit under the header: Overview, Samples, and Filaments.

Overview — is the evidence healthy?
The Overview subtab is a read-at-a-glance summary. Current Evidence is a row of metric cards:

Evidence Samples — included samples over total (e.g. 41 / 55), counting only samples with an accepted extraction and at least one included swatch.
Swatches — included swatches over total.
Excluded Samples — how many samples you have toggled to Exclude.
Excluded Swatches — how many individual swatches are currently sidelined.

Needs Attention lists concrete blockers to a good fit: any stale or missing model, and a Samples without accepted extraction count. If nothing is wrong it says No immediate blockers. Treat this list as your pre-fit checklist — clear it (accept the pending extractions, decide the exclusions), then fit.

Samples — curate one strip at a time
The Samples subtab is a table, one row per sample, with columns Sample, Strip, Filaments, Fit State, Extracted Appearance, and Fit Control. Above it are two filters:

A Filter dropdown: All, Included, Excluded, Has Excluded Swatches, Needs Extraction, Stale, Missing Model. (Stale and Missing Model only return rows when a model actually is stale or missing.)
A filament filter: Filaments… opens a Filter Samples by Filament picker; selected filaments show as chips, and Clear removes them. Use it to see every sample that a given filament appears in.

Including and excluding a sample
The Fit Control column holds one button per row: Exclude when the sample is currently included, Include when it is excluded. Clicking it flips that sample’s participation in the next fit. Excluding keeps the measurement intact — it is still in the workbook, still viewable — it is simply withheld from the fit. Excluding (or re-including) a sample marks the affected models stale; that is expected, and the fix is to re-run Fit Models.
The comparison drawer
Clicking anywhere on a row (outside the button) opens a read-only comparison drawer for that sample. It shows, per swatch, the measured colors beside each model’s prediction — Measured Colors, Predicted Colors (Color Model V2), and Predicted Colors (Color Model V1) — under a Color Comparison module. Two display toggles control what you see, they do not change any data:

An Appearance / Transmission toggle picks the domain the strips are drawn in (what the camera sees versus raw transmission — see Transmission vs Appearance).
A Color Corrections toggle switches the predictions between with- and without-corrections, so you can judge how much the corrections are doing (v1’s pair corrections and v2’s correction layer — Color Model v1, Color Model v2).

Use this drawer to decide whether a sample is trustworthy before you exclude it: if the model already tracks the measurement well, leave it in; if one swatch is wildly off, sideline that swatch.
Per-swatch exclusion
Excluding a single swatch rather than the whole sample is done on the sample’s own record, in its Model Fit controls (the Included / Excluded toggle per swatch, alongside the Exclude this sample from model fits checkbox) — reached by opening the sample from the Logbook, not from this comparison drawer. Swatches you sideline there show up here as the Fit State “N swatches excluded” pill and under the Has Excluded Swatches filter. See Processing and extraction for that surface.

Filaments — is each filament well covered?
The Filaments subtab answers a different question: does every filament have enough included evidence to be modeled well? It is a coverage table with columns Filament, Brand, Samples Containing It, Included Samples, Included Swatches, Excluded Swatches, Thickness Coverage, Role Coverage, and Health. Health is a colored pill summarizing the row:

Good — enough included swatch evidence.
Sparse — limited included evidence (few swatches); the fit for this filament is thin.
Excluded only — the filament appears in samples, but every one of them is excluded, so it contributes nothing.
Excluded — the filament carries the permanent Exclude from model fits and new generation flag from Managing filaments.
Stale — a model needs refitting.

Clicking a row opens the filament’s coverage detail: a Summary (health state and whether it is included in fits), a compact Coverage block (included/excluded sample and swatch counts), a Model State panel, and an Evidence Samples list of every sample containing the filament. Show In Samples jumps to the Samples subtab pre-filtered to this filament, so you can act on the thin cases directly.
Read this tab as a gap-finder: a Sparse or Excluded only filament is a signal to print and calibrate more strips for it, or to re-include a sample you sidelined too aggressively.

The usual loop

Overview — clear Needs Attention (accept pending extractions upstream, resolve stale/missing).
Samples — spot-check suspect rows in the comparison drawer, Exclude the bad ones.
Filaments — check for Sparse / Excluded only coverage; re-include or plan more strips.
Fit Models — rebuild Calibration’s three working models from the included evidence; the chips return to current.
Publish Models — copy the exact current set into a new immutable library, then activate it from Generator’s Models menu when ready.

prisma-calibration/technical-reference/u.title: Using the Calibration App
prisma-calibration/technical-reference/u.content:
The calibration app is a logbook. You register filaments and sample geometries, create samples, attach each sample its lightbox photographs, extract per-swatch color measurements, curate which measurements the models are allowed to trust, and fit the three color models the generator prints from. This section is the operator’s manual for that workflow — the screens, the controls, and the order of operations.
How It Works explains the phenomena behind each step; the Technical Reference is the code-level map. This tier stays at the level of what you click and why.
Running the app
In the packaged Suite, double-click Prisma Calibration.exe. The launcher creates or validates Calibration’s portable Workspace, starts the local server on port 8016 (or the next available local port), and opens the browser. Keep its console window open while you work; closing it stops Calibration. See Launching the Calibration App for the complete user-facing procedure.
The app is a single-page frontend served by a FastAPI backend. It is a single-user, single-process tool: one browser, one machine, one job at a time. Developers can run the source server directly, but that is not the release install or launch path. The window header reads Calibration Logbook.
The workspace at a glance
A topbar of global actions sits above five mode tabs:





























TabWhat you do thereLogbookThe master sample table. Create samples; open any sample to inspect or edit it.ImagesTwo subtabs: Assign Images (attach photos and blanks to samples) and Processing Queue (run extraction, then accept or reject the result).FilamentsThe filament library. Add and edit filaments and their print/model policy.GeometriesThe sample-geometry library. Define strip layouts, manage bundles, export files.ModelingCurate which samples and swatches feed the models, then fit them.
The topbar carries Refresh Data, Maintenance, and Backup / Restore.
The pages
Start here for the whole workflow end to end:

Driving the calibration app — the spine: how a sample goes from an idea to a fitted model, and how the app is wired underneath.

The library — the reusable things samples are built from:

Managing filaments — adding filaments and setting their white-cap, special-role, and model-exclusion policy.
Samples and geometries — defining strip geometries, managing bundles, and bulk-creating samples.

Measurement — turning photographs into color numbers:

Assigning images — the three-pane assign workspace, registering blanks, and bulk CSV assignment.

The Modeling page — the Overview, Samples, and Filaments subtabs; excluding and including evidence; fitting the models.

prisma-calibration/technical-reference/w.title: Web API and job orchestration
prisma-calibration/technical-reference/w.content:
In one sentence: server.py (calibration.server) is the calibration app’s one FastAPI process — it selects a storage backend explicitly (no silent fallback), serves the single-page frontend, exposes every /api route family, and guards each heavy operation behind a module-level lock so that only one backup, model fit, extraction write, or maintenance job can run at a time — the second caller gets an HTTP 409, not a queue.

This page is the code-level contract of the calibration server: how it boots, what its route surface looks like, and — the load-bearing part — how it enforces “one job at a time.” It is the backend counterpart to the operator-facing Driving the calibration app; where that page describes buttons and screens, this one describes the server the buttons talk to. For where data actually lives, see Data access and persistence; for the long-running operations the server dispatches, see The maintenance backend.
Related: calibration.server · calibration.csv_assignment_import · calibration.sample_mutations · Driving the calibration app
One process, one user, start-then-report
The whole app is a single FastAPI instance (server.py:200) launched by one uvicorn.run (server.py:9004). There is no task queue, no worker pool, no external broker. That shapes everything else on this page:

Heavy work runs on a daemon thread, not a subprocess or a queue. A “start” endpoint validates, acquires a lock, spawns a threading.Thread(..., daemon=True), and returns a job record immediately (e.g. start_photo_stack_fit server.py:8217; start_camera_transform_build server.py:8244). The client then polls a matching status endpoint (get_photo_stack_status server.py:8235, get_camera_transform_status server.py:8262) until the job record reports terminal state. This is the start-then-report model: the HTTP call that starts the job does not wait for it.
Job state is in-memory. Running/finished jobs live in module-level dicts — _photo_stack_jobs, _camera_transform_jobs, _profile_fit_jobs, _backup_jobs, _image_import_jobs, _maintenance_jobs, _reextract_jobs (declared server.py:204–233) — each with its own dict-guarding threading.Lock and a TTL for pruning stale records. A server restart forgets them.
The polling is chatty by design, so a log filter mutes the high-frequency status GETs from uvicorn’s access log (_PollingAccessLogFilter server.py:251, installed server.py:274).

Because there is exactly one process and (in practice) one operator, the concurrency model can be this simple. The lock/409 mechanism below is what actually keeps two conflicting operations from colliding.
Backend selection — explicit, never silent
The store is chosen at startup and validated up front. _configured_backend (server.py:305) reads PRISMA_CALIBRATION_BACKEND, falling back only to a local .backend file — and if neither is set it raises RuntimeError rather than defaulting (server.py:311). Only "json" and "sqlite" are accepted (_VALID_BACKENDS server.py:48); anything else is a hard error.
_create_store (server.py:336) turns that choice into a concrete store:

"sqlite" builds an SQLiteDataStore (calibration.sqlite_data_access) from a required database path and a required materialized asset root (server.py:368), each resolved through _configured_required_path, which likewise raises if the path is not configured. This is the production backend.
"json" builds a DataStore (calibration.data_access) over a data-root directory (server.py:356). Per the docstring (server.py:343–348), JSON “can still be constructed intentionally for migration tests/tools, but it is never selected as an implicit fallback.” Treat the JSON store as migration/test-only, off the production path.

At import time _store is None (server.py:203); the packaged calibration_launcher.py first resolves the portable layout, prepares/initializes the SQLite Workspace, applies the required environment, and then imports the server. A source-only main() or bare Uvicorn launch can still populate the store through the development paths. SQLite initialization records recovery context before constructing the store; if construction fails, _store remains unset and get_store (server.py:465) raises an error saying SQLite recovery is required. A successful store runs interrupted-maintenance scanning and the SQLite restore-point startup check (server.py:430-:436). GET /api/config (get_config server.py:947) echoes the resolved backend and paths back for the UI’s copy-path controls.

The supported Windows release path is Prisma Calibration.exe, whose desktop launcher defaults to local port 8016 and searches upward if that port is occupied. Commands and defaults in server.py are source-development interfaces, not end-user installation guidance (see Driving the calibration app).

The /api route surface
Routes are declared as decorated functions across server.py (the module exports well over a hundred endpoint handlers — see the Defines list on calibration.server). They group into a stable set of families, keyed by the first path segment:





































FamilyPurpose/api/samples, /api/bundles, /api/geometries, /api/stepsSample CRUD, batch creation, geometry/bundle/STEP management/api/filaments, /api/profilesFilament registry and fitted-profile read/activate/api/images, /api/blanks, /api/thumbnails, /api/previewsManaged image assets, blank registration, preview/thumbnail serving/api/processExtraction — process one/all samples, manual extract, status summary/api/fitting, /api/models, /api/photo-stack, /api/camera-transformModel fitting, review, and the Camera Transform build/api/maintenance, /api/systemLong-running maintenance jobs, re-extraction, SQLite restore points/api/backup, /api/raw-archivesBackup/restore and RAW image archive lifecycle
Read endpoints return JSON directly; the heavy families (backup, maintenance, photo-stack, camera-transform, profiles/fit-all, images/import-inbox) follow the start-then-poll pattern above. This page describes the families, not every route; the exhaustive list is the module’s Defines block on its Architecture node.
The SPA is mounted last, at /
_mount_static (server.py:8892) mounts the frontend directory at the root with StaticFiles(directory=..., html=True) (:8897). It is called by main after store initialization and after the API routes have been registered (:8998-:9002). Mounting it last means /api/... paths resolve to their handlers and everything else falls through to the SPA’s index.html.
Backup and restore orchestration
Backup and restore are SQLite-only (_require_sqlite_backup_store, server.py:1068). The server separates package validation from destructive application. Upload or local-path validation registers a preview token (/api/backup/validate-restore and /api/backup/validate-restore-path, server.py:3950-:4014); the preview records the source identity and validated package semantics. A restore request must claim that token before starting (_claim_restore_preview, server.py:3188); the claim prevents a preview from being reused or changed between validation and execution.
POST /api/backup/restore-job (server.py:4156) claims a validated preview and starts _run_restore_job (:3781) on a daemon thread after checking maintenance and backup blockers. The synchronous /api/backup/restore endpoint (:4182) performs the same claim and calls _execute_claimed_restore while holding _backup_restore_lock. The executor creates an emergency pre-restore package, stages and validates the ZIP, applies only the package semantics, runs a store smoke check, and reinitializes the SQLite store (_execute_claimed_restore, :3398). apply_restore restores displaced state when application or smoke checking fails. Once the smoke check succeeds, rollback cleanup handles read-only files; any residual cleanup failure is returned as a warning rather than re-entering rollback after the old tree may be partially deleted.
Backup creation has the same split: /api/backup/create runs synchronously under _backup_restore_lock, while /api/backup/create-job starts _run_backup_job and exposes in-memory progress through /api/backup/jobs/{job_id} (server.py:3732-:3793). RAW-archive creation, import, release, and restore-preview deletion use the same lock family and are not independent concurrent workers.
The lock / 409 blocker mechanism
This is the heart of “one job at a time.” Beyond the per-dict locks that just guard the job registries, a family of run locks serializes the operations themselves (declared server.py:234–242):

_backup_restore_lock — backups, restores, and RAW-archive work.
_model_fit_run_lock — spline fits, photo-stack fits, and Camera Transform builds (all “model fitting”).
_extraction_writer_lock — anything that writes extraction evidence (notably re-extraction).
_maintenance_run_lock — general maintenance operations.
_evidence_activity_gate_lock — a short-held mutex that makes the check-then-acquire of the model-fit and extraction-writer locks atomic (server.py:235).
_maintenance_resource_gate_lock — admission lock for queued/running maintenance reservations and ordinary writer leases. It protects the transition between “checked” and “owned,” not the filesystem or SQLite directly.

The pattern is uniform: a start endpoint asks whether a conflicting operation holds the relevant lock, and if so raises HTTPException(409, ...) immediately — it does not block or enqueue. Backup/restore endpoints additionally use preview tokens and a claimed-preview state before destructive work begins; the lock prevents overlapping backup, restore, and RAW-archive operations.
The model-fit and extraction-writer locks use a context-manager guard so acquire/release is exception-safe:

_model_fit_run_guard (server.py:2050) calls _try_begin_model_fit_run (server.py:2026); on failure it raises HTTPException(409, ...) with a blocker message (server.py:2054) and otherwise releases the lock in its finally (_end_model_fit_run server.py:2042).
_extraction_writer_guard (server.py:2088) mirrors that, and additionally cross-checks the model-fit lock so a model fit and an extraction write can never overlap (server.py:2098–2100).

The _try_begin_* helpers take _maintenance_resource_gate_lock and then _evidence_activity_gate_lock, inspect the other evidence-writer family, and attempt a non-blocking run-lock acquisition. Maintenance admission takes those locks in the same order, avoiding a model/extraction-start versus maintenance-start deadlock. A model or extraction worker also owns an ordinary resource lease for its full worker lifetime.
Each MaintenanceOperation.conflict_resources tuple drives the shared admission policy. start_maintenance_job_endpoint checks active ordinary leases and creates the queued job while still holding the resource gate; the queued job itself is therefore the reservation and closes the queue-to-worker race. Ordinary API mutations are classified into SQLite, image custody/preview, extraction evidence/sample visuals, geometry, and model categories. Middleware acquires the request’s lease before dispatch and releases it in finally. On-demand source/blank preview GET routes are classified as preview writers because they can create cache files. A conflicting request receives HTTP 409; unrelated reads and writes continue. Worker-start failure marks the queued job failed, which immediately removes it from the active-reservation set.
Net effect: the “one job at a time” behavior the operator sees in the UI is not a frontend nicety — it is enforced server-side by these locks, and a conflicting second request is rejected with a 409 the moment it arrives.
CSV bulk image↔sample assignment
csv_assignment_import.py (calibration.csv_assignment_import) is the one bulk-entry path: an operator uploads a CSV mapping sample IDs to sample/blank images and an orientation, instead of assigning each by hand. The template columns are fixed — Sample ID, Sample Image, Blank Image, Orientation (TEMPLATE_COLUMNS csv_assignment_import.py:14) — and orientation accepts U/D/L/R (plus T/B aliases) via ORIENTATION_MAP (csv_assignment_import.py:16).
It is a two-phase, validate-then-commit flow, and it is SQLite-only — both endpoints call _require_sqlite_assignment_store, which 501s on the JSON backend (server.py:1103):

Validate. POST /api/samples/assignment-import/validate (server.py:4317) runs validate_assignment_csv (csv_assignment_import.py:34), which resolves each row against live samples/images/blanks, accumulates per-row errors, and returns a preview plus a token that caches the valid rows’ commit specs server-side.
Commit. POST /api/samples/assignment-import/commit (server.py:4351) looks the token’s cached specs back up and calls commit_assignment_rows (csv_assignment_import.py:120), which re-validates against current state and raises CsvAssignmentError if the preview went stale (the server maps that to HTTP 409 with a stale flag). Existing-blank assignments use save_samples; when the operator confirmed one or more unregistered blanks, save_samples_with_blank_registrations (sqlite_data_access.py:3524) registers or resolves those blanks and writes every sample assignment inside one SQLite transaction. A registration, validation, or sample-save failure therefore rolls back the entire database mutation rather than retaining a partially registered blank.

Eligibility is deliberately strict: _sample_eligibility_errors (csv_assignment_import.py:569) rejects a row whose sample already has an image, a blank, an orientation, a non-unassigned status, or any extraction results — the importer only fills in genuinely empty samples, never overwrites work. Optionally, when the register_unregistered_blanks flag is set (csv_assignment_import.py:124), commit includes not-yet-registered blank images in the same transaction as their assignments.
Sample mutations — domain logic lifted out of the server
sample_mutations.py (calibration.sample_mutations) holds sample create/update domain logic pulled out of the HTTP handlers to keep them thin; its functions raise ValueError for domain errors and the server converts those to HTTPException (module docstring sample_mutations.py:1–7). The live functions — the ones server.py and csv_assignment_import.py actually import and call — are:

recompute_sample_status (sample_mutations.py:47) — sets a sample’s status to assigned vs unassigned from assignment completeness (used by both the server and the CSV committer).
invalidate_sample_processing (sample_mutations.py:83) — the profile-staleness / invalidation core. When a sample’s provenance changes (new filament, new STEP geometry, swapped source image, rejection), it clears the derived state (measurements, thumbnails, the extraction-result sidecar) and marks every dependent profile stale so downstream fits know their inputs moved. The server calls it on delete, swap, reject, and provenance edits (server.py:4649, 8454, 8531, 8609).
mark_profiles_stale_for_sample (sample_mutations.py:38) — the profile-ownership helper invalidate_sample_processing uses, exposed for direct use on delete.

Note the staleness marking is gated to the JSON backend inside invalidate_sample_processing (sample_mutations.py:99–103): on SQLite the store tracks profile dependencies itself, so the function skips the manual stale-flagging path.

Live vs dormant: three functions in this module — apply_sample_update (sample_mutations.py:132), create_samples_from_step_files (sample_mutations.py:239), and compute_fit_result (sample_mutations.py:292) — are not called anywhere in Prisma/ or tests/; a characterization test even refers to “the dead apply_sample_update” (tests/calibration/test_step_2_invalidation_review.py:7). The server’s update_sample handler (server.py:4439) reimplements sample-update logic inline rather than delegating to apply_sample_update. Treat those three as vestigial — superseded by inline server logic; only the three functions above are live.

Cross-references

Driving the calibration app — the operator’s view of these same endpoints (the UI that starts and polls the jobs).
Data access and persistence — the SQLiteDataStore/DataStore this server selects and reads through.
The maintenance backend — the long-running operations behind /api/maintenance and re-extraction.
Processing and extraction / Extraction — the operator guide and mechanism page for the /api/process family.
