prisma-calibration/technical-reference/i.title: Technical Reference
prisma-calibration/technical-reference/i.content:
The code-level map of the calibration subsystem. Where How It Works explains the phenomena and How To Use explains the workflow, this tier is for the developer tracing an exact detail — module boundaries, data contracts, and the functions that do the work. Pages here use real identifiers and file:line anchors, and they link to the auto-generated Architecture module nodes.
All code lives under Prisma/calibration/. The production backend is SQLite (sqlite_data_access.py); the JSON DataStore survives only for migration tools and tests.
The subsystems
Server and storage:

Web API and job orchestration — the FastAPI server: backend selection, the route families, and the one-job-at-a-time lock/blocker model.
Data access and persistence — the SQLite store and its materialized asset root, the JSON DataStore, the domain models, backups, and automatic restore points.

Measurement:

The extraction pipeline — from a raw lightbox photo to a committed per-swatch ExtractionResult.
Extraction artifact sinks and blank registration — derived thumbnail destinations and the SQLite/JSON blank-registration boundary.
Geometry and strip definition — the source-of-truth GeometryDefinition, its invariants and fingerprint, the body plan, and STEP/STL export.
Geometry-bundle role mapping and sample creation — SQLite material-slot mapping across geometry members and the sample creation contract.

Sample state and assignment:

CSV assignment import and commit lifecycle — preview validation, stale-commit protection, and managed-image blank registration.
Sample mutations, invalidation, and profile staleness — evidence/provenance mutation, derived-state invalidation, and SQLite persistence boundaries.

The models:

Spline model fitting (v1) — the legacy spline transmission fitter (Color Model v1).
Photo-stack model fitting (v2) — the photo-stack fit path (Color Model v2).
The camera transform fitter — building the transmission → camera-color map.
Model workflow, publication, and review — the unified fit fan-out, publication and staleness, and the modeling-review read side.

Upkeep:

The maintenance backend — the maintenance operation framework and the staged re-extraction backend.

Architecture nodes
The Architecture/ folder holds one auto-generated structural node per calibration module — its public definitions, its imports, and its importers — parsed from source by scripts/gen_docs_module_graph_calibration.py. They are regenerated from code, so they can’t silently rot; the prose above links into them. Re-run the script after code changes.

prisma-calibration/index.title: Prisma Calibration
prisma-calibration/index.content:
Prisma Calibration measures how 3D-printing filaments transmit light. It turns controlled photographs of printed calibration samples into working color models, then can publish an immutable model library for the Prisma Lithophane Generator.
Why calibration is needed
The color of a backlit print depends on the filament, its thickness, and the other filament layers around it. A filament’s name or displayed color is not enough to predict these effects. The generator needs measurements from real printed samples.
Calibration builds a reusable library of these measurements. You add to it when you introduce new filaments or need better coverage; you do not repeat the full calibration process for every lithophane.
What the app does
The calibration workflow has four main stages:

Define your filaments and the sample strips you will print.
Print the samples and photograph them on a lightbox.
Assign and process the photographs to measure each swatch.
Review the measurements and fit Calibration’s current working models.
When that exact model set is ready to use, publish it as a new Generator library.

The app manages the samples, photographs, measurements, model-fitting process, and publication step. Printing and photography happen outside the app. Calibration never edits a model library after Generator has installed it.
Where to begin

Getting Started — prepare the app and complete the calibration workflow for the first time.
How To Use — instructions for the tasks and screens in the app.
How It Works — explanations of sample measurement, color models, and the camera transform.
Technical Reference — implementation details for developers.

prisma-lithophane-generator/getting-star.title: Installing Prisma
prisma-lithophane-generator/getting-star.content:
Prisma is a portable Windows application. It does not use a conventional installer: download one ZIP, extract the whole folder, and keep that folder together.
Choose a download

Prisma Generator is for making lithophanes with published model libraries. It includes the Prisma Standard Model Library and starts with Prisma.exe.
Prisma Suite contains the same Generator plus Prisma Calibration for building and publishing your own model libraries. Its two launchers are Prisma Generator.exe and Prisma Calibration.exe.

You can install later model-library updates in either version. You need the Suite only if you want to capture calibration data or build your own models.
Extract it

Download the Windows ZIP from Prisma’s GitHub Releases page.
In File Explorer, right-click the ZIP and choose Extract All. Do not run Prisma from inside the ZIP preview.
Move the extracted Prisma folder to a normal writable location, such as Documents. Do not put the live folder in Program Files, a cloud-synchronized folder, or a network share.
Keep the entire folder together. The executables, bundled runtime, settings, images, exports, libraries, and Calibration data use paths inside this one portable folder.

No Python, PyCharm, VS Code, CAD package, FFmpeg installation, or command-line setup is required. The Windows packages bundle the runtime Prisma actually uses; development-only tooling and the unused video/CAD stacks are not part of the packaged application.
Windows warning
Prisma is not currently code-signed, so Windows SmartScreen may call it an unrecognized app. Only use a ZIP obtained from Prisma’s official GitHub Releases page. If you trust that download, choose More info and then Run anyway.
Extracting a newer Prisma release does not update an older live folder in place. Until a documented migration procedure accompanies a future release, keep each extracted version separate and keep independent copies of important data.

prisma-lithophane-generator/getting-star.title: Launching Prisma
prisma-lithophane-generator/getting-star.content:
Open the extracted Prisma folder and double-click the Generator launcher:

Prisma.exe in the Generator-only download.
Prisma Generator.exe in the Suite.

A console window opens, Prisma starts a server available only on your computer, and your default browser opens the interface. Keep the console window open while you use Prisma. Closing it stops the local server; it does not delete your work.
The launcher normally uses http://127.0.0.1:8010. If that port is busy, it chooses another local port and prints the actual address in the console. Starting the same app a second time reopens the already-running Generator rather than creating a second writer for its Workspace.
The folders Prisma creates
On first launch, Generator creates these folders beside the executable:

























FolderWhat belongs thereGenerator\ImagesSource artwork. Add images through the app or copy supported images here.Generator\ExportsCompleted 3MF/STL exports, one folder per export.Generator\Model LibrariesValidated, installed published libraries. Manage these through the Models menu.Generator\WorkspaceApp-managed settings, saved runs, caches, and logs. Do not rearrange individual files inside it.
Generator keeps its normal state inside the extracted Prisma folder, not %LOCALAPPDATA%. You may move or copy the entire Prisma folder while the app is closed. Do not manually combine one installation’s Workspace or Model Libraries with another.
If the browser does not open
Read the address printed after Address: in the console and enter it in your browser. If Prisma reports a startup error, leave the window open long enough to read the message. The application accepts desktop-launcher connections only from the local computer (127.0.0.1); it is not a hosted website or a server for other devices.

prisma-lithophane-generator/getting-star.title: Getting Started
prisma-lithophane-generator/getting-star.content:
The generator app turns a source photo into a printable color lithophane — a stack of filament layers that reproduces the image when it is backlit. This page walks one image the whole way through the wizard: pick it, build a palette, solve, and export the print files. For the reasoning behind each stage see How It Works; for the details of each screen, How To Use.
What you need

A source image — an ordinary photo. Nothing to prepare; you pick or upload it in the app.
A valid published model library. The Windows download begins with the Prisma Standard Model Library installed; you can later install another published library from Model Library → Manage in the Generator’s left panel. A filament unavailable in the active library can’t be used in a palette.
A multi-color printer with an AMS and OrcaSlicer, for the print files and swap plan the app produces.
The app itself — see Installing and Launching. The Generator-only download starts with Prisma.exe; the Suite starts it with Prisma Generator.exe. Neither requires Python, an IDE, or a manual dependency installation.

It opens on a four-step wizard: 1 Image → 2 Palette → 3 Preview → 4 Export. It’s a single-user tool — one browser, one job at a time — and the long jobs (a solve, a palette suggestion, an export) run in the background: the app kicks the job off, then polls for progress, so two tabs would fight over the same session.
Walk one image through
1 — Pick a source image
On step 1 Image, choose a photo from the image library, or use Add Image to upload one from your computer. The placeholder reads Select an image until you pick one; the preview and the framing controls fill in once you do.
2 — Build a palette
On step 2 Palette, the beginner path is Auto-Suggest: pick the filaments the suggester may draw from under Select Filaments for Auto-Suggest, set Max colors and Extra color loads, and press Suggest Palettes. Candidates land in the Suggested Palettes staging pad, each already pre-scored with a Suggest dE figure (lower is a closer fit) so you can compare them; Add to Deck promotes the one you like into the Palette Deck (the live palette the solve uses). See Palette.
3 — Solve and review
With a palette in the deck, press Solve (top bar) to run step 3 Preview. The solve runs the staged pipeline in the background and reports progress; when it finishes, the Predicted view shows the print’s predicted lit appearance beside the source, with a color-error figure (an RMSE % — lower is closer) in the run header. The view toggles — White Cap, Color Regions, Top Surface, Thickness Maps — let you inspect what the print actually lays down. The blocky look is deliberate: the preview honors the true solve resolution and never fakes detail the print won’t have. For what happens inside a solve, see How a Solve Works.
4 — Export print files
On step 4 Export, pick the finished run under Select Run, then Generate Print Files. Choose the Output format — Single 3MF file (default) or Individual STL files — for OrcaSlicer. Generate the Swap Instructions to get the AMS loading order and pause plan (Copy to Clipboard for the slicer), and Download .zip to collect the files. See Export.
From here

How To Use — the full walkthrough of every screen and control.
How a Solve Works — what the pipeline does between pressing Solve and the predicted render.
Palette and Export — the two ends of the workflow in depth.
Settings — the controls behind the defaults (solve mode, resolution, preprocessing, color regions, and white cap).
How It Works — the model and the math under the whole thing.
Prisma Calibration — where personal model libraries are built and published.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.filePath: Prisma Lithophane Generator/How It Works/Color Model/Appearance provider.md
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.title: Appearance provider
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.content:
Before Prisma can solve an image it has to answer one question, over and over: given this stack of filament layers at these thicknesses, what color comes out when it is backlit? The appearance provider is the part of the system that answers it — the single color contract the rest of the solve is written against. Every stage that needs to know “what will this stack look like lit?” phrases the question the same way and gets back a predicted color, without having to know how the prediction was made.
Why it is a separate piece
There is more than one way to predict a stack’s color, and Prisma ships two. Routing every prediction through one agreed contract keeps the rest of the pipeline model-agnostic: the recipe search, the preview, the accuracy check, and the white cap all ask the same question and accept the same kind of answer, so the model underneath can be swapped without disturbing any of them. You choose the model once — the Appearance Model setting — and that choice flows through the whole solve.
The two models

Color Model v1 treats each filament as an independent sheet that dims and tints light by a fixed amount per thickness, and composes a stack by multiplying those transmissions. Order does not matter, and it needs nothing beyond the per-filament profiles already calibrated. This is The Transmission Model.
Color Model v2 — the default — is the interaction-aware model, built from photographs of real printed stacks. Because it models how layers interact, layer order matters and it cannot be reduced to per-filament profiles; it loads the v2 bundle from Generator’s one active published model library. This is The photo-stack v2 model.

The two differ in machinery but present the same interface, which is the whole reason the provider exists.
What asks it, and what it answers
You hand the provider a physical stack — a white base, the ordered color layers, and a white cap, each with a thickness — and it returns the color that stack produces, as backlit linear color (convertible to OKLab for distance work). Four parts of the pipeline rely on it, exactly the four its own setting names:

Recipe lookup — filling The Color LUT with the predicted color of thousands of candidate stacks.
Previews — turning the solved layers into the predicted backlit image shown on screen.
Diagnostics — predicting the solved result and measuring its color distance from the solve target, to report where the print lands and where it had to compromise.
Luminance-cap response — in Luminance mode, sampling the white filament’s behavior to build the cap that carries the image’s tone (see Solve Modes and White Cap).

Staying current
Every answer carries a fingerprint derived from the chosen model and its calibration data — the per-filament profiles for the spline model, or the published bundle and its correction data for the photo-stack model. The active published library cannot change underneath a running Generator. If you switch the appearance model or activate a different complete library, the fingerprint changes and Prisma treats an earlier solve as belonging to different model inputs rather than silently reusing it.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.filePath: Prisma Lithophane Generator/How It Works/Color Model/The Transmission Model.md
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.title: The Transmission Model
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.content:
Every color decision rests on one prediction: given a stack of filament layers at chosen thicknesses, what color comes out when light passes through? The transmission model is the simpler of Prisma’s two answers — the appearance model labeled Color Model v1 in the settings.
Light leaves the backlight white, then passes through a white base, one or more colored layers, and a white cap. Each layer absorbs part of the light; the model predicts the color that survives the full stack.
One filament, many colors
A filament does not have a single color — it has a family of colors indexed by thickness. A thin layer barely tints the light; piled on, it reads deep and saturated, closing toward black. Prisma learns this curve for each filament by measuring printed swatches, not from a physical absorption law. The measured transmission at a handful of thicknesses — the knots — is fitted, one curve per red, green, and blue channel, with a monotone cubic spline (PCHIP), so transmission can be read off at any thickness in between. Zero thickness returns perfectly clear (transmission 1). Past the thickest measured swatch the curve has no data, so there it falls back to a Beer-Lambert exponential extrapolated from the last two measurements — the only place a physical formula enters.
Stacking is multiplication
To get a full stack’s color you do not simulate light bouncing through layers — you multiply what each layer transmits, one channel at a time:
T_\text{total} = T_\text{base} \cdot \prod_i T_{\text{color},i} \cdot T_\text{cap} \quad (\text{per channel})
The base trims the light, each color trims it further, the cap trims it last. Because multiplication commutes, stacking order does not change the result — the solver only chooses how much of each filament, never the sequence.
Where filaments interact
Real filaments are not perfectly independent: stack two and they interact in ways a plain per-layer multiply cannot capture. This model corrects for that with pair corrections — small empirical per-channel multipliers measured for specific two-filament combinations. They are not applied in the multiply above; they enter when the catalog of candidate stacks (The Color LUT) is built, adjusting only two-layer combinations, and only when the Color corrections setting is on. They belong to this model alone; the alternative model carries its own separate correction.
That alternative is Color Model v2 — the photo-stack model — which predicts a whole stack’s color directly from photographs of real prints, capturing interaction without per-pair patches. It is the newer, context-aware option and now the generator’s default; Color Model v1 remains available and works from the per-filament profiles alone, with nothing else required. Both are reached the same way, through the Appearance provider.
Why it matters
This prediction is the loop the solver runs across the whole image: propose a stack, predict its color, measure the distance to the target, choose. Predictions and targets are compared in OKLab; colors no stack can reach are steered onto reachable ones first by Gamut mapping.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.filePath: Prisma Lithophane Generator/How It Works/Color Model/The photo-stack v2 model.md
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.title: The photo-stack v2 model
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.content:
Prisma has two ways to predict the color a backlit filament stack will show. The simpler one, The Transmission Model, treats each layer independently and multiplies their transmissions — a good first approximation, but real filaments are not that well-behaved. The photo-stack model is the context-aware alternative: it predicts a whole stack at once, accounting for how each layer’s contribution depends on what surrounds it. A blue layer reads differently depending on what sits above it, what sits below it, how much white caps it, and which other colors share the stack. That neighbor-dependence is the point, and it is why this model cannot be reduced to one curve per filament.
It is the default. The Appearance Model setting offers Color Model v1 (the transmission model) and Color Model v2 (this model, the default); a solve uses Color Model v1 only when you select it. Either way the model is reached through the Appearance provider.
Where it comes from
You do not build this model by hand. It is the product of a calibration fit: the calibration side of Prisma photographs real printed stacks under backlight, measures the colors they produce, and fits a runtime bundle plus a separate correction layer and supporting files. A separate Publish Models action then copies the exact current fit into a complete published model library.
There is a deliberate firewall. The research code that fits the model and the Generator that uses it share no mutable state at runtime: Generator reads only the immutable library selected in its Models menu, never Calibration’s working model directory. Refitting or editing Calibration cannot change a library already installed in Generator. To use newer data, publish a new library, install it, and activate it as one coherent unit. Generator validates the library’s schema and every manifested file before use.
What it computes during a solve
The model answers one question repeatedly: for this exact stack of layers at these thicknesses, what color comes out the back? It builds the answer in stages.
The first stage works in optical density — the negative log of transmission — where stacking layers is addition rather than multiplication. It sums each layer’s optical density and adds extra terms for the effects a plain multiply misses: white behind the colors darkening them more when color is present, the front white cap behaving differently from the base, and two distinct colors interacting. Converting that total back to color, through a floor that bounds how dark the stack can read, gives the base prediction. Strip the extra terms and the floor and this stage is the multiply model; everything added is the context-awareness.
The remaining stages refine that prediction in OKLab, each pulling it toward measured evidence: keeping lower color layers from washing out under what is stacked above them; for single-color stacks, reconciling the white cap against the base and leaning on direct measured sandwiches of that one color; and for two-color stacks, pulling the result toward the physically supported one-color endpoints it sits between.
The correction layer
On top of the staged prediction sits an optional correction layer — a final residual nudge learned from the calibration photos. For a given stack it gathers training samples from the same context, weights them by similarity, and shifts the prediction toward the residual those real measurements showed, within a bounded amount. It is governed by the Color corrections setting, the same checkbox that enables the transmission model’s pair corrections, with each model applying its own correction data.
These predicted colors fill the lookup table the solver searches (The Color LUT) and are compared in OKLab on the way to choosing layers in The Solve.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.filePath: Prisma Lithophane Generator/How It Works/Color Model/index.md
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.title: Color Model
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.content:
.hiw-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.hiw-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.hiw-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.hiw-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}ColorModelThe Color LUT


The color model is Prisma’s calibrated account of how filaments behave when stacked and backlit: given a stack of specific filaments at specific thicknesses, it predicts the color that stack transmits. Every decision the solver makes rests on these predictions, so the model’s accuracy sets the ceiling on how faithfully a print can reproduce an image. The filaments a given print may draw from are its Palette; the model can predict any stack they form.
The question the model answers
A lithophane is a layered stack — a white base, one or more colored layers, a white cap — lit from behind. The model answers one question, repeatedly: given this stack, these filaments at these thicknesses, what color emerges? The solver evaluates this many times while searching for the layer assignment that best matches each region of the image, and the same model renders the on-screen preview, which is its prediction displayed as an image.
Two models behind one boundary
Prisma began with the transmission model. Each filament has a transmission curve per color channel, measured at a handful of thicknesses from calibration swatches and interpolated smoothly between them; a stack’s transmission is the per-channel product of its layers’ curves. Because multiplication is order-independent, this model is insensitive to layer order, and it remains a clean, defensible baseline. See The Transmission Model.
Real filaments, however, interact in ways a pure product cannot express: the spectral character of one dye shifts how the next layer reads, a white cap washes out saturation, and order matters at the margins. Prisma’s production model is therefore the photo-stack model, fitted directly from photographs of printed stacks rather than from idealized per-layer curves. It carries explicit terms for white context, color-on-color interaction, cap attenuation, and ordering, and pairs them with a residual correction that pulls any remaining systematic error back toward the measured truth. See The photo-stack v2 model.
The two never collide because nothing in the system addresses either one directly. They sit behind an appearance provider — a single interface that accepts a physical stack description and returns a predicted color. One provider wraps the transmission model, another the photo-stack model; selecting the model in force is just selecting a provider, and nothing downstream changes. Each provider also carries a fingerprint identifying the model and its calibration, so a result computed under one model can never be silently reused under another. See Appearance provider.
What this feeds
Evaluating the model one stack at a time is expensive, so the solver does not query it afresh for every region. Instead Prisma samples the model across the palette’s filaments and thicknesses and bakes the answers into a lookup table the solver can read almost instantly; that table is built next, in The Color LUT. The model is also what the Camera Transform renders into a display color for previews, and what the Target Colors stage inverts to bring a source image into the model’s domain.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.filePath: Prisma Lithophane Generator/How It Works/Export/index.md
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.title: Export
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.content:
.hiw-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.hiw-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.hiw-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.hiw-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}Runs withSwapsExportSTL / 3MF


Export is the final stage. By now the generator has solved the image into a stack of filament layers and capped it with white. Export turns that abstract result — a set of per-point height maps, one per material — into a 3D model a slicer such as OrcaSlicer can open and print. Each export produces one chosen output: a set of STL files, or a single 3MF.
From height maps to solid geometry
The solve describes the lithophane as a stack of materials, each with a thickness at every point: a flat white base beneath everything, one map per color filament, and a white cap on top. Export builds these into solid, watertight shells. The base is a simple plate; each color material and the cap is a solid that rests on whatever lies beneath it, so the running floor rises as materials stack and the geometry reflects the true print order — even though, optically, order does not matter. Every footprint comes directly from the point grid and the physical spacing between points, so the printed panel matches the solved image one-to-one. A requested border adds a rectangular frame and insets the content within it.
A run with swaps (Runs with Swaps) adds two things. The white fill that tops each filament band up to its flat ceiling becomes real geometry — folded into the same white material as the cap, never a separate filament or file. And the stacking order stops being cosmetic: a mid-print swap is valid only if its band ends at one flat height everywhere, so the material order must match the solved swap plan exactly. Export enforces this — the order is checked against the plan, an audit confirms every band starts at its constant floor and every color stays inside its band, and a mismatch is refused rather than shipped.
Why the meshing must be careful
Naively triangulating a blocky height map produces a mesh that looks closed but is not reliably so. Where two raised regions meet at only a single corner or edge — a pinch contact — a slicer tends to weld the touching points and report a non-manifold solid, which can break slicing.
The generator therefore uses a rectilinear mesher designed for this kind of stepped field. It resolves each shared corner consistently, keeps touch-only contacts from being re-welded into pinches, and closes and orients each material shell before packaging it. These geometry rules preserve the solved dimensions while producing objects the slicer can treat as solids.
Field-derived vs exact geometry
How the white cap surface is built is a choice — the Mesh method setting — and it is where the field-derived vs solve-grid distinction lives.
The exact solved raster option builds every material, colors and cap alike, straight from the solve-grid height maps: one mesh cell per solved point. It is faithful to the solve but inherits its blockiness.
The default, field-derived white cap, rebuilds only the white cap — not from the blocky grid, but from continuous scalar fields, and on a grid several times finer than the solve grid (currently four times). This lets the cap surface carry smoother tonal relief than the solve resolution alone would allow — which matters most for the cap’s fine detail (see White Cap) — while the colored geometry stays locked to the solve grid, exactly where the color decisions were made. The reconstruction is the same mechanism in both solve modes: the cap is rebuilt from a single canonical target upper-surface field, filling the layers between the color ceiling and that surface with white. It also cleans sub-printable artifacts as it goes — tiny internal air voids and isolated white specks too small to print.
In both cases the white cap is meshed as two parts of the same material — a rigid guard that shields the color stacks’ exposed walls, and a freeform surface for the rest — and in a banded print the between-band white fill merges into this same object as a third part.
STL versus 3MF
Both formats describe the same geometry; they differ in how material is recorded. An STL carries only triangles, with no notion of material, so the STL export writes one file per object — white base, each color material, the cap, the border — into a shared folder, to be loaded together and assigned a filament by hand. A 3MF is a container that can record a material assignment per object: the 3MF export packs every object into one file and tags each with a filament slot, so the model opens with materials already assigned. The assignment is per object, not per print layer — every object is one filament — and objects printed in the same physical material, such as a shared white base and cap, collapse onto a single slot, so the slot count matches the real number of materials loaded. This is what lets a multicolor lithophane open ready to slice.
Alongside the geometry, export writes a manifest recording the panel dimensions and each object’s material assignment.
The swap-banded materials feeding this stage come from Runs with Swaps.
Figure for review

Export turns each solved material map into a solid shell, preserves the true print order, and packages the same geometry as either STL objects or a material-aware 3MF.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.filePath: Prisma Lithophane Generator/How It Works/How a Solve Works.md
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.title: How a Solve Works
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.content:
A solve is the whole journey from a photograph to a set of printable files. You pick a source image and a palette of filaments, press Solve, and Prisma decides — at every point in the image — which filaments to stack and how thick each layer should be, so that when the finished panel is backlit it reproduces the picture. This page walks the entire arc at a glance; each stage links down to the page that explains it properly.
The principle underneath is the one the whole system rests on: backlit filament behaves as a subtractive color filter, and thicker colored layers transmit less light, reading darker and more saturated. A solve is the search for the stack, at each location, whose transmitted color lands nearest the target while still being something a printer can build.
The arc, stage by stage
1. Condition the image and compute its targets. The source photo is first framed and graded, then run through an optional clean-up pass that steers it toward colors the chosen palette can actually reproduce. Every pixel is then translated into a perceptual color space and mapped onto the set of colors the palette can physically reach. What comes out is a field of target colors — the goal the solve aims at. See Target Colors.
2. Precompute what the palette can reach. In parallel, the palette’s calibrated color model is used to predict the backlit color of every printable stack of those filaments, and the results are gathered into a lookup structure — the joint color table. Because each candidate color can then be read from the table instead of recomputed from the optical model, the solve can score thousands of candidate recipes cheaply. See The Transmission Model and The Color LUT.
3. Solve a recipe per color region. The solve does not choose each pixel independently — that would yield a speckled, unbuildable field. Instead it partitions the image into contiguous regions of similar target color and picks one filament recipe per region, balancing color fidelity against clean geometry: a recipe is penalized both for missing its region’s color and for leaving a tall height step against its neighbors, since a sharp height jump prints as a visible seam. The result is a set of per-filament thickness maps.
4. Add the white cap. A white layer is authored over the colored stacks. It sets overall brightness and diffuses the backlight, and it reinforces the structural shell every viewing surface needs. The Solve Mode setting governs how it is built: in Color mode the cap follows the brightness each recipe implied; in Luminance mode it is reconstructed from the photo’s own luminance, carrying tone and fine relief like a classic lithophane. See White Cap.
5. Plan swaps when the palette exceeds the printer. If all colors fit, nothing extra is needed. Otherwise a scout solve divides the palette among flat, white-filled filament bands that can be loaded in sequence. See Runs with Swaps.
6. Export the print files. Finally the layered thickness field is turned into a printable mesh and written out as an STL or 3MF model the slicer can open.
One thing worth knowing about the code
When you press Solve in the web app, the color decomposition is performed by the staged backend — an ordered pipeline of stages that plan the color regions, choose recipes, and synthesize the cap. An older command-line engine still exists in the codebase and is described by some stale docstrings, but the web app never runs it; every web-app solve takes the staged path.
Where to go next
The stages above are conceptual signposts; follow any of them into its own page for the detail. The color decisions themselves live in The Solve; the optics that make them possible in The Transmission Model.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.filePath: Prisma Lithophane Generator/How It Works/Image Adjustments/index.md
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.title: Image Adjustments
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.content:
.hiw-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.hiw-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.hiw-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.hiw-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}SourceImageImageAdjustmentsPreprocessing


Image Adjustments are the alterations to a source image that modify it before it enters the lithophane generation pipeline. The appearance of the adjusted source image is what the pipeline will try to replicate in the finished, backlit lithophane. A source image is adjusted in two ways: its framing and its grading. The frame specifies what portion of the image is used, how it is oriented, and what size it will be when printed. The grade is the set of tonal and color transformations applied to the frame.
Adjusting a source image is purely about how the finished product should look. This is distinct from Preprocessing, where the image may instead be modified to suit the lithophane generation process itself, or to make the printed result more amenable to printing.
Adjustments are non-destructive
Image adjustments do not modify the source image file. Each setting is stored as a parameter. The browser renders a live preview by approximating those parameters with display-side filters, so the preview is only an approximation of the adjusted image the pipeline will actually act on. The framed and graded raster is reconstructed from the original source image only when a solve or export runs. This keeps any quirk of browser rendering from affecting the lithophane itself.
The frame
Beyond selecting which portion of the source image is used, the frame fixes how pixels on screen relate to the lithophane as a physical object. The frame’s dimensions are the dimensions of the printed lithophane. A lithophane should not be rescaled in a slicer: scaling the model alters the layer thicknesses, and it is those thicknesses that produce the image, so a rescaled print no longer reproduces it.
The frame’s dimensions, together with the solve pitch — the physical spacing between the points the pipeline solves for — also fix the print-scale raster: the version of the image the pipeline actually operates on, and the one shown in the preview. Working at print scale keeps the pipeline from solving for detail finer than the printer can render. That raster can look slightly blocky, but the blockiness is an honest depiction of how the image will resolve once printed.
The grade
The grade is a fixed-order chain over the sRGB raster:

Grayscale, if black-and-white mode is selected, applied first so every later operation acts on a luminance image.
Exposure, contrast, and saturation, as multiplicative gains of the form 1 + v for v ∈ [−1, 1]. Contrast pivots about the image’s mean gray level; saturation interpolates between the image and its grayscale.
Tint, a recolor toward a chosen hue that preserves each pixel’s luminance. The target hue is rescaled so its luminance (Rec. 709 weights) matches the pixel’s, then blended in by the tint strength. The effect shifts chroma without altering brightness, and is skipped in black-and-white mode.
Highlights and shadows, additive offsets gated by a luminance ramp. Highlights act only above mid-gray and shadows only below, each ramping to full strength at the extreme — at most ±80 levels on the 0–255 scale. This is a masked offset, not a tone curve.
Temperature, an opposing per-channel shift: warm raises red and lowers blue, cool the reverse, by up to ±30 levels.

The result is clamped to eight bits per channel. This graded raster is the image the rest of the pipeline receives, beginning with Preprocessing and then The Solve.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.filePath: Prisma Lithophane Generator/How It Works/Palette/index.md
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.title: Palette
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.content:
.hiw-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.hiw-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.hiw-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.hiw-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}PaletteThe Color LUT


A palette is the set of filaments chosen for a print. The Color Model can predict any stack of filaments, but a given lithophane draws only from its palette, plus the fixed white used for the base and the cap. The palette is the working set the rest of the pipeline is restricted to: The Color LUT enumerates only stacks the palette allows, and every solved recipe uses only its filaments.
What a palette holds
A palette is a small list of colored filaments together with the white assigned to the base and cap. When every color fits beside white in the printer’s loaded slots, they remain available throughout the print. A larger palette requires Runs with Swaps, which divides the colors among fixed-height bands. Restricting the prediction table and solve to the selected working set keeps the search tractable and the preview honest about what the print will actually use.
Palette suggestion
Choosing filaments by hand is hard, because the best palette for an image depends on how its colors combine when stacked, not only on which colors appear in it. Prisma can suggest a palette automatically from the source image.
The suggester works in the perceptual color space the solve uses. It first summarizes the image as a set of weighted color clusters — representative colors, each weighted by how much of the image it covers — so common colors count for more than rare ones. For each candidate filament it precomputes the colors that filament can produce alone, at every thickness and a sampled spread of caps. It then scores whole palettes: every combination of the allowed size is evaluated against the weighted clusters, and the best few are kept — only when the number of combinations grows very large does it fall back to a seeded greedy search refined by local swaps. Because stacked filaments make colors that neither makes alone — a cyan over a yellow yields greens — each palette’s reachable set includes sampled two-filament pairs, so a pair that unlocks a needed mixed color is credited for it. The finalists are then rescored once more with sparsely sampled three-filament stacks, so a color reachable only by mixing three filaments is credited before the final ranking.
The search does not stop at one palette size. It sweeps the sizes each extra filament reload makes possible, keeps the best palette of each size, and recommends the smallest size whose remaining gap a larger one does not close by a worthwhile margin per added color — bigger is suggested only when bigger genuinely earns it. The result is a ranked shortlist rather than a single answer — the final choice is left to the user. Each candidate carries an estimated color error, and the default ranking also weighs worst-case misses, so a palette with one badly-missed region ranks below one that is uniformly close. The same Color and Luminance distinction the solve uses applies here: a Color-target suggestion aims directly at the photo’s colors, while a Luminance-target one emphasizes the image’s vivid regions and largely ignores its brightness structure — brightness is the white cap’s job in that mode.
Figure for review

Broad color reach is not the same as useful coverage. A palette tailored to the source image can place more reachable stack colors near the colors the image actually uses.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.filePath: Prisma Lithophane Generator/How It Works/Preprocessing/Preprocessing Modules.md
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.title: Preprocessing Modules
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.content:
The five preprocessing modules, and what each one actually does to the image. The chain they run in — fixed order, single common working space — is described on Preprocessing; the settings-drawer presets and fields are covered in Preprocessing Module Settings. All five ship disabled.
Noise Reduction
An edge-preserving smoother. Each pixel is replaced by a weighted average of its neighborhood, where a neighbor’s weight falls off with two distances at once: how far away it is, and how different its color is. Nearby, similar-colored pixels blend; pixels across a strong color edge contribute almost nothing. Grain and sensor noise — small, low-contrast fluctuations — average away, while real boundaries survive untouched.
The three fields map directly onto the mechanism: Filter radius sets the neighborhood size, Color similarity sets how large a color difference still blends, and Spatial reach sets how quickly influence decays with distance. The filter is purely spatial and palette-free; it neither knows nor cares what will be printed.
Print-Scale Smoothing
The same edge-preserving filter, but its scale is anchored to the printer rather than to pixels. The anchor is a physical feature scale of twice the nozzle diameter — 0.4 mm at the standard 0.2 mm nozzle, encoding that a reliably printed feature is about two extrusion widths wide — converted into solve-grid pixels through the solve resolution. Smoothing at that radius removes exactly the detail the print could never carry, before the solver spends effort chasing it.
Feature scale multiplies the anchor: below 1 preserves more detail, above 1 flattens beyond print scale. Color similarity works as in Noise Reduction, and Passes repeats the filter, strengthening the flattening at some cost in edge crispness.
Flat-Area Smoothing
A total-variation smoother: it seeks an image that stays close to the source while minimizing the total amount of change from pixel to pixel. Minimizing that quantity has a characteristic effect — gradual texture and gentle gradients collapse into flat patches, while genuine edges, which are worth their cost, remain. At stronger settings the result reads as deliberately graphic, closer to a screen print than a photograph.
Flattening strength is the weight on the flatness objective. Scale strength to print width ties that weight to the same nozzle-derived feature scale used by Print-Scale Smoothing, so the flattening tracks what is printable. Flattening mode picks what gets flattened: lightness only (texture goes, color stays), lightness and color together in perceptual coordinates, or all three color channels directly. Iteration limit caps the optimization.
Palette Tone Fit
The first palette-aware module. The palette determines the darkest and lightest the print can actually go; a photograph usually spans more. Rather than letting the out-of-range tones clip, this module remaps the image’s lightness into the achievable range with a smooth three-anchor curve: the image’s shadow and highlight anchors — set as percentiles of its lightness distribution via Shadow anchor and Highlight anchor — map onto the palette’s achievable black and white, with a midpoint whose placement Midtone curve bends lighter or darker. Beyond the anchors the mapping continues linearly and clamps at the achievable limits.
Only lightness is rewritten; hue and saturation pass through unchanged. Tone fit strength blends between the original and the remapped lightness, from no effect to the full fit. With no palette selected — or a palette whose tonal range collapses — the module does nothing.
Palette Saturation Fit
A palette’s reachable saturation is not one number: it varies with hue and with lightness — a palette can be rich in reds and starved in cyans, and richer in the midtones than in the shadows. This module reads the palette’s map of maximum reachable saturation across hue and lightness, and for each pixel looks up the bound at that pixel’s own hue and lightness, interpolating around the hue wheel and across the lightness range. The bound is served generously — biased high rather than low — so real saturation is never destroyed here; anything still beyond the palette’s true reach is caught later by gamut mapping.
Compression is a soft knee against that bound. Below Compression start — a fraction of that local bound — colors pass through unchanged. Above it, saturation follows a smooth saturating curve that approaches the bound but never crosses it; Compression softness sets how gradually the curve bends. Hue and lightness are preserved exactly — only saturation is scaled — so an over-vivid color moves straight inward toward what the palette can print rather than shifting toward a different color. A palette with no usable chroma information leaves the image untouched.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.filePath: Prisma Lithophane Generator/How It Works/Preprocessing/index.md
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.title: Preprocessing
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.content:
.hiw-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.hiw-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.hiw-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.hiw-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}ImageAdjustmentsPreprocessingTargetColorsNoiseReductionPrint-ScaleSmoothingFlat-AreaSmoothingPaletteTone FitPaletteSaturation Fit


Preprocessing is the optional first step of the lithophane generation pipeline. It occurs after Image Adjustments and before the image is reduced to a set of Target Colors. Its operators modify the image to make it better suited for conversion into a lithophane: they either alter the spatial variability of color within the image, or adjust the image’s tone and color to better match the chosen palette. Whether preprocessing should be used at all — and with what settings — depends on the source image and on user preference. By default, no operators are enabled.
The mismatch it resolves
A stack of translucent filament, backlit, is a bounded medium. It spans a limited gamut and a limited dynamic range, and it reproduces detail only down to the size of a printed feature. A photograph routinely exceeds all three: colors more saturated than any stack can make, a contrast range wider than a panel can transmit, and sensor noise and fine texture that carry no information once the image is quantized into layers but that resurface as visible speckle. Preprocessing reconciles the image with the medium before the solver commits to it, so the solver is not forced to chase content that was never reproducible.
Preprocessing operators
Five operators are available, in two groups.
Reducing spatial detail the print cannot carry:

Noise Reduction (denoise) — removes small image noise so color regions come out less fragmented.
Print-Scale Smoothing (flatten) — smooths features down to the scale the printer can reproduce, yielding larger, simpler color regions.
Flat-Area Smoothing (flatten) — flattens gradual texture into broad areas, a more graphic look at stronger settings.

Fitting tone and color to the palette:

Palette Tone Fit (tone) — compresses the image’s tonal range into the range the palette can reproduce.
Palette Saturation Fit (color) — softly pulls colors the palette cannot reach inward, preserving hue.

How each module actually transforms the image is explained in Preprocessing Modules.
The preprocessing chain
Any number of operators may be enabled at once. When several are, they are applied in a fixed order — denoise, then flatten, then tone, then color — the same order they appear in the settings, regardless of the order they were switched on. When consecutive operators work in different color spaces, the image is converted between them through a single common space, sRGB in 32-bit float, rather than through direct conversions between every possible pair. Preprocessing never modifies the source image; its result is passed only to Target Colors.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.filePath: Prisma Lithophane Generator/How It Works/Runs with Swaps/index.md
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.title: Runs with Swaps
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.content:
.hiw-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.hiw-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.hiw-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.hiw-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}White CapRuns withSwapsExport


A normal run keeps every colored filament loaded from the first color layer to the last. When the palette exceeds the active printer’s color slots, Prisma instead divides those filaments among a sequence of fixed-height bands. The printer pauses at each band boundary so the next set of colors can be loaded.
This happens automatically during the solve. There is no user-facing planning choice and no alternate swap method.
Why the bands must be flat
A slicer pause occurs at one Z height across the entire panel. The lower set of filaments therefore has to finish at the same height everywhere before any slot can be reassigned.
The colored stacks do not naturally end on a flat plane. Prisma fills the unused height inside each band with the same white used for the base and cap. Every point then reaches the band’s fixed ceiling, making the next set of colors physically printable above it.
That white fill is also the central compromise. It changes the light passing through the color stack, usually making some combinations lighter or less saturated. The bands consume part of Max Total Thickness as well, leaving less freedom for the cap and color recipes. A swap run is therefore more constrained than an otherwise identical run with every color continuously available; it cannot improve the underlying optical search space, even when the larger palette makes the final result better than a smaller no-swap palette.
The scout solve
Prisma cannot choose useful band heights from filament names alone. It first performs a reduced-resolution scout solve with the full palette and no bands. The scout estimates how much of each filament the image wants and where those thicknesses occur.
The palette is already in the canonical dark-first print order. Prisma considers valid ways to assign those filaments to the available color slots across the required number of bands. Each candidate band’s height is estimated from almost all of its active scout usage and quantized to whole printed layers. The chosen plan minimizes total band height first and predicted white fill second.
This is why filaments that are heavily used in different parts of the image may share a compact band, while filaments that need to stack thickly in the same places tend to require more height.
The final constrained solve
The scout does not become the printed result. Once the band plan is fixed, Prisma builds new color lookup tables whose recipes obey those bands and already include the required white fill. The full-resolution solve then runs against those tables.
Including the fill during the final solve matters: the solver evaluates the color that the physically printable, white-filled stack will transmit. It does not solve an unconstrained image and patch the bands in afterward.
The completed run stores the band assignments, their exact layer counts, and the resulting pause heights. That plan is part of the run just like its palette and cap settings.
From bands to Swap Instructions
Each pause height is the white-base thickness plus the completed band heights below it. On Export, Swap Instructions turns the stored plan into:

the initial filament assigned to each slot;
the Z height for every slicer pause;
which filament to unload and load in each affected slot; and
which slots remain unchanged.

Export presents the plan; it does not optimize it again. If the active printer has fewer usable slots than the completed solve assumed, the plan is incompatible and the run must be solved again with the correct printer configuration.
The practical workflow and its trade-offs are covered in Runs with Swaps under How To Use. The stored bands then flow into Export like any other solved geometry.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.filePath: Prisma Lithophane Generator/How It Works/Settings/Color Solver.md
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.title: Settings: Color Solver
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.content:
Color Solver settings control two related decisions: which printable recipes are considered good matches, and which solve points initially share one recipe decision. The first group changes recipe search; the second changes the region map on which the staged solve begins.
Recipe Search
The Appearance Model supplies predicted colors for every candidate stack. Color corrections select the calibrated correction layer associated with that model. Max colors per region limits how many distinct colored filaments one recipe may contain, reducing or expanding the candidate set before matching begins.
Out-of-gamut handling changes unreachable target colors before recipe lookup. Nearest reachable color selects the closest modeled stack color directly. Preserve hue reduces saturation, and adjusts lightness only when necessary, so the target moves without rotating to another hue. Color mismatch tolerance decides when that remapping is required. Chroma weight then changes the relative cost of lightness error and chromatic error during matching; it does not alter the source image.
Region Construction
The same image can be partitioned three ways before recipes are chosen:

Image regions use an image-segmentation method that permits unequal, irregular regions. Strong image structure tends to become a region boundary, while locally similar areas can stay together over a larger span.
Superpixels produce compact, approximately even regions whose borders can still bend around image edges. They offer a more regular patchwork than Image regions without becoming independent of the picture.
Fixed grid assigns uniform square planning cells. It is predictable and structurally simple, but an image edge has no influence on where a cell ends.

Color region target sets the intended physical width of these initial regions. Internally it is converted to solve-grid points and raised when necessary to meet the printer’s minimum line-length and extrusion-width floor. Region planning scale builds the initial map on a coarser raster and expands it back to the solve grid, trading edge fidelity for broader regions and lower planning cost.
Regions are initial commitments, not permanent walls. Local recipe corrections can replace small areas inside a region when another recipe improves the target match enough; printability checks then grow useful corrections into printable footprints or return them to the owning region.
Boundary mutation
Boundary mutation operates after the initial region recipes and local corrections. At every four-connected recipe boundary, each solve point tests only the recipe immediately across that boundary. If the neighboring recipe lowers that point’s modeled color error, the point becomes part of a candidate run for that specific original-and-borrowed recipe pair.
Candidates are accepted as connected boundary runs rather than isolated points. Mutation current-dE percentile can restrict testing to the worst current boundary errors. Mutation min gain requires the run’s average improvement to clear a threshold. Mutation min contact requires enough shared edge with the region supplying the borrowed recipe. Together these controls let a contour move where the evidence is coherent while rejecting weakly attached flecks.
One Mutation pass can move a recipe boundary by one solve point. Later passes recompute candidates and error thresholds against the newly mutated map, allowing a contour to advance farther while stopping early when no accepted improvement remains. Mutation never invents a new stack: every accepted point borrows a recipe already present directly beside it.
For the drawer controls and day-to-day guidance, see Color Solver Settings.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.filePath: Prisma Lithophane Generator/How It Works/Settings/Essentials.md
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.title: Settings: Essentials
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.content:
The Essentials settings establish the coordinate system and physical envelope every later stage must obey. They do not merely resize the final mesh: they determine the raster the image is sampled onto, how thickness becomes printed layers, and how much vertical space remains for color and the white cap.
Solve Pitch and the working grid
Solve Pitch is the physical spacing between neighboring solve points. Together with the framed print dimensions, it determines the width and height of the working raster. A smaller pitch creates more target points and can preserve finer image structure, but every later image, region, recipe, and height field becomes larger. The image sampling pitch and solver pitch are a coupled pair in the live pipeline, so there is no hidden finer image grid behind the solve grid.
Color region target is independent of Solve Pitch. Pitch says how far apart solve points are; the region target says how many of those points should normally share an initial recipe decision. The effective region target is never allowed below the active printer’s feature-size floor.
The vertical budget
Max Total Thickness is a ceiling shared by the white base, colored layers, boundary cap, and detail cap. Increasing it can expose more printable color recipes and more cap authority, but no stage owns the added height exclusively. A thicker color stack leaves less room above it; a larger cap reservation narrows the color-plus-cap combinations that fit.
Base Thickness is spent first and uniformly. The remaining height becomes the working budget for color and cap. The white base has no per-point thickness map because it is constant across the panel.
Layer Height is quantization
The solver expresses printable thicknesses as whole layers. Layer Height therefore defines the vertical step size of every recipe and cap decision, not only an export preference. A smaller value offers more possible optical thicknesses within the same budget; a larger value makes the set coarser. Slicing at a different layer height changes the physical recipe and invalidates the predicted color.
White materials and Solve Mode
The selected White Base/Cap Filament supplies calibrated optical behavior to the Color Model. White is not treated as a neutral mathematical constant: its measured transmission influences every predicted stack and the Luminance-mode cap response.
Solve Mode applies a coordinated preset rather than switching to a separate color solver. Color and Luminance use the same target colors and recipe machinery, but assign different authority to the white cap and reserve the thickness budget differently. See Solve Modes for the full mechanism.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.filePath: Prisma Lithophane Generator/How It Works/Settings/Preprocessing.md
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.title: Settings: Pre-processing
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.content:
Pre-processing settings alter the print-scale image before Target Colors are built. They do not change the source file, and they do not repair a solve afterward. Their purpose is to remove image variation the print cannot carry or to move the image toward the selected palette before recipe lookup begins.
Two kinds of intervention
Noise Reduction, Print-Scale Smoothing, and Flat-Area Smoothing change spatial variation. Noise Reduction uses color and distance to average small fluctuations while retaining strong edges. Print-Scale Smoothing anchors that edge-preserving operation to the printer’s physical feature scale. Flat-Area Smoothing instead minimizes gradual pixel-to-pixel variation, producing broad patches at stronger settings.
Palette Tone Fit and Palette Saturation Fit are palette-aware. Tone Fit remaps image lightness into the palette’s printable dark-to-light range while preserving hue and saturation. Saturation Fit applies a soft knee at the palette’s hue- and lightness-dependent saturation boundary, pulling over-vivid colors inward while preserving hue and lightness.
The detailed algorithms and the meaning of every Custom field are covered in Preprocessing Modules.
Fixed order, independent enablement
Modules are independently enabled, but their execution order is fixed:
Noise Reduction → Print-Scale Smoothing → Flat-Area Smoothing → Palette Tone Fit → Palette Saturation Fit
This order first removes irrelevant spatial variation, then fits the surviving image to the palette. Presets are named parameter bundles for one module; choosing Custom exposes the same parameters directly and does not change the module’s place in the chain.
Resample kernel
The Resample kernel acts before the module chain when the framed image is reduced to the solve grid. Lanczos retains more high-frequency contrast and therefore hands the modules a sharper raster. Area integrates source pixels over each destination point, handing them a more strongly anti-aliased raster. Once the print-scale raster exists, all enabled modules operate on that same grid.
For when to enable each module and practical starting values, see Preprocessing Module Settings.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.filePath: Prisma Lithophane Generator/How It Works/Settings/White Cap.md
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.title: Settings: White Cap
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.content:
White Cap settings divide the available white thickness between a continuous structural surface and localized additional relief. They do not sit after the color solve as a cosmetic filter: cap thickness participates in predicted appearance and shares the same total-height budget as the colored recipes.
Minimum coverage
Min Cap Layers is converted to a physical thickness by multiplying it by Layer Height. The product gate quantizes the minimum upward to a whole layer and enforces at least one white layer above every color stack. This minimum belongs to the continuous boundary cap.
Boundary cap modes
In Color mode, Boundary cap chooses how the upper surface is shaped:

Detail Aware begins from the optically preferred per-region cap and allows smoothing only while the modeled appearance remains within Appearance budget. It keeps the continuous boundary cap structurally sufficient and leaves more localized correction to the detail cap.
Smooth prioritizes a clean, continuous upper surface. Smoothing radius sets the physical neighborhood over which the upper profile is smoothed; image and recipe edges reduce that smoothing locally. The underside still follows the color stacks exactly.

Luminance mode forces the smooth boundary-cap path because broad image tone is authored directly into that surface.
Detail authority
The detail-cap stage always runs. Detail depth sets the maximum number of whole white layers it may add above the boundary cap; it is an authority limit, not a requested thickness. At each point the stage keeps an added layer only when the Appearance Model predicts an improvement, and later printability checks may suppress or enlarge features. A depth of zero leaves the stage no additional layers to place, but does not bypass the stage or the required boundary coverage.
In Luminance mode, Shading balance divides the image-derived tonal structure between the smooth boundary cap and the detail cap. Moving toward Smooth gives the broad surface more of the luminance range; moving toward Detail lowers that broad authority and reserves more of the remaining target for localized relief.
The complete cap construction, including Color and Luminance differences, is described in White Cap. For operational guidance, see White Cap Settings.
