prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.filePath: Prisma Lithophane Generator/How It Works/Settings/index.md
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.title: Settings: How They Work
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.content:
Settings are a cross-cutting view of the generation pipeline. Some establish the print’s physical limits, some transform the image before solving, and others alter how recipes, regions, and the white cap are constructed. The Settings drawer explains what to choose; these pages explain what each group changes inside the pipeline and why its tradeoffs appear in the result.
The pages mirror the four sections in the drawer while using distinct titles to avoid collisions with the How To pages:

Settings: Essentials — the physical grid, vertical thickness budget, layer quantization, white materials, and Solve Mode preset.
Settings: Pre-processing — resampling, the fixed module chain, and the distinction between spatial simplification and palette fitting.
Settings: Color Solver — recipe matching, region construction, local recipe corrections, and Boundary mutation.
Settings: White Cap — the continuous boundary cap, detail-cap authority, smoothing, and Luminance-mode Shading balance.

When settings take effect
The browser keeps a mutable settings collection, but a solve receives a frozen snapshot. Changes therefore apply to the next solve and cannot alter a solve already in progress or a result already stored. Settings profiles save and restore that collection; they do not create a second processing path.
Several product guarantees are enforced independently of the visible controls. The source always enters through the Camera Transform, the detail-cap stage always runs, and the printability gates always protect color regions and white-cap features. User settings tune the work those stages perform, but cannot bypass those guarantees.
For the operational controls, profile workflow, and recommended starting values, see Settings.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.filePath: Prisma Lithophane Generator/How It Works/Target Colors/Camera Transform.md
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.title: Camera Transform
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.content:
The Camera Transform is the calibrated bridge between two ways of describing a color: the transmission a filament stack passes — the quantity the Color Model reasons in — and the display color a camera or screen renders that transmission as. Prisma crosses between the two constantly: to show a predicted print on screen, and to translate a source image into targets the model can match. The Camera Transform is what makes those crossings faithful to how the calibration photographs were actually captured.
Two directions
The transform is defined in the forward direction: given a stack’s predicted transmission, it produces the display color that transmission appears as. This is what turns a solve into the on-screen preview, and the form in which the model’s appearance predictions are expressed.
Its inverse runs the other way: given a display color, it recovers the transmission that would appear as that color. This inverse is what the Model-domain ingress step uses to carry each source pixel from screen color into the model’s transmission domain, so that targets and predictions can be compared in the same terms. Because inverting the transform for every pixel would be costly, the inverse is precomputed once as a dense lookup grid and sampled.
How it is calibrated
The transform is fitted from calibration data — printed swatches photographed under the backlight — so it captures the specific response of that camera and lighting rather than an idealized one. The fit is a color-correction matrix, expanded so it can absorb the nonlinear way a camera renders saturated colors, followed by a smooth, monotonic curve per channel. Calibration stores one current working transform. Generator sees it only after all three model families and the filament catalog are published together as a new immutable library, and keeps using its selected library until you explicitly activate another one.
Because everything the solver compares passes through this transform, a print is only as faithful as the transform is accurate. It is the link that makes the model’s transmission-domain reasoning correspond to what a viewer actually sees.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.filePath: Prisma Lithophane Generator/How It Works/Target Colors/Gamut mapping.md
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.title: Gamut mapping
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.content:
With a given set of filaments, only so many colors can be made by stacking them and shining light through. That reachable set is the palette’s gamut, and a source image almost always asks for colors outside it — a saturated neon, a deep electric blue, a vivid orange that no stack of these filaments backlit can reach. Gamut mapping resolves this before the solver runs: it finds the targets that lie outside the gamut and moves each toward a color the palette can make, so the solver works from a set of reachable targets instead of chasing ones that do not exist.
Doing this first makes the compromise deliberate. Left alone, the solver would still produce something for an impossible color — whatever reachable color happened to score best — but the result would drift unpredictably. Deciding up front how to give up the unreachable part keeps the colors that matter recognizable.
Where the boundary is
The reachable set is not abstract: it is The Color LUT, the catalog of every printable filament stack and the color each one produces. A target counts as reachable when some catalog color lies within a small tolerance of it; a target farther than that from every printable color is out of gamut. The catalog’s outer surface — the convex hull of all those colors in OKLab — serves as the projection surface for the default mode below. (The print’s white is handled separately, below, and comes from the Appearance provider rather than the catalog.)
Two ways to compromise
The Out-of-gamut handling setting picks the strategy, and the two differ in what they protect:

Nearest reachable color (the default) projects the target straight onto the closest point of the gamut’s outer hull. All three axes can move — lightness shifts a little along with the color — but the result lands closest overall to the original, giving the lowest color error along saturated edges. One deliberate exception: a flagged target that already sits inside the hull is left in place — pushing it outward to the boundary would invent a more saturated color — and the solver’s own nearest-color matching handles it instead.
Preserve hue pulls the color inward along a ray toward gray, scaling its vividness down by a single factor — the hue never shifts. Lightness holds too, except when the target is darker or lighter than the print can reach, in which case it yields exactly as far as needed. It never makes a target worse: if no point along the ray comes within tolerance, the target is replaced only if the best point found still improves it. This protects hue and, as far as possible, brightness — which matters most for things like skin tones — at the cost of visibly muting strongly saturated regions.

Both modes decide which targets to touch the same way: a target is out of gamut when no printable color lies within the allowed tolerance of it, measured as plain color difference (the Chroma weight setting does not bend this test). That tolerance is the Color mismatch tolerance setting — the same color-difference threshold the solve later uses to judge coverage, not a gamut-only knob. The modes differ only in where a flagged target is moved.
Re-anchoring to paper white
Separately, the White-point rescale option re-anchors every target to the print’s actual white — the slightly-off-white seen through the thinnest white stack, rather than the ideal white of the source image. It is off by default. When on, it predicts that paper white from the Appearance provider and scales every target toward it one channel at a time, a von Kries adaptation. It does nothing when there is no white base or the print’s white is already neutral. Because it shifts the whole image toward the real paper white, predicted previews read slightly darker and warmer with it enabled.
All of this happens in OKLab, so “nearest” means nearest as the eye judges it. Gamut mapping runs after the catalog is built and just before the layers are solved — see The Solve.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.filePath: Prisma Lithophane Generator/How It Works/Target Colors/Model-domain ingress.md
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.title: Model-domain ingress
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.content:
The colors in a source photo are not the colors the solver should aim for. They have to be translated first. This page covers that translation and why it exists.
Two color domains
Everything Prisma knows about its filaments came in through a camera: swatches were printed, backlit on a lightbox, and photographed. So the color a stack of layers is predicted to produce is expressed in the domain the camera handed back — the model domain, a transmission-color space anchored to those measurements. The entire solve lives there: the targets it chases, the colors it predicts, the distances it measures.
A source photo lives in a different domain — ordinary display sRGB, the encoding any image on a screen uses. Taken at face value its numbers would point the solver at the wrong targets, because the filament knowledge was never expressed in display sRGB. The two domains do not coincide.
Pulling the photo in
Before anything else reads the image, ingress maps every pixel from display sRGB into the model domain. It is not a gamma curve: it is a trilinear lookup into a baked 33×33×33 table that inverts the calibrated Camera Transform. Where the Camera Transform carries a model-domain color out to its photographed display appearance, ingress runs that mapping backward to carry a display color in. After ingress the image and the filament model finally speak the same language, and the targets the solver chases are these translated colors (measured in OKLab).
Ingress is not optional — it is what makes the calibrated filament model apply to the actual picture, and every solve runs it. (Earlier builds exposed an advanced switch that skipped the table and fell back to a legacy gamma-2.2 target domain for side-by-side comparison; that control has been removed.)
Coming back out
The reverse direction matters for previews. The solve produces colors in the model domain, which are not meant for a screen, so a preview of what the lit print will look like is made by running the prediction forward through the Camera Transform to its true backlit appearance. This happens only when the preview images are baked. The Appearance provider supplies the model-domain prediction that feeds this step; it does not itself produce the displayed appearance.
Both directions come from one calibrated, fingerprinted Camera Transform built by the calibration app. If that artifact is missing, malformed, or its contents do not match its recorded hashes, Prisma refuses to solve and tells you to rebuild it — it never silently guesses. For the transform’s internals in both directions, see Camera Transform.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.filePath: Prisma Lithophane Generator/How It Works/Target Colors/OKLab.md
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.title: OKLab
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.content:
The solver has to answer one question millions of times: how far is this candidate stack’s color from the color this pixel asked for? Distance between raw red, green, and blue values is a poor judge of that, because equal steps in RGB do not look equally different to the eye. A small numeric gap in one part of the range is glaring; a larger gap elsewhere is invisible. A solver that trusted RGB distance would spend its effort on differences no one can see and ignore ones that stand out.
OKLab is a perceptual color space built so that equal numeric distance corresponds to roughly equal perceived difference. Every color becomes a point on three axes — one lightness axis and two color-opponent axes — arranged so that the straight-line distance between two points tracks how different they look. The transform from linear RGB is fixed: a 3×3 matrix into an intermediate cone-response space, a cube-root compression, and a second 3×3 matrix out. Lightness here runs on a 0–1 scale, not the 0–100 of textbook Lab.
Why the solver lives here
Putting both sides into OKLab turns “find the closest printable color” into ordinary nearest-point search. Prisma converts the image’s per-pixel targets into OKLab once, up front, and stores every candidate filament stack’s predicted color in OKLab too — that is what fills The Color LUT. Choosing a recipe for a region then reduces to finding the stored point nearest the target. The distance used is plain, unweighted Euclidean:
\Delta E = \sqrt{(\Delta L)^2 + (\Delta a)^2 + (\Delta b)^2}
That same distance, taken between each pixel’s target and the color the solved stack is predicted to produce, is the solve’s quality measure. The headline figure is the root-mean-square of those per-pixel distances over the image; the interface reports it as RMSE % — the RMS distance times 100 — so a raw OKLab error of 0.03 shows on screen as about 3. Lower is better, everywhere.
The one control that bends the metric
By default the three axes count equally. The Chroma weight control changes that, but only inside the recipe search: it divides the lightness axis by its value, so a setting above 1 makes the search favor hue and saturation over brightness when deciding which stored stack is nearest. It reshapes which recipe gets chosen, nothing more — the quality number that comes back is always measured in true, unweighted OKLab, so it stays comparable whatever the weight. Aside from this, the metric is fixed; nothing else lets you change it.
A caution on comparing numbers
This is the generator’s yardstick. The calibration half of Prisma scores its own color accuracy with a different one — CIE76 difference in CIE Lab, whose lightness runs 0–100. These are different metrics in different spaces on different scales, so a generator figure and a calibration figure are not comparable even when they happen to print similar digits. Within a single solve, though, the OKLab distance is the consistent measure of how close the print lands.
The space underlies everything the solver touches: how targets first arrive (Model-domain ingress), what happens when one cannot be reached (Gamut mapping), and how recipes are scored (The Solve).

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.filePath: Prisma Lithophane Generator/How It Works/Target Colors/index.md
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.title: Target Colors
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.content:
.hiw-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.hiw-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.hiw-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.hiw-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}PreprocessingTargetColorsThe Solve


After Preprocessing, the image is still an sRGB array — a description of how to render the picture on a screen. That on-screen appearance is the goal: it is what the lithophane should look like when backlit. The solver must reproduce it, but it cannot operate on screen colors directly. This stage turns each pixel into a target the solver can match, through a change of domain and a change of metric, then projects any unreachable target onto what the palette can actually produce.
The transmission domain
The color model is built from calibration data — printed swatches photographed under a backlight. It does not reason about screen colors; it reasons about transmission, the fraction of light a stack passes per channel. Transmission is intrinsic to the filaments, independent of the appearance any particular backlight produces, and it is the quantity the model both predicts and composes. A screen sRGB value is not a transmission, so each pixel must be carried into the transmission domain before the model can be asked to match it.
That conversion is ingress, and it always runs. It applies the inverse of the model’s calibrated appearance transform, the Camera Transform — the mapping that turns a predicted transmission into a displayed, backlit-looking color, run backward — giving the transmission that would reproduce each pixel’s appearance. After ingress, the targets and the model’s predictions describe the same physical quantity, which is the only basis on which the solver can compare them. See Model-domain ingress.
Perceptual distance
The solver selects a recipe for each region by minimizing color difference, and raw transmission coordinates are a poor yardstick for that: equal numeric steps do not correspond to equal perceived change. So the transmission-domain targets are re-expressed in OKLab, a space constructed so that straight-line distance tracks perceived difference (a separation of about 0.02 is roughly one just-noticeable difference). The model’s catalog of predicted stack colors is expressed in the same OKLab space, so a nearest-color search compares like with like and “nearest” means perceptually nearest. Every later color comparison happens here. See OKLab.
Projecting onto the achievable gamut
A palette of real filaments can transmit only a bounded set of colors — its gamut — and a vivid target may fall outside it. Rather than let the solver chase a color it cannot reach, each out-of-gamut target is first moved to the nearest reachable one. Only colors genuinely outside are moved, within a small tolerance, so interior colors are not dragged onto the boundary. Two projections are offered: the default treats the achievable colors as a solid body in OKLab and moves each target to its nearest surface point, incurring the smallest total change; the alternative holds hue fixed and reduces saturation, giving up lightness only when the target is darker or lighter than the print can reach. Moved targets are flagged, so the result can report which regions of the image exceeded the palette’s reach. An optional white-point rescale (off by default) can first re-anchor every target so the image’s white maps to the print’s actual paper white, keeping pale tints in gamut. See Gamut mapping.
The surviving colors — in the transmission domain, expressed in OKLab, every one achievable — form the target cloud the solver reproduces.
Figure for review

Each source pixel is pulled through the inverse Camera Transform into the transmission domain, re-expressed in OKLab, and projected onto the active palette’s gamut when it falls outside.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.filePath: Prisma Lithophane Generator/How It Works/The Color LUT/index.md
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.title: The Color LUT
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.content:
.hiw-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.hiw-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.hiw-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.hiw-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}PaletteColorModelThe Color LUTThe Solve


Before matching the photo, Prisma computes in advance every filament stack the Palette permits and the color each one transmits, and stores the result as a lookup table. With that catalog built, the solver never evaluates the model during its search: for any color the image asks for, it finds the nearest stored color and reads off the stack that produces it.
The motivation is cost. The color model is expensive to evaluate, and a single solve poses the same kind of query for hundreds of thousands to millions of image points. Running the model per point would be intractably slow; building the catalog once converts every per-point query into a fast nearest-neighbor lookup. The model still does the expensive work, but only once, against a fixed set of candidate stacks, rather than repeatedly inside the solve.
What an entry holds
Each entry is one printable stack — which colored filaments are present, the thickness of each, and the thickness of the white cap — paired with the color that stack produces, stored in the perceptual space the solver searches (see Color Model). The cap is stored jointly with the colored layers rather than chosen in a later pass: because the cap governs brightness, a single lookup answers the whole question at once — which filaments, at what thicknesses, under how much cap. The white base beneath is fixed, so its effect is folded identically into every entry, and the query target is prepared in that same base-included space; only the cap and the colored layers vary.
Building the catalog
Prisma enumerates filament subsets — one filament, two, and small stacks up to a configured limit on how many colors may share a single point. For each subset it steps through cap thicknesses, and for each cap through every assignment of colored-layer thicknesses that still fits within a total height budget; a taller stack absorbs more light and costs more material, so a thicker cap leaves fewer colored layers affordable beneath it. Each candidate is composed through the Color Model and expressed in the perceptual space. Measured corrections are folded in here, per the active model: under Color Model v1, pair corrections — which capture how two stacked filaments interact beyond a simple product of their transmissions — and under Color Model v2 (the default), that model’s own residual correction layer. Both answer to the same Color-corrections setting.
Two refinements keep the catalog lean. Many distinct stacks land on nearly the same color, so Prisma retains one entry per color cell, preferring the stack that uses the least colored material and breaking ties toward the thinner cap, which reads brighter. And the nearest-color search can be told to weight hue above lightness, which helps when an exact brightness match is unavailable but the hue must still land.
Caching
Building the catalog is the slow step, so the finished table is written to disk and keyed to everything it depends on: the exact palette, the filament measurements, the layer height, the cap and budget settings, and the hue-weighting choice. If any of those change, the table is rebuilt; otherwise a later print with the same setup loads it almost instantly. A larger palette, or more colors allowed per point, enlarges the table and slows that first build alone.
How the solve uses it
For each image point the solver hands the table a target color and receives the nearest stored stack — filaments, thicknesses, and cap — together with the distance of the match, a direct measure of color error. Because every lookup is a nearest-neighbor search rather than a model evaluation, the whole image is matched quickly. See The Solve.
Figure for review

Prisma evaluates each printable candidate once, stores its stack and predicted color together, then answers the solve’s repeated color queries with nearest-neighbor lookups.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.filePath: Prisma Lithophane Generator/How It Works/The Solve/Solve Modes.md
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.title: Solve Modes
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.content:
Prisma offers two Solve Modes, chosen on the settings page: Color (the default) and Luminance. What differs directly is how the white cap is built — and as a result, how the print carries brightness and fine detail. The color solver, its targets, and its recipe table are the same code in both modes; but because Luminance mode reserves part of the height budget for the cap, the recipe table is built over a narrower range of cap thicknesses and the chosen recipes can come out different (see below).
The fundamental difference
The white cap sets a print’s brightness, and the two modes derive its thickness from different sources.
In Color, the cap is a by-product of the color solve. For each region the solver already chose a cap thickness jointly with its color recipe — the cap that lands the region’s target brightness — and the cap simply realizes those heights. The source image’s own luminance plays no direct role; brightness is whatever the color decision implied.
In Luminance, the cap is reconstructed from the source image’s brightness. Each point’s luminance is mapped through the white filament’s measured darkening curve to a cap thickness, so the cap physically reproduces the photo’s tonal structure. The result is split in two: a smooth boundary cap carrying the broad tone, held below an image-derived ceiling so it does not consume the whole height budget, and a detail cap of extra white layers placed wherever they measurably improve the predicted result, carrying fine relief the boundary cap cannot. A print made in Luminance mode reads partly like a classic relief lithophane — tone encoded as white thickness — layered on top of color.
One subtlety: Luminance mode does not steer recipe choices toward brightness — it runs the same solver against the same targets, and the shipped preset leaves the solver’s luminance tie-break off. But the two modes do not produce identical recipes. Luminance mode reserves a share of the height budget for the white cap — an image-derived boundary authority — and that reservation is baked into the recipe table before the solve: it narrows the range of cap thicknesses each color stack may be paired with, so fewer color-plus-cap combinations fit under the total-thickness ceiling, and the solver’s best reachable recipe can differ from the one it would pick in Color mode.
What switching modes changes
Choosing a Solve Mode is a preset: it flips a bundle of related settings at once, and the same bundle is independently enforced on the server, so a run’s mode can never be half-applied. Selecting Luminance turns on the source-luminance cap, forces the boundary cap to its smooth form, and arms an extra printability check; selecting Color turns the source-luminance cap off. Because of this, several controls appear, disappear, or change meaning with the mode:

Shading balance — visible only in Luminance, and the only luminance-specific knob exposed. It sets whether the broad luminance shading is carried more by the smooth boundary cap or by fine detail-cap relief: higher values put more shading in the smooth cap, lower values reserve more for fine relief. (A 0–100 slider between Detail and Smooth, default 75.)
Boundary cap — Detail Aware (default) or Smooth — is a Color-mode control; in Luminance it is hidden and forced to Smooth. See White Cap.
Detail depth — shown in both modes: the most extra white layers the detail cap may add above the boundary cap.
Smoothing radius and Appearance Model — meaningful in both modes. Smoothing radius smooths the boundary cap’s top surface in either mode; the Appearance Model (the color model used for lookups and previews) also drives the luminance cap’s response in Luminance mode.

How the cap is constructed in each mode
In Color, the boundary cap realizes the per-region cap heights the color solve already chose. By default (Detail Aware) it keeps that boundary structural and preserves the solved appearance — departing from the raw optical cap only as far as the Appearance budget in predicted color allows — and pushes the remaining tonal variation up into the detail cap; the alternative, Smooth, instead smooths the solved heights into one continuous outer surface. Either way the mandatory detail cap then adds whole white layers, up to Detail depth, wherever they measurably improve the predicted result.
In Luminance, the boundary cap follows the image’s broad luminance, clamped down to an image-derived ceiling — with Shading balance governing how much of the tone the smooth cap carries versus the detail cap — to leave budget for detail. The detail cap then searches, point by point, for how many extra white layers (up to Detail depth) most improve the predicted color and brightness, keeping white only where the gain is real. A printability check unique to Luminance then clamps that freely-authored detail back within the height budget so it cannot create unprintable features. The mechanics of both caps are detailed in White Cap.
One downstream consequence: because the two modes produce structurally different caps, the export step reconstructs the cap geometry differently for each — see Export.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.filePath: Prisma Lithophane Generator/How It Works/The Solve/index.md
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.title: The Solve
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.content:
.hiw-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.hiw-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.hiw-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.hiw-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}TargetColorsThe Color LUTThe SolveWhite Cap


The solve is where a prepared image becomes a printable plan. Given the per-point color targets from Target Colors and a palette of calibrated filaments, it decides, at every point in the image, which filaments to stack and how thick each should be, so the backlit panel reproduces the photo. Thicker colored layers transmit less light and read darker and more saturated; the solve is the search for the stack that lands nearest each target while remaining something a printer can build.
It does not decide each point independently — that would yield a speckled, unbuildable field of single-point recipe changes. Instead it runs as an ordered sequence of stages, each handing a finished result to the next, and each trading raw color accuracy against clean, printable geometry.
Solve modes
The solve runs in one of two Solve Modes, Color (the default) or Luminance. The color solver, the targets, and the recipe table are the same machinery in both, but Luminance reserves cap budget up front, so its recipe table spans a narrower range of cap thicknesses and the chosen recipes can come out different. What changes deliberately is how the white cap is built. In Color, the cap follows the brightness each region’s recipe implied. In Luminance, the cap is instead reconstructed from the source image’s luminance, carrying the photo’s tone and fine detail as white relief, like a classic lithophane, on top of color. The two modes are compared in depth in Solve Modes, and the cap mechanics in White Cap.
Why staged
Two goals pull against each other. Matching color exactly wants the freedom to change the recipe at every point; printing well wants large regions of constant recipe and gradual changes in height. The staged structure resolves the tension by fixing color in coherent regions first and adding refinement and fine detail only where it earns its place, rather than satisfying both goals everywhere at once.
Throughout, the solve leans on The Color LUT: instead of recomputing a candidate stack’s transmitted color from the optical model, it reads the answer from the precomputed table. Because each lookup is nearly free, the solve can score many candidate recipes per region, and many height options per recipe, without becoming slow.
What each stage contributes
Compile the settings. The run’s settings are first resolved into a fixed, self-consistent plan: the resolution it will solve at, the spacing of the color regions it aims for, and the printability limits it must respect. Every later stage reads this one compiled plan, which makes a run reproducible and internally consistent.
Plan the color regions. The image is partitioned into contiguous patches of similar target color, and adjacent patches are recorded as neighbors. Each patch is destined for a single recipe. Working in regions rather than points is what keeps the result buildable; the neighbor map is what later lets the solve reason about the seams between regions.
Choose a recipe per region. This is the core decision. For each region the solve scores candidate stacks under three competing pressures: how closely the stack reproduces the region’s color, how small a height step it leaves against its neighbors, and a preference for the thinnest stack that still suffices. The second pressure compares the total visible height of adjacent regions and penalizes the square of the gap between them — a sharp height jump prints as a visible seam — so a slightly imperfect color that sits nearly flush with its neighbor often beats a perfect color that leaves a step. Each candidate is scored at its best achievable cap brightness, so color and overall lightness are decided together rather than in separate passes. Where a region’s color varies internally, the solve may grant finer sub-region recipes within it.
Build the white cap. A white layer is authored over the colored stacks. It sets overall brightness and, in Luminance mode, carries much of the image’s tone and fine relief; it also reinforces the structural shell every viewing surface requires, and runs the printability checks that grow, trim, or refuse features the printer could not reliably produce. See White Cap.
Assemble the output. The layered plan is converted into the per-filament thickness maps the rest of the pipeline expects — one height map per colored filament plus the white cap — together with a report of how closely the predicted colors matched their targets and how much of the image landed within tolerance.
When the palette overflows the printer
Everything above describes one pass, and one pass is all it takes when the palette fits the printer’s loaded slots. When it does not, the solve runs twice: a quick reduced-resolution scout solve measures how the image actually uses each filament, the colors are divided into slot-sized bands of exactly the height they need — each topped up to a flat ceiling with white — and the final solve then runs the full staged sequence against recipe tables constrained to those bands, with each candidate stack’s white fill already included so its dilution is priced into the choice. The reserved band heights also come out of the total thickness budget, leaving the cap correspondingly less room to spend. How the bands are chosen, and why their flatness is what makes mid-print filament swaps valid, is covered in Runs with Swaps.
What comes out
The result is a set of height maps, one per filament plus the white cap, specifying how tall each material stands at every point, alongside the quality and printability summary. These maps flow onward to become the printable mesh.
Figure for review

The solve moves from one compiled plan to coherent color regions, region recipes, white-cap geometry, and finally the per-filament thickness maps used by export.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.filePath: Prisma Lithophane Generator/How It Works/White Cap/Thickness map.md
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.title: Thickness map
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.content:
Once the solver has decided which filaments go where, the result takes the form of a thickness map: a set of per-filament height fields, one for each filament in the palette. Each field is the same shape as the image, and every cell holds a thickness in millimeters — how much of that filament stands at that point. This is the solve’s primary geometric output.
Pull the layers apart and you have one field per filament — not one per color channel, but one per actual palette filament. Where a field reads zero, that filament is absent there. Where it stands tall, that color is doing the work: thicker material transmits less light, so it reads darker and more saturated. Stacked together, these fields are the recipe for the print.
The white cap rides along
A finished lithophane needs a white skin over the colored stack, and the cap’s height travels in the same bundle as another field, beside the color maps. In the production solver the cap may be split into two fields — a broad boundary cap and a fine detail cap — that downstream steps add back together when needed. Either way the cap’s thickness is not a setting stored here; it is decided during cap construction, which depends on the solve mode — the color solve sets it in Color mode, image luminance drives it in Luminance mode. The full account is in White Cap.
(There is no white-base field: the base is a single fixed thickness under everything, folded into the color model rather than mapped per pixel.)
It also carries the solve’s report card
The same bundle holds two diagnostic fields: a per-pixel color-error map, recording how far each point’s predicted color landed from its target, and an out-of-gamut mask marking pixels whose target was unreachable. These travel with the geometry, so the solve’s own quality record is part of its output rather than a separate artifact.
Why it is the hinge
The thickness map is where color matching becomes physical geometry, and two stages depend on it directly:

Export reads each height field and builds it into printed material at the right places and depths. See Export.
Color checking runs the maps back through the color model to predict what the lit stack will actually look like, then compares that against the target — that is how Prisma knows where it matched the color and where it had to compromise. The prediction comes from the Appearance provider.

No control reads or writes the thickness map; it is pure solve output. It is produced at the end of the solve — see The Solve — and flows two ways from there: out to the printer as geometry, and back through the color model as a check.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.filePath: Prisma Lithophane Generator/How It Works/White Cap/index.md
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.title: White Cap
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.content:
.hiw-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.hiw-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.hiw-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.hiw-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}The SolveWhite CapRuns withSwaps


When the solver finishes, its output is still a set of color decisions. This stage turns them into geometry: a Thickness map of colored material, and a white cap over the top that sets the print’s brightness and protects the color. See The Solve for how the colors are chosen.
The cap is built in two stacked tiers above the color stack. The boundary cap is the cap: a closed white surface that covers the color stack. It is always present (with a one-layer minimum), it closes over the colored material so no color edge is left exposed, and its thickness is what sets how bright each region reads — thicker white passes less light, so it reads darker. Its underside fits the color stack exactly; only its upper surface is shaped. The detail cap is the second tier — whole extra white layers added on top of the boundary cap. Where the boundary cap is the structural surface, the detail cap adds fine extra white only where it earns its place — gated on image detail and on whether the added white measurably improves the result, up to a layer ceiling — and it can be suppressed feature by feature for printability. It never lowers the boundary cap; it only adds above it.
From colors to heights, and the budget
Each solved color is a recipe of stacked colored layers; summed at each point they give the colored stack’s height above the white base. The top of that stack is the color ceiling. Total object height is a hard ceiling that includes the white base, so the cap may use only the budget left between the color ceiling and the target height — and the boundary tier is held within part of that budget, reserving room for detail. Cap thickness is quantized to whole printed layers and held at the one-layer minimum.
In a run with swaps, the color ceiling is different: every filament band is filled with white up to a flat, panel-wide ceiling, so the top of colors-plus-fill sits at one constant height everywhere rather than following each point’s own stack. The cap’s budget is measured from that flat ceiling, and it is a hard limit of its own — whatever the brightness arithmetic below asks for, the cap can never spend more than the height left above the bands. See Runs with Swaps.
The cap settings
A handful of settings shape the cap:

Boundary cap — Detail Aware (default) or Smooth. Smooth shapes the boundary cap into one continuous outer surface that carries the tonal relief directly. Detail Aware keeps the boundary cap structural, preserves the solved appearance against the active color model, and places the remaining tonal relief in the detail cap instead — bounded by the Appearance budget. This is a Color-mode choice; Luminance always uses the smooth boundary cap.
Appearance budget — for the Detail Aware boundary cap: the most extra predicted color error (in the model’s color space) allowed as the smoothed boundary cap departs from the raw optical cap. Lower values preserve the solved appearance more aggressively. (Default 0.008.)
Smoothing radius — how much the boundary cap’s upper surface is smoothed. Lower values keep more tonal relief in the surface; higher values produce a cleaner, more contiguous cap. The smoothing is edge-aware — pulled back toward the unsmoothed surface near strong color or recipe edges — and the underside still fits the color stack exactly.
Detail depth — the most whole white layers the detail cap may add above the boundary cap. It permits detail height; it does not force the detail cap to use every layer. (Default 5.)
Shading balance — used in Luminance mode (below): whether the broad luminance shading is carried more by the smooth boundary cap or by fine detail-cap relief.

Color mode vs Luminance mode
The cap is built fundamentally differently depending on the Solve Mode — covered in full in Solve Modes.
In Color, the boundary cap is the brightness the color solve already chose: for each point, the cap thickness whose predicted stack best matched the target color. The source image’s own luminance plays no direct role. With the default Detail Aware boundary cap that solved surface is kept structural and appearance-preserving, its tonal relief carried by the detail cap; with Smooth it is smoothed into one continuous surface instead. The mandatory detail cap then adds a little extra white — up to Detail depth layers — wherever it measurably sharpens the result.
In Luminance, the source image’s brightness drives the cap. The boundary cap is held under a ceiling derived from that brightness — it cannot exceed the cap thickness the image’s own luminance implies, and Shading balance sets how much of the tone the smooth cap carries versus the detail cap — which keeps the smooth tier from consuming the whole budget. The detail cap then adds white toward the fuller luminance-derived relief, point by point wherever it measurably improves the predicted result, up to Detail depth layers; a printability check unique to this mode keeps that freely-added detail within budget. Together the two tiers reproduce the photo’s tonal structure as white relief — like a classic lithophane — on top of color.
Band fill changes the brightness arithmetic in a banded print, because white inside a band dims the light just as cap white does. In Color mode this takes care of itself: the solve chose every recipe with its band’s fill already included, so the cap those recipes imply is already correct. In Luminance mode the cap is derived from the source image’s brightness, so the fill must be subtracted explicitly: the cap targets are thinned by exactly the fill thickness beneath them, and fill and cap together — not the cap alone — reproduce the intended tone. Without that subtraction a banded Luminance print would come out darker than the photo asks.
Covering every surface
However the cap heights are derived, the cap is meshed as two parts of the same white material. A rigid guard sits one layer above each colored point and extends a short way to the side, shielding the exposed side walls of the color stacks so no color cliff faces the viewer bare. A freeform surface carries the rest of the cap up to its target height away from the colored regions. Before the result is accepted, every print layer is checked for exposed color and for white features — specks or pinholes — too small to print reliably; tiny faults are grown into printable footprints where possible and suppressed otherwise.
The finished cap heights, with the colored stacks, pass onward to be meshed. In a swap run, the filament bands were already fixed before the cap was built (Runs with Swaps). How the cap surface becomes mesh, and why it can carry finer detail than the solve grid, is covered in Export.
Figure for review

The color ceiling follows the top of each solved stack. Above it, the boundary cap provides continuous white coverage with a layer-quantized upper profile; localized detail layers add relief on top within the remaining height budget.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.filePath: Prisma Lithophane Generator/How It Works/index.md
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.title: How It Works
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.content:
A color lithophane is a thin printed panel that shows almost nothing in reflected light but resolves into a full-color picture when lit from behind. Prisma’s job is to decide how to stack translucent colored filaments — layer by layer, point by point — so that the light transmitted through the panel reproduces a target photograph.
This section explains what the system does internally, and why. None of it is required to make a print; How To Use covers the actual workflow. The goal here is a working mental model, so that the settings have meaning and an unexpected result is easier to diagnose.
The principle it rests on
Backlit, a stack of colored filament behaves as a subtractive optical filter — much like stacked panes of stained glass. The color emerging at any point is governed by two things: which filaments are stacked there, and how thick each layer is. Thicker filament transmits less light, so it reads darker and more saturated. Reproducing a photograph therefore reduces to a dense per-point problem: at every location, choose the filaments and thicknesses whose transmitted color best matches the target. Everything below exists to pose that problem well, solve it efficiently, and turn the solution into geometry a printer can actually produce.
The pipeline
The image moves left to right through a sequence of stages. A second stream — the chosen palette, the calibrated color model, and the lookup table built from them — feeds into the solve, supplying the predicted color of every printable filament stack.

The main flow runs left to right; the palette’s color model and the lookup table feed the solve from below. Select any stage to read how it works.
The stages

Image Adjustments — the framing and color grading you apply to the source photo in the first tab, before the automatic pipeline begins.
Preprocessing — an optional, configurable clean-up pass that conditions the image toward what the chosen palette can actually reproduce.
Target Colors — translating every pixel into a perceptual color space and onto the set of colors the palette can physically reach.
The Solve — the core step: choosing a filament recipe for each region of the image so the backlit result matches the targets while staying printable.
White Cap — converting the solved colors into a thickness map and adding a white layer that sets overall brightness.
Runs with Swaps — planning flat filament bands when the palette contains more colors than the printer can hold at once.
Export — turning the finished layers into an STL or 3MF model the slicer can open.

Feeding the solve from the side:

Palette — the filaments chosen for a print, and how Prisma can suggest them from the image.
Color Model — the calibrated model of how your filaments transmit light when stacked.
The Color LUT — a precomputed table of every printable stack and the color it produces, so the solver can look colors up instead of recomputing them.

Settings as a cross-cutting view
The pipeline pages follow the image from stage to stage. Settings: How They Work reorganizes the same system around the four Settings drawer sections — Essentials, Pre-processing, Color Solver, and White Cap — and explains how their controls change those stages internally.
Each page stands on its own; start with any stage and follow the cross-links from there.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-to-use/c.title: Configuration
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-to-use/c.content:
.htu-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.htu-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.htu-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.htu-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}ConfigurationImage


One-time setup: choosing the published model library Prisma predicts from, telling it which of that library’s filaments you own, and describing your printer. These controls live together near the bottom of the panel on the left edge of the app: Model Library, Active Filaments, then Printer.
That left panel is also the app’s dashboard: a thumbnail of the selected image, the Palette Deck (see Palette), and a small badge under the title showing whether the browser is connected to the app (“offline” means it isn’t — see Launching Prisma).
Model Libraries
A published model library is one self-contained, read-only snapshot: its public filament catalog, Color Model v1 profiles and corrections, Color Model v2 bundle and corrections, and Camera Transform all belong to the same calibrated generation. Generator uses exactly one installed library at a time; it never mixes models or filaments from different libraries.
The Model Library section in the left panel names the current library and shows whether it is In Use, needs a restart, is invalid, or has not been selected. Press Manage to open Model Libraries. The list marks the library currently In Use, any library selected for the next launch, and any package that failed validation. Select a valid library to see its version, publisher, filament count, compatibility, and release notes.

Install Library… accepts a published Prisma model-library ZIP and validates every required file before installing it. Installing does not switch the running Generator.
Activate and Restart Prisma selects the library and restarts Generator so every backend model loader changes together. Unsaved session history is cleared by the restart.
Remove Library is available only for a library that is neither currently loaded nor selected for the next launch. Removing the installed copy does not delete the original ZIP you downloaded.
Open Folder opens Generator\Model Libraries. Use the app for install, activation, and removal rather than manually rearranging this folder.

If the selected library is missing or invalid, Prisma opens the manager in Library Recovery mode. You can inspect or replace libraries, but lithophane generation remains unavailable until a complete valid library is selected.
Switching libraries changes the filament catalog and all three calibrated model families together. Earlier runs remain stored, but they cannot silently stand in for a solve made with the newly active library.
Active Filaments
Active Filaments is the subset of the current model library that the rest of the app offers you. You probably don’t own every calibrated filament in the library, so this filter lets you hide the ones you don’t have without changing the installed model library.
Press Manage next to Active Filaments in the left panel. A window opens with every available filament as a card; click a card to enable or disable it. All and None set everything at once, and the counter at the top shows how many are enabled. Close the window when you’re done — changes apply immediately.


                  
                  📸 Screenshot to capture 
                  
                

The Active Filaments window, with a mix of enabled and disabled filament cards visible and the “N / M enabled” counter at the top.


Disabling a filament just hides it — nothing is deleted, and you can re-enable it any time.
Printer Configuration
Prisma needs to know your printer’s basic facts: how big it can print, how many filament slots it has, and what nozzles you use. These set the limits the app works within — the maximum print size, how many colors a palette can hold at once, and the finest detail a solve should attempt.
Press Configure next to Printer in the left panel. The Printer Configuration window opens:

Printer list (top) — if you have more than one printer, pick which one to edit here. + New adds a printer; Delete removes the selected one.
General — the printer’s Name, its Print Area X / Y in millimeters (caps how large a lithophane you can make), AMS Units, and Slots per AMS. Units × slots is the total number of filaments the printer holds at once — this is what decides how many colors fit without swaps (see Palette).
Nozzle Profiles — one row per nozzle you own, with its usable layer-height range and the finest feature it can print. + Add creates a row. These drive the app’s recommendations — most importantly the recommended solve resolution.

Changes save automatically; just close the window.


                  
                  📸 Screenshot to capture 
                  
                

The Printer Configuration window, showing the General fields and a couple of Nozzle Profile rows.


Picking the active printer and nozzle
Back in the left panel, the Printer area shows the active printer (a dropdown if you have several) and the active nozzle on the same row. Set these to match your actual machine before solving — the nozzle choice changes the recommended solve resolution and what the app considers printable.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-to-use/e.title: Export
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-to-use/e.content:
.htu-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.htu-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.htu-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.htu-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}PreviewExport3D Printing


The Export tab turns a finished solve into the files your slicer needs, plus the filament-change plan for the print. The tab is laid out as numbered steps, left to right.


                  
                  📸 Screenshot to capture 
                  
                

The whole Export tab after generating files: the run list on the left, the Print Files options, the Generated Files list, and Swap Instructions.


1 — Select Run
The left column lists your completed solves — the same cards as the Preview tab’s history. Click the run you want to print. Export uses that run’s frozen solve, palette, and settings, so later changes in the drawer do not alter it.
2 — Print Files
Three choices, then Generate Print Files:

Output format — Single 3MF file (default) bundles everything into one file, the convenient choice for OrcaSlicer. Individual STL files gives one file per filament instead.
Mesh method — how the 3D shape is built. Field-derived white cap (default) produces a cleaner, smoother cap surface. Exact solved raster reproduces the solve’s blocky grid exactly.
Mesh detail — for the default method, how finely the cap surface is rebuilt, from 2x large/fast to 16x maximum detail. Higher looks better and takes longer to generate, with bigger files. 4x balanced is right for most prints.

Generating takes a little while for large prints; progress shows while it runs.
3 — Generated Files
The finished files appear here. Download .zip grabs them all in one archive, or click a single file to download just it. They’re also written to Generator\Exports beside the app, in a per-export subfolder. These are what you open in the slicer — see 3D Printing.
Swap Instructions
If the print needs mid-print filament changes, this panel is the plan: which filaments to load in which slots, and what to change at each pause. Generate builds it from the selected run — you can do this without generating print files — and Copy to Clipboard takes it with you. It uses your current printer’s slot configuration, so make sure the right printer and AMS setup are active in Configuration.
Runs with swaps need a little more preparation and judgment than runs whose colors all fit at once. See Runs with Swaps for the complete workflow.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-to-use/i.title: Adjustments
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-to-use/i.content:
.htu-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.htu-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.htu-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.htu-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}ImageAdjustmentsPalette


The Adjustments panel on the Image tab controls the print’s size and framing (Size) and the picture’s tone and color (Image). Changes show live in the framing canvas and the Preview pane. Reset returns everything here to defaults.
Size


                  
                  📸 Screenshot to capture 
                  
                

The Size sub-tab with an image loaded: the framing canvas above, and the Direction / Aspect Ratio / Scale / Rotate / Width / Height controls below.


The canvas shows your photo with a bright window over it — the part that will print. Drag inside the window to move it; drag its edges to resize it (when the aspect ratio allows).

Direction — Landscape or Portrait. Flips the frame’s orientation.
Aspect Ratio — the frame’s shape. W×H lets you set width and height independently (drag any edge freely). Ratio asks for a custom proportion. Image matches the photo’s own shape, and 3:2, 4:3, 5:4, 1:1 are fixed shapes.



                  
                  📸 Screenshot to capture 
                  
                

The Custom Ratio dialog (opens from the Ratio button).



Crop Fit — three one-click framings: fit the whole image centered, fill the frame’s width, or fill its height.
Scale — zooms the photo inside the frame (100% = whole image visible). Use it to crop in on the part you want.
Rotate — fine rotation in degrees, plus one-click 90°L, 90°R, H-Flip, and V-Flip buttons.
Width / Height — the print’s physical size in millimeters. The lock buttons hold one dimension fixed while the other follows the aspect ratio. Limited by your printer’s print area.
Border — adds a raised frame around the lithophane. Width is how far it extends outward; Border Height is how tall it stands. The border prints in the same white as the cap.

Bigger isn’t just bigger: at a larger print size the same photo spreads over more solve points, so the print can carry more detail. Check Rendered Size in the info bar.
Image


                  
                  📸 Screenshot to capture 
                  
                

The Image sub-tab, showing the Mode toggle and the adjustment sliders.


These tune the picture before Prisma reproduces it. They work like the basic controls in any photo app, and the effect shows live:

Mode — Color or B/W. B/W removes color from the target image, but it does not automatically remove colored filaments from the active palette. Use a white-only or otherwise deliberately limited palette when you want a truly single-color print.
Exposure — overall brightness.
Contrast — the spread between darks and lights.
Highlight / Shadow — brighten or darken just the light areas, or just the dark areas.

In Color mode there are four more:

Tint and Tint Strength — wash the whole image toward a chosen hue, by a chosen amount.
Saturation — how vivid the colors are.
Temp — warmer (toward orange) or cooler (toward blue).

A practical use: if the preview after solving shows your palette can’t reach the photo’s most saturated colors, easing Saturation down here can produce a cleaner, more even result than letting the solver clip them.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-to-use/i.title: Image
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-to-use/i.content:
.htu-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.htu-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.htu-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.htu-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}ConfigurationImagePaletteAdjustments


The Image tab is step 1: pick the photo, decide how big the print will be, and frame the part of the picture you want. Everything else in the app works from what you set here.


                  
                  📸 Screenshot to capture 
                  
                

The whole Image tab with an image selected: Library and Preview on the left, the Adjustments panel with the framing canvas on the right.


Library
The Library pane holds your source photos. Each thumbnail shows the file’s name, pixel dimensions, and size; click one to select it (or drag it onto the framing canvas). Add Image uploads a photo from your computer; the refresh button re-reads the folder; the expand button enlarges the pane when you have many images.
Switching to a different photo resets the framing — crop, scale, and rotation start fresh for the new image.
Prisma accepts ordinary image formats such as JPEG and PNG. Almost any photo can be solved, but that does not mean every photo will make an equally good lithophane. A sharp source with readable contrast and important details large enough to survive the print resolution is a stronger starting point.
The library is the photos folder inside Prisma’s own folder on your computer — Add Image copies your photo into it, and you can also drop files there directly (then press refresh).
Preview
The Preview pane shows the framed and adjusted target image that the rest of the app will use, with the physical dimensions marked. It is not yet a prediction of the printed result. If something important is cut off here, fix the framing before moving on.
Adjustments
The Adjustments panel on the right is where you set the print’s size and shape and, optionally, tune the picture itself. It has two sub-tabs:

Size — orientation, aspect ratio, physical width and height, crop framing, rotation, and an optional raised border.
Image — brightness, contrast, color adjustments, and a black-and-white mode.

Both are covered control by control in Adjustments. Reset (top right of the panel) returns everything to defaults.
The info bar
Under the controls, three figures summarize the setup:

Image Size — the source photo’s pixels.
Print Size — the physical size the lithophane will be.
Rendered Size — how many solve points the print works out to at the current resolution. This is the real detail level of the print: if it’s much smaller than the image size, fine detail in the photo won’t survive, no matter how sharp the source is.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-to-use/p.title: Palette
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-to-use/p.content:
.htu-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.htu-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.htu-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.htu-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}ImagePaletteSettingsRuns withSwaps


The Palette tab is where you choose the colored filaments available to the solve. Palette choice has a large effect on the result: Prisma can mix the colors you provide by stacking them, but it cannot make every target equally well from every set of filaments.
The white used for the base and cap is selected separately under Settings → Essentials. It appears on palette cards for context but is not one of the palette’s color filaments.
Both creation modes use the enabled Active Filaments from the currently active model library. If a filament is missing, check Configuration first; use Model Library → Manage in the left panel only when you mean to switch the complete published model library.


                  
                  📸 Screenshot to capture 
                  
                

The Palette tab in Auto-Suggest mode: the filament picker on the left, the controls and Suggest Palettes button on the right, and a few results in the Suggested Palettes column.


Auto-Suggest
Auto-Suggest tests combinations from the filaments you allow and stages promising palettes for the selected image.

Under Select Filaments for Auto-Suggest, select the filaments Prisma may consider. All and None are quick starting points.
Set the limits on the right.
Choose a Target that matches the Solve Mode you intend to use.
Press Suggest Palettes.
Compare the results and use Add to Deck on the palettes you want to solve.

The controls are:

Max colors — the most colored filaments in one printer load. Prisma caps this to the color slots available after reserving the white slot.
Extra color loads — allows suggestions that use additional groups of colored filaments. 0 keeps every color loaded for the whole print. Values above 0 create runs that require mid-print swaps.
Suggestions — how many alternatives to request.
Target — Source color evaluates palettes against the adjusted image’s colors. Luminance detail evaluates them for the Luminance workflow, where the white cap carries more of the light-and-dark structure.

Each result shows Suggest dE. dE means delta E, a perceptual color-difference estimate; lower indicates a closer estimated fit to the suggestion target. It is useful for narrowing the field, not for declaring a winner. Palettes with similar scores can distribute their errors very differently, so solve the promising options and compare their predicted images.


                  
                  📸 Screenshot to capture 
                  
                

A single card in the Suggested Palettes column, showing its filament swatches, Suggest dE, and the Add to Deck button.


The collapsible Palette Suggestion Settings panel contains two less-common controls:

Min added-color gain — how much improvement another color or load tier must provide before Prisma recommends continuing.
Compute all load tiers — tests every allowed tier even when the improvement falls below that threshold.

If the selected white is unavailable to the color model, suggestion cannot run. Filaments excluded from modeling are also ignored even if selected as candidates.
Cancel requests a stop at the next safe search boundary. The progress bar remains visible as Cancellation requested until the worker actually stops; any partial suggestions returned by the search are still shown.
Manual
Manual mode is for building a palette directly. Select filaments under Select Filaments for Palette; the Manual Palette panel shows the current set and whether it fits in one load. A manual palette may contain more colors than the available color slots, but that run will require swaps.
Press Add to Deck when the set is ready. Clear empties the manual palette.


                  
                  📸 Screenshot to capture 
                  
                

The Palette tab in Manual mode: the filament library on the left, and the Manual Palette panel on the right with several filaments filling the slots.


Suggested Palettes and the Palette Deck
The Suggested Palettes column is a temporary staging area. Suggestions arrive there first so you can compare them without filling the app’s main deck. Add to Deck promotes one; Clear empties the staging area.
The Palette Deck in the left rail contains palettes ready to use. Click a card to make it active. The highlighted palette is the one the next solve uses. Hover over a card to see its filament names, white filament, and suggestion score when available.


                  
                  📸 Screenshot to capture 
                  
                

The Palette Deck in the app’s left panel: two or three cards, one highlighted as active, with the hover preview popped out on one of them.


Use Save on a deck card to keep that palette under a name. Removing the card from the deck does not delete its saved copy.


                  
                  📸 Screenshot to capture 
                  
                

The Save Palette dialog.


Load in the deck header opens saved palettes. Select one to return it to the deck, or delete a saved palette from that list. Clear empties the active deck.


                  
                  📸 Screenshot to capture 
                  
                

The Load list open, showing a few saved palettes with their color chips.


Once a palette is active, press Solve. For a first comparison, favor palettes that fit in one load. Extra colors are worthwhile only when the predicted improvement justifies the slower solve, white-fill trade-offs, and manual changes required by a swap run. See Runs with Swaps before printing one.

For the optical reason stacked filaments can produce colors that none of them makes alone, see Palette in How It Works.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-to-use/p.title: Advanced Modes
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-to-use/p.content:
.htu-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.htu-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.htu-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.htu-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}Preview CardModesAdvancedModesExport


The Advanced button at the end of the mode bar reveals two extra views. They’re diagnostic — most prints never need them — but they answer specific questions the everyday modes can’t.
Thickness Maps
One map per filament in the palette, showing how thick that filament is laid down across the print — brighter is thicker. The White cap selector picks which cap portion (Total / Boundary / Detail) appears in the white filament’s map.
Use it to see what each filament is contributing — for example, whether an expensive color is barely used, or which filament is producing an unexpected region.


                  
                  📸 Screenshot to capture 
                  
                

The Thickness Maps grid showing the per-filament maps for a solved run.


Highpass
Shows only the parts of the print’s surface above a height you choose with the Threshold slider, and reports how many layers that leaves. Slide it down and the tallest features appear first.
Use it to spot isolated tall spikes — small lonely peaks print poorly, and this view finds them before the printer does.


                  
                  📸 Screenshot to capture 
                  
                

The Highpass view with the threshold pulled partway down so only the tallest features show.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-to-use/p.title: Preview Card Modes
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-to-use/p.content:
.htu-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.htu-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.htu-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.htu-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}PreviewPreview CardModesAdvancedModes


The bar above the preview switches what a solved run displays. Predicted is the everyday view; the others show the physical print behind it. Where a view maps thickness or height, a scale bar below explains the colors, and views with sub-options show them in a row under the mode bar. Click any image to enlarge it.
Predicted
What the print should look like lit from behind — the app’s best prediction of the finished lithophane. This is the view to judge results by: compare it against the source column and decide with your eye.


                  
                  📸 Screenshot to capture 
                  
                

The Predicted view beside the source image.


White Cap
Maps of the white cap’s thickness — brighter means thicker white. View picks which part:

Total — the whole cap.
Boundary — just the continuous covering layer.
Detail — just the fine relief on top.

Contours: On/Off overlays lines marking each printed-layer step. In Luminance mode this view shows where the image’s brightness structure is being carried by white thickness.


                  
                  📸 Screenshot to capture 
                  
                

The White Cap view with the Total/Boundary/Detail selector and contours on.


Color Regions
Two looks at the color stack under the cap, switched by View:

Color Ceiling — a height map of where the colored layers top out across the print.
Recipe Viewer — the print rendered from its colors alone, plus the “cookbook”: which filament combination produces each region. Click around to see what’s actually printed where — useful when a color surprises you and you want to know which filaments made it.



                  
                  📸 Screenshot to capture 
                  
                

The Recipe Viewer with a region’s recipe visible.


Top Surface
The final printable outer surface — the actual heights the printer will build, everything included. Contours: On/Off marks the layer steps. This is the closest thing to holding the unlit print and looking across it.


                  
                  📸 Screenshot to capture 
                  
                

The Top Surface view with contours on.


Explorer
A horizontal slice through the print: pick a Height with the slider and see which material sits at that height everywhere in the print, within a Band ± window you can widen or narrow. Like peeling the print down to a chosen layer — the way to answer “what is the printer putting down at 1.4 mm?”


                  
                  📸 Screenshot to capture 
                  
                

The Explorer view mid-height, with the Height and Band controls visible.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-to-use/p.title: Preview
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-to-use/p.content:
.htu-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.htu-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.htu-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.htu-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}SettingsPreviewExportPreview CardModesAdvancedModes


The Preview tab is where lithophanes actually get built and judged. You start a solve, Prisma works out the filament stack for every point, and the results land here for inspection — before you’ve spent any plastic.
A lot happens under the hood during a solve; you don’t need any of it to use the app. If you’re curious, How It Works explains the whole machine.
Starting a solve
Press Solve in the top bar. It needs two things: a selected image and an active palette in the Palette Deck — it stays grayed out until both exist. Progress shows while the solve runs, typically a minute or two depending on size and settings; you can cancel and keep using the app.


                  
                  📸 Screenshot to capture 
                  
                

The Preview tab with a completed solve: the source and predicted result side by side, the view-mode bar above, and the Solve History column on the right.


Preview cards
A finished solve appears as columns in the main area — your source photo beside the solved result. The bar above switches what the result shows: the predicted appearance, the white cap, the color regions, and more. Each view is described in Preview Card Modes; the extra diagnostic views behind the Advanced button are in Advanced Modes. Source Image: On/Off hides the source column when you want more room. Click any image to enlarge it.
One thing to know up front: the result can look blocky compared with the photo. That view shows the solve grid honestly rather than inventing image detail between solved points. A field-derived white-cap export may reconstruct a smoother physical cap surface, but it does not create new color decisions beyond the solve resolution.
Solve History
Every solve becomes a card in the Solve History column on the right, newest on top. Each card shows the run’s name, its palette colors, and RMSE %, the run’s overall color-error score. Lower is closer to the target, but use the predicted image rather than the number alone when choosing between runs. Details unfolds the settings the run used.
Click a card to show or hide that run in the main area. Showing two or more runs puts them side by side — the easiest way to judge whether a settings or palette change actually helped.


                  
                  📸 Screenshot to capture 
                  
                

Two Solve History cards selected, with both runs displayed side by side next to the source.


To keep a run deliberately, save it. Clear removes the cards from the current Solve History display only. It does not delete automatic saves, cached run data, or explicitly saved runs; automatic saves remain available through Load.
Saving and loading solves
Press Save on a card and give it a name to keep that run permanently — result, settings, palette, everything.
Load (top of Solve History) opens the Saved Runs window: your saved runs plus recent automatic saves (each solve is quietly auto-saved, so a good result is usually recoverable even if you forgot to save). Select one to Load it back — it behaves exactly like a run you just solved, including being exportable. Save keeps an automatic save permanently, Rename and Delete manage the list, Download hands you the run as a file, and Load from file… brings a downloaded run back in — handy as a backup or to move a run to another computer.


                  
                  📸 Screenshot to capture 
                  
                

The Saved Runs window with a few saved and automatic runs listed.




                  
                  📸 Screenshot to capture 
                  
                

The Rename saved run dialog.


When the result isn’t right
Compare the predicted view against the source and trust your eye. Colors falling short usually mean the palette can’t reach them — try another suggestion, more colors, or easing the photo’s saturation (see Adjustments). Missing fine detail usually traces to solve resolution or the white cap’s detail depth (see Settings). Change one thing, solve again, and compare the two runs side by side.
