prisma-lithophane-generator/how-to-use/r.title: Runs with Swaps
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-to-use/r.content:
.htu-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.htu-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.htu-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.htu-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}PaletteRuns withSwapsSettings


A run needs swaps when its palette contains more colored filaments than the active printer has color slots. Prisma plans these runs automatically; there is no separate mode or setting to choose.
Swaps increase the available palette, but they are not a free upgrade. The solve takes longer, the band structure consumes part of the thickness budget, white fill between bands can dilute color, and the print requires correctly timed filament changes. A palette that fits in one load is the more reliable baseline and will generally produce an equal or better result when it can cover the image well enough.
Before solving

Open Configuration and confirm the active printer, material-system units, and slot count.
Select the white filament under Settings → Essentials. White occupies a slot throughout the print.
Build a palette that exceeds the remaining color slots. In Auto-Suggest, allow this with Extra color loads. In Manual mode, simply select the additional colors.
Keep a no-swap palette available when possible so you can compare whether the extra colors actually help.



                  
                  📸 Screenshot to capture 
                  
                

Auto-Suggest with Extra color loads above 0, showing the slot preview and a suggested palette that exceeds one load.


Solve and compare
Press Solve normally. Prisma first runs a lower-resolution scout to estimate how the image uses the palette, then plans the swap bands and runs the final solve. This takes longer than a run whose palette fits at once.
On Preview, compare the swap run with the no-swap baseline. Look at the predicted image, not only RMSE %. Extra colors are useful when they make a visible improvement in important parts of the image; a slightly better score alone may not justify the added constraints and print handling.
The swap plan is fixed as part of the completed run. If you change the printer’s slot capacity, solve again under the new configuration.
Generate Swap Instructions

Open 4 Export and select the completed swap run.
Under Swap Instructions, press Generate.
Confirm the initial slot assignments and each later unload/load instruction.
Use Copy to Clipboard to carry the plan into OrcaSlicer.
Generate the print files from the same selected run.

Swap-instruction generation is a short request that runs to completion once started. Its progress bar does not offer a misleading Cancel action.


                  
                  📸 Screenshot to capture 
                  
                

Swap Instructions for a completed run, including the initial slot loading, pause heights, and per-slot changes.


Follow the slot identities and pause heights exactly. The instructions assume the printer configuration used for the solve and do not redesign the plan at export time.
Practical guidance

Prefer the smallest palette that gives a meaningful visual improvement.
Limit Extra color loads while exploring; more tiers increase search time and print handling.
Keep the white filament loaded in its assigned slot for the entire print.
Check that each required filament is ready before slicing and printing.
Treat a swap run as a deliberate second option, not the default path for every image.

For the reason the solve uses flat filament bands and white fill, see Runs with Swaps in How It Works.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-to-use/s.title: Color Solver Settings
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-to-use/s.content:
.htu-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.htu-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.htu-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.htu-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}PreprocessingModulesColorSolverWhiteCap


These control the heart of the process: how Prisma decides which filaments to stack, and how thick, at every point of the print. The section has two parts — how colors are matched (Recipe Search) and how the image is carved into color patches (Region Construction).


                  
                  📸 Screenshot to capture 
                  
                

The Color Solver section of the settings drawer with Advanced: On, showing both the Recipe Search and Region Construction tables.


Appearance Model
The calibrated prediction of what color a stack of filaments makes when backlit. Color Model v2 (default) is the newer, more accurate model; Color Model v1 is the older one, kept for comparison. This choice affects everything downstream — the solve, the suggested palettes, and every preview.
Recipe Search

Out-of-gamut handling (advanced) — what happens to photo colors your palette simply can’t make. Nearest reachable color (default) substitutes the closest color the palette can print. Preserve hue keeps the hue, mutes the vividness, and nudges brightness only when a color is too dark or bright to print — often gentler on skin tones and skies.
White-point rescale (advanced) — scales the image so its white matches the brightest white the print can make. Keeps pale tints (light skies, whites with a hint of color) from being flattened to plain white. Previews will read slightly darker and warmer with it on — that’s the print’s reality.
Color corrections — applies the calibration’s measured correction data when predicting stack colors. Leave on; turning it off makes predictions less accurate.
Max colors per region — how many different colored filaments may stack at a single point (1–7). More lets tricky colors be mixed better, but slows the solve and makes busier stacks. 3 is a good middle.
Color mismatch tolerance (advanced) — how far off a color must be before it counts as unreachable and gets remapped. The difference is measured as dE (delta E), a perceptual color-difference estimate; lower is stricter.
Chroma weight (advanced) — a slider from Tone to Color. Center is balanced; drag toward Color to make the matching favor hue and vividness, toward Tone to favor brightness. Each step doubles or halves the weight shown.

Region Construction
Prisma doesn’t pick a recipe per pixel — it first divides the image into small color patches (regions) and solves those. These settings set how that patchwork is drawn.

Region method (advanced) — how regions are drawn. Image regions (default) and Superpixels follow the picture’s own structure; Fixed grid uses uniform squares.
Region planning scale (advanced) — plan the regions on a coarser version of the image (1× = full resolution). Higher makes broader, simpler regions and faster solves, but follows fine edges less closely.
Color region target — the intended size of a color patch, in millimeters. Smaller follows the image more faithfully; larger gives simpler, cleaner prints.
Local recipe corrections (advanced) — lets small spots inside a region use a better-matching recipe when the improvement is strong. Preserves fine detail, at the cost of more small patches. On by default.

Boundary mutation
Boundary mutation (advanced) lets boundary points borrow a recipe from the region immediately across the border when that recipe matches the photo better. It is on by default. The change is accepted in connected boundary runs, so the result shifts a contour instead of scattering unrelated points.

Mutation passes — the maximum number of refinement passes (1–16). Each pass can move the boundary one solve point farther; processing stops early when nothing else improves.
Mutation current-dE percentile — only consider boundary points whose current dE is among the worst. Empty considers all boundary candidates; the cutoff is recalculated each pass.
Mutation min gain — the minimum average color-error improvement a connected run must achieve. Empty uses the default shown in the field.
Mutation min contact — the minimum length along which a proposed run must touch the region whose recipe it borrows. Raising it rejects short, weakly attached shifts.

Figures for review

Image regions form unequal patches around image structure; Superpixels favor compact patches that still follow edges; Fixed grid uses uniform cells regardless of the picture.

Boundary mutation refines an existing recipe boundary; it does not introduce a new recipe. Each pass can advance a boundary by one solve point.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-to-use/s.title: Preprocessing Module Settings
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-to-use/s.content:
.htu-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.htu-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.htu-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.htu-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}SettingsPreprocessingModulesColorSolver


Preprocessing changes the image before color solving starts. It can reduce noise, simplify detail that will not survive printing, or move tones and saturation toward what the selected palette can reproduce. These are creative controls as much as cleanup tools: use the preview and compare runs rather than assuming stronger is better.


                  
                  📸 Screenshot to capture 
                  
                

The Pre-processing section of the settings drawer, with the module toggles visible and one module set to Custom so its fields show.


Resample kernel (advanced)
How the photo is shrunk onto the solve grid. Lanczos (default) keeps things sharper; Area gives a softer, smoother result that can suit coarse prints. It only matters when the photo is larger than the solve grid — which it almost always is.
The modules
Five modules run in a fixed order, each switched on or off independently:
Noise Reduction → Print-Scale Smoothing → Flat-Area Smoothing → Palette Tone Fit → Palette Saturation Fit
All five start off on a fresh install. Each module has strength presets plus Off and Custom; picking Custom reveals its individual fields. The first three change spatial detail. The last two change the target’s tone or saturation and do nothing until a palette exists.
Noise Reduction
Softens fine grain and noise while trying to preserve edges. It is a useful first step when texture or sensor noise is fragmenting the solved color regions. Custom fields:

Filter radius — how large an area each point is smoothed over.
Color similarity — how different two colors can be and still get blended. Higher smooths across stronger color differences.
Spatial reach — how far the smoothing extends, in pixels.

Print-Scale Smoothing
Off by default. Smooths away detail finer than your printer can physically render, producing larger, simpler color patches. Its strength automatically tracks your nozzle size and solve pitch. Custom fields:

Feature scale — scales the smoothing radius: below 1 keeps more detail, above 1 flattens more.
Color similarity — as above.
Passes — how many times the smoothing is applied.

Flat-Area Smoothing
Off by default. Collapses gradual texture into broad flat areas — at higher strengths the image takes on a painted, graphic look. Custom fields:

Flattening strength — how aggressively texture is flattened.
Scale strength to print width — ties the strength to your printer’s real resolution so it tracks what’s printable.
Flattening mode — what gets flattened: lightness only, lightness and color, or everything.
Iteration limit — a cap on how long the flattening computation runs.

Palette Tone Fit
Off by default. Needs a palette. Remaps the photo’s brightness range to the darkest and lightest your palette can physically print, so shadows and highlights land where the filaments can reach instead of being clipped. Custom fields:

Tone fit strength — how fully the remap is applied (0 = none, 1 = full).
Shadow anchor — how much of the darkest part of the image is treated as “black.”
Highlight anchor — how much of the brightest part is treated as “white.”
Midtone curve — bends the in-between tones lighter or darker.

Palette Saturation Fit
Off by default. Needs a palette. Gently pulls colors that are more vivid than your palette can print back within its reach, keeping their hue and brightness. Softer than letting the solver clip them. Custom fields:

Compression start — how close to the palette’s limit a color must be before it starts getting pulled in. Lower starts earlier and affects more of the image.
Compression softness — how gradual the pull-in is.

Figure for review

The first three modules simplify spatial detail in different ways. The palette-aware modules instead move tone or saturation toward what the selected palette can reproduce.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-to-use/s.title: White Cap Settings
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-to-use/s.content:
.htu-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.htu-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.htu-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.htu-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}ColorSolverWhiteCapPreview


Every lithophane has a white cap above the color stack. The cap diffuses the backlight, affects the predicted appearance, and forms the viewing surface. It has two required parts: the boundary cap, which continuously covers the solved color stacks, and the detail cap, which adds localized white relief above that boundary where the image calls for it.


                  
                  📸 Screenshot to capture 
                  
                

The White Cap section of the settings drawer with Advanced: On, showing the Boundary and Detail sub-sections.


Min Cap Layers
The minimum number of boundary-cap layers everywhere above the colors. Its minimum thickness is this count multiplied by Layer Height. The app requires at least one layer so every solved color stack has continuous white cover.
Boundary

Shading balance (Luminance mode only) — where light-and-dark variation is carried. Toward Smooth, more of it goes into the broader boundary-cap surface; toward Detail, more goes into localized detail relief. Suggest proposes a balance from the selected image.
Boundary cap (advanced) — the cap’s character. Detail Aware (default) keeps the cap as thin as it can wherever thickening it would visibly change the image. Smooth prioritizes a clean, continuous outer surface instead.
Appearance budget (advanced, Detail Aware only) — how much visible color change you’ll tolerate in exchange for a smoother cap. Lower protects the image more aggressively.
Smoothing radius (Smooth only) — how far the cap’s top surface is smoothed, in millimeters. Lower keeps more tonal relief; higher gives a cleaner surface. The cap’s underside always fits the colors exactly either way.

Detail

Detail depth — the maximum number of white layers the detail cap may add above the boundary cap. It is a limit, not a target: the detail cap can appear as separated bumps and ridges rather than covering the entire surface. At 0, the detail-cap stage still runs but has no extra height available to place.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-to-use/s.title: Settings
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-to-use/s.content:
.htu-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.htu-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.htu-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.htu-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}PaletteSettingsPreviewPreprocessingModulesColorSolverWhiteCap


Settings control how Prisma builds the lithophane — its thickness and resolution, any preprocessing applied to the image, how colors are matched, and how the white cap is built. The defaults are sensible: you can make a good print without opening this drawer at all.
The settings drawer
Press the Settings gear (top right) to slide the drawer in from the right — it works from any tab. Pills along the top of the drawer switch between sections: Essentials, Pre-processing, Color Solver, and White Cap. The square button expands the drawer to full width; the × closes it.
Advanced: Off / On (in the drawer header) hides or reveals the less-common settings. Leave it off at first — everything you need day to day is visible without it.


                  
                  📸 Screenshot to capture 
                  
                

The settings drawer open on Essentials, with Advanced: Off — the section pills, the profile bar, the stack diagram, and the Essentials table.


There’s no OK or Apply — changes take hold as you make them, and they apply to the next solve. A solve already running or finished keeps the settings it started with. Exporting an older run uses that run’s frozen settings rather than whatever is currently in the drawer.
Profiles
The bar at the top of the drawer manages settings profiles — named saves of the entire settings collection. The current profile’s name is shown, with a marker when you’ve changed something since it was saved.

Profiles… opens the profiles window: pick a profile from the list to load it, or Restore System Defaults to go back to a factory state.
Save stores your current settings into the current profile.
Save As… stores them under a new name.



                  
                  📸 Screenshot to capture 
                  
                

The Settings Profiles window with a few profiles in the list.




                  
                  📸 Screenshot to capture 
                  
                

The Save Settings Profile As window.


Profiles are how you keep useful setups around — for example, a high-detail profile and a quicker draft profile — and switch between them in two clicks. When you find settings that work, save them.
Essentials
The everyday section: the print’s physical envelope and the one big quality choice. The diagram at the top shows the stack these settings describe — white base on the bottom, color layers, white cap on top, viewed from the cap side.

Solve Mode — the biggest single choice in the app. Color aims the filament stacks directly at the image’s colors. Luminance lets white-cap thickness carry more of the image’s brightness and fine detail, with color underneath. Compare both when subtle light-and-dark structure matters; the better choice depends on the image and palette.
Solve Pitch — the size of one solve point, in millimeters. Smaller = more detail but slower solves and exports. The recommended value follows your active nozzle; there’s little point going finer than the nozzle can print.
Max Total Thickness — the print’s total thickness budget. Thicker gives the solver more layers to work with — deeper darks and richer color — at the cost of print time.
Layer Height — must exactly match the layer height you’ll slice with. If these disagree, the printed colors won’t match the preview.
White Base/Cap Filament — the white used for the solid base and the top cap. This is chosen here, not in the palette (see Palette).
Base Thickness — the solid white plate the print sits on.

The line under the table shows what these work out to — how many color layers the budget leaves, and the resulting stack.
The other sections
Each has its own page describing every setting and what it does to the print. The short version:

Preprocessing Module Settings — optional clean-up of the photo before solving: noise reduction, smoothing toward printable detail, and reshaping tones and saturation toward what your palette can reproduce. Each module is a simple preset picker; all start off.
Color Solver — how colors are matched. The everyday controls: the Appearance Model (the calibrated color prediction — v2 is the default), Color corrections (leave on), Max colors per region (how many filaments may stack in one spot), and Color region target (how fine the color patchwork is).
White Cap — the white layer above the colors. Day to day: Min Cap Layers (never below 1) and, in Luminance mode, Shading balance (whether broad shading comes from smooth cap thickness or fine relief).

There is no separate swap-planning setting. When a palette needs more colors than your printer can hold at once, Prisma plans the required filament bands automatically during the solve. See Runs with Swaps for when to use them and how to carry the plan into the slicer.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-to-use/i.content:
.htu-diagram svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.htu-diagram a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.htu-diagram a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.htu-diagram a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}Set up onceMake each lithophaneConfigurationImagePaletteSettingsPreviewExport3D Printing


A color lithophane is a thin printed panel that reveals a color image when lit from behind. You give Prisma a photo and the filaments available to you; it works out a printable stack and exports the files your slicer needs.
This section is the practical guide to the app. It explains what to do and what each choice changes. For a conceptual view of the machinery underneath, see How It Works.
The workflow in the app
The conceptual workflow and the controls are nearly the same, but a few decisions live outside the numbered tabs:





































In the appWhat you are decidingConfiguration in the left railWhich calibrated filaments and printer setup are available. This is mostly one-time setup.1 ImageWhich image area to print, its physical size, and any image adjustments.2 PaletteWhich colored filaments the solve may use.Settings gearOptional solve, preprocessing, region, and white-cap behavior for the next run.Solve → 3 PreviewBuild a run, inspect the prediction, and compare it with earlier runs.4 ExportChoose a completed run and generate its 3MF or STL files and any Swap Instructions.3D PrintingMove the generated files into the slicer, prepare the printer, and light the finished panel.
Most iteration happens between Palette, Settings, and Preview. Change one meaningful thing, solve again, and compare the runs side by side.

New here? Getting Started covers installing and launching the app and walks through a first solve.

Setup

Configuration — tell Prisma which filaments you own and which printer setup is active.

Make a lithophane

Image — choose a photo, set the physical print size, and frame it.
Palette — choose colored filaments manually or ask Prisma to suggest them.
Settings — tune print thickness, solve behavior, preprocessing, and the white cap when needed.
Preview — build and compare predicted results.
Export — generate print files for a selected completed run.

Special workflow

Runs with Swaps — use more colored filaments than the printer can hold at once and carry the resulting Swap Instructions into the slicer.

After export

3D Printing — slice, print, and light the result.
Tutorials — worked examples from start to finish.

Clear Temp Files in the top bar removes accumulated working files, solve history, automatic saves, and internal caches. It does not delete exported files or runs you explicitly saved.

prisma-lithophane-generator/technical-re.title: Color-core library
prisma-lithophane-generator/technical-re.content:
In one sentence: the Prisma/lib/ color core is the shared, framework-free toolbox of color-space conversions, two non-interchangeable ΔE definitions, the spline transmission model (build / predict / compose / pair-correct), adjacent-layer collapsing, the filament-registry accessor, and the Camera Transform loader (forward fit, Newton inverse, trilinear LUT) that both the generator and calibration apps build on.

This page documents the modules under Prisma/lib/ that the generator solve path depends on. These are pure helpers — no FastAPI, no disk writes beyond reading JSON/.npz artifacts. If you are wiring a new solve stage, this is the layer you import from. For how these pieces compose into a render, see The Transmission Model and generator.model; for the color-domain contracts, see Model-domain ingress.
Related technical references: Model-domain ingress and display conversion.
Related architecture nodes: lib.transmission, lib.color, lib.stack_geometry, lib.filaments, lib.camera_transform.

Two ΔE definitions — not interchangeable
The repo has two distinct color-difference functions that live in different modules, use different color spaces, and serve different consumers. Mixing them up is a real trap. (One wiring caveat: the generator’s deltaE_ok path is live, but the lib/color.py compute_dE_from_linear shown here is a dormant copy — the calibration app consumes an identical duplicate; details below.)























FunctionSpaceFormulaSourcedeltaE_ok(lab1, lab2)OKLabEuclidean distance in OKLablib/transmission.py:59compute_dE_from_linear(measured, predicted)CIE Lab (CIE76)Euclidean distance of CIE-Lab tripletslib/color.py:95

deltaE_ok operates on OKLab coordinates produced by linear_to_oklab (lib/transmission.py:40). It is the generator’s perceptual metric — the solver imports linear_to_oklab directly (generator/model.py:22, used at generator/model.py:160) and compares candidates in OKLab. The module docstring’s claim that OKLab is “faster than CIEDE2000” is a design note, not a guarantee — what matters is it is a different space from CIE76.
compute_dE_from_linear converts each linear-RGB triplet to CIE Lab via linear_to_lab (lib/color.py:77, an approximate D65 transform) and returns the plain CIE76 distance (lib/color.py:99). This is the calibration metric in spirit, but watch the wiring: the calibration fitting and composition paths import a byte-for-byte duplicate from calibration/fitting/color_math.py (defined at calibration/fitting/color_math.py:93), not this lib/color.py copy. The current lib/color.py importer is the modeling-review linear_to_hex call described below; it does not make this CIE76 helper live.

Practical rule: a “ΔE 3.3” reported by the generator’s OKLab metric and a “ΔE 3.3” from the calibration CIE76 metric are not the same number. Never compare them across the two systems. See Delta E definitions.

OKLab round-trip (lib/transmission.py)

























FunctionWhat it doesSourcelinear_to_oklab(rgb_linear)linear-sRGB (...,3) in [0,1] → OKLab; vectorised over arbitrary leading dims via the _M1/_M2 matriceslib/transmission.py:40oklab_to_linear(lab)OKLab → linear-sRGB; inverts _M2, cubes LMS, inverts _M1, then clips to [0,1]lib/transmission.py:51deltaE_ok(lab1, lab2)scalar Euclidean OKLab distancelib/transmission.py:59
Note the round-trip is not loss-free at the gamut edge: oklab_to_linear clips its output to [0,1] (lib/transmission.py:56), so OKLab values that map outside the unit cube are clamped. The matrices are the standard Björn Ottosson OKLab coefficients hard-coded at lib/transmission.py:27 and :33.
linear_to_oklab is the generator’s entry point into perceptual space — generator/model.py:160 wraps it as to_oklab(...) and casts to float32.

sRGB / linear / Lab helpers (lib/color.py)
These are the scalar, stdlib-only conversions (the module imports only math). They are the calibration-flavored cousins of the vectorised numpy helpers above.

Liveness: lib/color.py is only partially wired. The calibration modeling-review path imports its linear_to_hex helper (calibration/modeling_review.py:13, used at :225), and the server reaches that review builder (calibration/server.py:111, :8285). The other helpers below, including compute_dE_from_linear, linear_to_lab, and the interpolation functions, have no current importer found in the production tree; the calibration fitting path uses its duplicate calibration/fitting/color_math.py instead. Treat this module as a mixed boundary: linear_to_hex is live for modeling-review presentation, while the remaining functions are dormant reference utilities.
















































FunctionDirectionNotesSourcelinear_to_srgb(c)linear [0,1] → sRGB [0,255] intexact sRGB piecewise transfer (0.0031308 / 2.4 gamma)lib/color.py:54linear_to_hex(r,g,b)linear [0,1] → #RRGGBBwraps linear_to_srgblib/color.py:64srgb_to_linear(c)sRGB [0,255] int → linear [0,1]inverse sRGB transferlib/color.py:69linear_to_lab(rgb_linear)linear RGB → CIE Labapproximate D65, sRGB→XYZ matrix + f(t)lib/color.py:77interp_single(knots, values, d)scalar interpolationlinear interp; log-linear extrapolation past the last knot (lib/color.py:20)lib/color.py:12interpolate_pchip(knots, values, d_dense)vector PCHIPfalls back to interp_single when <2 knots or scipy missing (lib/color.py:36, :50)lib/color.py:31
interp_single / interpolate_pchip are the single-value interpolators of the calibration color pipeline (live via the calibration/fitting/color_math.py duplicate, not this module — see the liveness note above); they are distinct from the three-channel build_spline/predict pair in transmission.py. Note linear_to_srgb here is the exact sRGB transfer with the 2.4 exponent, whereas transmission.to_srgb uses a plain gamma=2.2 power (see below) — two different gamma conventions in the core, used in different places.

Spline transmission model (lib/transmission.py)
This is the heart of The Transmission Model: measured (thickness, T_rgb) knots interpolated with monotone cubic (Pchip), not Beer-Lambert. Composition is multiplicative and order-independent (the corrections term excepted).
Build / predict






























FunctionContractSourcebuild_spline(knots_mm, T_r, T_g, T_b)returns {'r','g','b'} of PchipInterpolator with extrapolate=False; asserts knots_mm[0] == 0.0 (lib/transmission.py:81) and clips T to [0,1]lib/transmission.py:67predict(profile, d)linear-RGB (3,) transmission at thickness d. d<=0 → ones(3); d>d_max → _extrapolate; otherwise clipped spline evallib/transmission.py:89_get_splines(profile)lazily builds and caches splines under profile['_splines']lib/transmission.py:138_extrapolate(profile, spl, d, d_max)Beer-Lambert slope extrapolation from the last two knots when d exceeds the measured rangelib/transmission.py:120

De-facto public despite the underscore. _get_splines and _extrapolate are imported by name across the generator and are part of the real contract, not private internals:

generator/palette/suggest.py:57 (vectorised T sampling)
generator/lut.py:2025 (legacy cap-fixed-color helper)
generator/pipeline/staged_solver_helpers.py:60 (the staged backend solve path — see generator.pipeline.staged_runner)

They are duplicated, not shared, in calibration/fitting/fitting.py:171,189 — calibration carries its own copy. Treat the transmission.py pair as the canonical generator-side definitions.

Compose / pair-corrections



































FunctionContractSourcecompose(layers, corrections=None)multiply predict over an ordered [(profile, d), ...] stack; optionally apply a per-pair correction factor C(d_overlay); final clip [0,1]lib/transmission.py:146_interpolate_correction(corr, d)linear interp of C_r/C_g/C_b over the correction’s knots_mm; anchored C=1 at d=0, holds constant past the last knotlib/transmission.py:183to_srgb(T_linear, gamma=2.2)gamma-encode linear transmission (plain pow(1/gamma))lib/transmission.py:196profile_from_dict(d)pre-build splines and return the (mutated) dictlib/transmission.py:203profile_to_save_dict(profile)drop the non-serializable _splines key for JSON savinglib/transmission.py:209
Pair-correction key format (verify before constructing one): when len(layers) >= 2, compose builds the lookup key from the first layer as overlay and the rest as base (lib/transmission.py:168-179):
pair_key = f"{overlay_fid}|{base1_fid}@{d1:.2f}+{base2_fid}@{d2:.2f}..."

i.e. "overlay|base@0.20" with thicknesses formatted to two decimals. Each profile must carry a filament_id for this to match; absent it, the key uses an empty string and the correction silently no-ops.
compute_pair_corrections lives elsewhere. The compose/build_spline docstrings reference compute_pair_corrections(), but that producer is not in this module — it is defined in calibration/fitting/fitter_core.py and writes data/filaments/pair_corrections.json. The generator only consumes the resulting dict: it loads the JSON through generator/server.py and threads it through the solve configuration to the active provider/LUT paths. See Pair corrections.

Adjacent-layer collapsing (lib/stack_geometry.py)
For prediction, a light path through A 0.40 + A 0.20 + W 0.20 sees A 0.60 + W 0.20 — adjacent same-filament runs are one contiguous region, but non-adjacent repeats stay separate because interface order matters.

























FunctionContractSourcecollapse_adjacent_layers(layers, *, precision=5, drop_zero=True)merge adjacent same-filament runs, preserving order; rounds thickness to precision, drops sub-epsilon and (optionally) zero layerslib/stack_geometry.py:31canonicalize_filament_stack(filaments, thicknesses_mm, *, ...)zip parallel lists then collapselib/stack_geometry.py:62unzip_layers(layers)inverse: a layer sequence → parallel (filaments, thicknesses) tupleslib/stack_geometry.py:82
Live in the generator: generator/appearance_model.py:29 imports collapse_adjacent_layers and calls it at appearance_model.py:294 before predicting a stack. Also used calibration-side: calibration/fitting/physical_stack.py:255 (imports at :16/:18) and lib/photo_stack_model/predictor.py:1478 (imports at :25/:27). The example transforms in the docstring (stack_geometry.py:40-41) match the code behavior.

Note: appearance_model’s appearance-named methods are pass-through after the projection-slot retirement — they return model-domain values, not display values. Collapsing happens regardless; the naming is the stale part, not the geometry. See generator.appearance_model.


Filament registry accessor (lib/filaments.py)
Thin JSON reader over data/filaments/registry.json. No caching — every call re-reads the file.

























FunctionReturnsSourceload_registry(registry_path)the full dict keyed by filament_idlib/filaments.py:9list_filament_ids(registry_path)sorted list of IDslib/filaments.py:15get_filament(registry_path, filament_id){"filament_id": id, **info} or None if absentlib/filaments.py:20
get_filament injects filament_id into the returned dict (lib/filaments.py:26) — convenient, because compose’s pair-correction key needs exactly that field. All three take an explicit registry_path: Path; the module hard-codes no location. See lib.filaments.

Camera Transform artifact (lib/camera_transform.py)
The Camera Transform (CT) is the color bridge between the model domain (predicted transmission RGB) and display sRGB. It has two directions:

Forward F — model RGB → camera-rendered display sRGB. A Finlayson degree-2 root-polynomial matrix (rp_features) followed by monotone PCHIP curves.
Inverse G — display sRGB → model RGB, used for image ingress. Baked once into a 33³ trilinear LUT.

The on-disk schema is camera_transform_v1 carrying a v2 fit model (camera_transform.py:20, :183-187). See Camera Transform and Model-domain ingress.
Artifact layout, generation-pinning, sha256



































ConstantValueSourceCAMERA_TRANSFORM_JSONcamera_transform.json (fit params)camera_transform.py:21CAMERA_TRANSFORM_LUTinverse_lut_33.npz (baked G)camera_transform.py:22CAMERA_TRANSFORM_MANIFESTmanifest.json (hashes)camera_transform.py:23CAMERA_TRANSFORM_CURRENTCURRENT (generation pointer)camera_transform.py:24N_KNOTS=10, N_W=18, N_PARAMS=48, LUT_SHAPE=(33,33,33,3)model dimscamera_transform.py:26-32
Generation pinning. A CT directory holds dated gen-* subdirs plus a CURRENT file naming one of them. _read_current_generation (camera_transform.py:69) reads CURRENT, and rejects anything that is absolute or not a single local path component (camera_transform.py:80) — a guard against pointer traversal. _resolve_artifact_file (camera_transform.py:88) transparently follows CURRENT when the path is a directory, so callers pass the CT root and get the pinned generation’s file.
SHA-256 integrity. When a generation dir is resolved, _verify_generation_hashes (camera_transform.py:160) loads manifest.json, requires an artifact_hashes map containing both filenames, and recomputes each file’s SHA-256 (_sha256_file, camera_transform.py:139) — raising CameraTransformError on mismatch (:175). Both load_camera_transform and load_inverse_lut run this verification before reading (camera_transform.py:205, :337). Separately, load_camera_transform records the raw JSON bytes’ SHA-256 on the returned CameraTransform.sha256 (camera_transform.py:223) for downstream provenance.
Caching. Both loaders cache by (resolved_path, mtime_ns) and clear the cache on every miss (camera_transform.py:225, :351) — a deliberate single-entry cache, not an unbounded one.
Runtime ownership. In the packaged Generator, PRISMA_PUBLISHED_LIBRARY_MODE=1 and the launcher-provided model-library root keep Camera Transform resolution inside the one active immutable published library. _resolve_data_root_default therefore does not consult Calibration or re-root that active path. _configured_data_root and the legacy Prisma/calibration/.data-root pointer remain only as a source-development/compatibility fallback when published-library mode is not active (camera_transform.py:127-:160).
Validators




















ValidatorChecksSourcevalidate_camera_transform_payload(payload, *, path)dict; schema == "camera_transform_v1"; model_version == "v2"; used_lattice falsy (lattice unsupported, :188); params shape (48,) and finite; n_params/n_knots matchcamera_transform.py:178validate_inverse_lut(lut, *, path)shape (33,33,33,3); all finitecamera_transform.py:325
Both raise CameraTransformError whose message appends the actionable "Rebuild via Calibration -> Camera Transform." (camera_transform.py:34, :136).
Forward F, Newton inverse, trilinear LUT


















































FunctionRoleSourcerp_features(linear_rgb)degree-2 root-polynomial features [r,g,b,√(rg),√(gb),√(rb)]camera_transform.py:244unpack_params(params)split the 48-vector into the (3,6) matrix w and the 3×10 curve knotscamera_transform.py:254_decode_knots(raw)monotone-positive PCHIP knot decode (softplus deltas, capped at OUT_MAX)camera_transform.py:230apply_forward(linear_rgb, params)F: root-poly matrix → clip → per-channel PCHIP curvecamera_transform.py:259invert_curve_channel(y_col, raw)invert one PCHIP curve (swap knot axes)camera_transform.py:273invert_forward(display_srgb, params, *, n_newton=4)G analytic: curve-invert, then Newton iteration on the root-poly residual with a hand-built Jacobiancamera_transform.py:279load_inverse_lut(path)load + validate the baked 33³ LUTcamera_transform.py:333apply_inverse_lut(img_srgb, lut)trilinear interpolation of the LUT over an sRGB image (auto-normalizes uint8 → [0,1])camera_transform.py:356
Where each runs — the load-bearing distinction. The generator’s image ingress does not call invert_forward. It loads the pre-baked LUT and trilinearly interpolates it:

generator/model.py:21 imports apply_inverse_lut, load_inverse_lut; calls them at model.py:120 / :125.
generator/model_domain_display.py:28 imports apply_forward, load_camera_transform; applies F at model_domain_display.py:44 (model RGB → display, for previews).

invert_forward (the Newton inverse) is called only at calibration bake time — calibration/fitting/camera_transform/lut.py:17 runs it over the 33³ grid to produce inverse_lut_33.npz. Grep finds no generator caller of invert_forward. So: the generator consumes the trilinear LUT; the Newton solve lives in the calibration bake. Do not expect invert_forward on a hot solve path.

Quick map: who imports what (generator side)

prisma-lithophane-generator/technical-re.title: Model-domain ingress and display conversion
prisma-lithophane-generator/technical-re.content:
In one sentence: the live solver converts source display-sRGB pixels through the committed Camera Transform inverse LUT into model-domain RGB before target-cloud construction, while generated preview artifacts convert model-domain predictions forward through the same transform for display.

This page is the implementation reference for the two domain boundaries. The conceptual explanation lives in Model-domain ingress and Camera Transform; this page records the actual runtime ownership, artifact contract, and failure behavior.
The domains and the boundary
The calibrated appearance model and the staged solver compare colors in model-domain RGB, then convert those values to OKLab for target matching and dE calculations. A source image arrives as display-encoded sRGB. The live product path therefore has this boundary:
loaded / adjusted display-sRGB image
  → Camera Transform inverse LUT G
  → model-domain RGB
  → OKLab target cloud
  → LUT / gamut / staged solve
The reverse boundary is used only for display-facing artifacts:
model-domain prediction
  → Camera Transform forward transform F
  → display-encoded sRGB PNG
The names predicted.png and target_transmission.png are consequently important: they are model/transmission-domain views encoded as PNG, not necessarily what a viewer would see on screen. predicted_appearance.png and predicted_color_only_appearance.png are the forward-transformed display-appearance views.
Ingress: source image to solve targets
The live solve calls compute_solve_target_cloud (pipeline/target_cloud.py:64) during the Load phase (pipeline/runner.py:1034). It calls image_to_target (model.py:128), then to_oklab (model.py:155), and finally projects the observation-grid OKLab values onto the solve grid with project_observation_to_solve_grid (target_cloud.py:80-90). The resulting SolveTargetCloud carries both observed_oklab and solve_oklab, their shapes, the fixed domain name model_oklab, and whether ingress was applied (target_cloud.py:18-28, :91-106).
image_to_target uses the configured inverse LUT when model_domain_ingress is true (model.py:148-151). The current server forces that setting on at product ingress and again while building SolveConfig (server.py:817-835, :1008-1018, :1104-1107). The False branch remains compatibility code: it returns ordinary sRGB-to-linear values (model.py:152) and is not a selectable current webapp product mode.
The image is already framed, resampled, and adjusted before this boundary. F1 preprocessing also runs before target-cloud construction. Therefore “ingress” is not the first operation on the raw upload: it is the domain conversion after source loading/adjustment and preprocessing, immediately before OKLab target construction.
Camera Transform artifact contract
The generator loads the transform through lib.camera_transform.load_camera_transform (lib/camera_transform.py:201) and the inverse LUT through load_inverse_lut (:333). A directory with a CURRENT pointer resolves to one generation; the loader verifies that generation’s manifest.json hashes before accepting camera_transform.json and inverse_lut_33.npz (lib/camera_transform.py:70-96, :142-176).
The accepted payload is camera_transform_v1 with model_version="v2", used_lattice=false, exactly 48 finite parameters, and ten monotone-curve knots per channel (lib/camera_transform.py:20-28, :178-199). The inverse LUT must have shape (33, 33, 33, 3) and finite values (:325-331).
Missing, malformed, schema-incompatible, or hash-mismatched artifacts raise CameraTransformError with the actionable instruction to rebuild through Calibration → Camera Transform (lib/camera_transform.py:44, :136). The generator does not silently fall back to gamma-only ingress when the product path requests the transform.
apply_inverse_lut performs trilinear interpolation over the 33³ table, accepts integer sRGB input by scaling it from [0,255] to [0,1], clamps coordinates, and returns float32 model-domain values (lib/camera_transform.py:356-389).
Display conversion and generated artifacts
After the staged solve produces a SolveResult, the server writes the normal model-domain predicted.png and then calls bake_view_domain_images (server.py:5028-5058). That helper:

recovers model-domain linear RGB from the gamma-2.2 encoded predicted.png;
applies the forward Camera Transform through apply_appearance_transform (model_domain_display.py:37-44); and
writes predicted_appearance.png as display-encoded sRGB.

For the source-side comparison, the same helper applies the inverse ingress LUT to the source image and writes target_transmission.png using the model-domain PNG encoder. Its return value contains the display-transform path and transform SHA-256, which the server stores under run_metadata["model_domain_display"] (server.py:5452).
The color-only recipe-viewer render follows the same forward transform through bake_appearance_png (model_domain_display.py:47-70, invoked at server.py:5075-5084). SolveResult.predict_image_color_only first zeroes white-cap terms and reuses the model-domain composition path (facade.py:406-417); the server then bakes that result into predicted_color_only_appearance.png.
The raw predicted.png remains available for transmission/model-domain inspection. The UI’s predicted-print view uses the appearance artifact when it is present, while the technical artifact bundle retains both domains so a run can be diagnosed without guessing which conversion occurred.
Provenance and current-path boundaries

The transform parameters and inverse LUT are one committed calibration generation selected by CURRENT; the loader caches them by resolved path and modification time (lib/camera_transform.py:201-224, :333-354).
The solve target cloud records domain="model_oklab"; gamut mapping and dE calculations operate on that cloud, not directly on display-sRGB values (pipeline/target_cloud.py:18-28, pipeline/runner.py:232-325, :327-445).
appearance_model.py prediction methods are model-domain pass-through APIs after the retired projection-slot conversion; display conversion belongs at the generator ingress/display boundary (appearance_model.py:218-221, :425-430).
The legacy CLI and compatibility constructors still expose model_domain_ingress=False defaults in lower-level helpers. That is not evidence of a live product fallback; the web server’s product configuration forces ingress on.

Related

Model-domain ingress — conceptual source-image explanation.
Camera Transform — conceptual calibration and transform explanation.
Color-core library — shared Camera Transform loader and color primitives.
The pipeline orchestrator and shared state — target-cloud placement in the Load phase.
The staged backend (Stage 0-5) — consumes model-domain targets.

prisma-lithophane-generator/technical-re.filePath: Prisma Lithophane Generator/Technical Reference/Conditioning/Image preprocessing the F1 slot.md
prisma-lithophane-generator/technical-re.title: Image preprocessing the F1 slot
prisma-lithophane-generator/technical-re.content:
In one sentence: the F1 slot takes the loaded image, runs an ordered, contract-enforced chain of preprocessing operators (each declaring its own color domain), and hands the result forward to target computation — inserting color-space conversions at every domain boundary and refusing to start if the chain is mis-wired.

Image preprocessing — the F1 slot
The F1 preprocessing slot is the stage that conditions the source image after filament profiles are loaded and before the solve target is computed. It is a pure function over image data: raster plus read-only context in, transformed raster plus an audit trace out. The actual operators that do the conditioning live on Preprocessing operators; the F2 shared service (palette metadata) that some operators consume lives on Palette metadata and protect masking. This page is about the runner that drives the chain and enforces the contract.
The slot runner is preprocessing/runner.py; its public types are preprocessing/types.py; the boundary converters are preprocessing/color_convert.py.
Where the slot sits in a solve
The slot is driven from the staged-backend pipeline runner, not the legacy CLI engine. run_pipeline (pipeline/runner.py:736) loads profiles, resolves preprocessing state, builds the LUTs and target cloud, and then hands off to the staged backend via run_staged_backend_path (pipeline/runner.py:1222–1225). The F1 slot executes inside run_pipeline, in between:















Before the slotThe slotAfter the slotProfiles loaded into state.profiles; appearance provider created during the Load phase.run_preprocessing_pipeline(...) called at pipeline/runner.py:1016.compute_solve_target_cloud(image, ...) at pipeline/runner.py:1034 computes the OKLab solve target from the post-preprocess raster.
Profiles load first so palette-aware operators can resolve their F2 context (pipeline/runner.py:997, resolve_palette_metadata_for_chain); the slot runs before target computation so the target OKLab reflects whatever conditioning the chain applied. This ordering is documented inline at pipeline/runner.py:985.
Liveness. The slot is live on the webapp solve path. The chain is resolved from live module state by _resolve_preprocessing_from_state (facade.py:438) and threaded into PipelineConfig.preprocessors (facade.py:645), which the webapp facade hands to run_pipeline (facade.py:845, facade.py:965). The whole F1 block is gated on if config.preprocessors: (pipeline/runner.py:991) — when no operators are enabled, the block is skipped entirely and the original raster flows through unchanged.
The runner contract — five things it does
run_preprocessing_pipeline (preprocessing/runner.py:210) does exactly five things, in order:

Sort enabled operators (preprocessing/runner.py:232).
Validate the chain shape before any work (preprocessing/runner.py:233).
Convert the raster at each operator’s input boundary (preprocessing/runner.py:247).
Run each operator and validate its output per-boundary (preprocessing/runner.py:252–253).
Preview: emit a per-operator snapshot frame, view-only (preprocessing/runner.py:273).

It returns (image, trace, accumulated_debug_maps) (preprocessing/runner.py:217): the post-preprocess raster in the last operator’s declared output domain, a list of one PreprocessingTraceStep per executed operator, and a dict of debug maps keyed <module_name>:<map_name> (preprocessing/runner.py:266).
1. Sort: (order, class qualname)
_sort_operators (preprocessing/runner.py:111) does a stable sort keyed on (float(getattr(op, "order", 1000.0)), f"{type(op).__module__}.{type(op).__qualname__}") (preprocessing/runner.py:117–123). So the primary key is the operator’s declared order (default 1000.0 on the base class, pipeline/base.py:93), and ties break deterministically on the fully-qualified class name — matching the registry’s lexical import-path discovery order.
Operators advertise their position with conventional order bands (documented at pipeline/base.py:80): Wing A 100–199, Wing B 200–299, Wing C 300–399, Wing D 400–499. For example, c2_soft_gamut_compress declares order = 330.0 (operators/c2_soft_gamut_compress.py:381), placing it in the Wing C band.
2. Validate the chain before running anything
_validate_chain (preprocessing/runner.py:126) enforces one rule: the last enabled operator must emit an sRGB output domain. It checks getattr(tail, "output_domain", None) against SRGB_OUT_DOMAINS (preprocessing/runner.py:136) and raises PreprocessingContractError otherwise (preprocessing/runner.py:137). SRGB_OUT_DOMAINS is frozenset({"srgb_u8", "srgb_f32"}) (types.py:35).
This check runs before any apply() call (preprocessing/runner.py:233, ahead of the loop at :243), so a mis-wired chain fails loudly with zero partial work. The error message is actionable — it names the offending operator and tells you to disable it or add a tail converter (preprocessing/runner.py:138–142). An empty chain is a legal no-op: _validate_chain returns immediately when not operators (preprocessing/runner.py:132), and the runner short-circuits with return image, [], {} for an empty sorted chain (preprocessing/runner.py:235–236).
3 & 4. Convert at boundaries, then run + validate per operator
The run loop (preprocessing/runner.py:243) carries a current raster and a current_domain. The ingress domain is inferred from the input raster’s dtype by _infer_ingress_domain (preprocessing/runner.py:189): uint8 → srgb_u8, float32 → srgb_f32 (preprocessing/runner.py:200–203); any other dtype raises PreprocessingContractError (preprocessing/runner.py:204). In practice the slot is entered from the post-load srgb_u8 raster, while many direct tests feed srgb_f32 (preprocessing/runner.py:194–197).
For each operator, the runner reads its declared input_domain (preprocessing/runner.py:244) and, if current_domain != in_dom, converts the raster to match (preprocessing/runner.py:247–248). The runner owns every boundary, including the very first one — the first enabled operator receives its declared input domain without normalizing inside apply().
After op.apply(...) (preprocessing/runner.py:252), _validate_apply_result (preprocessing/runner.py:146) enforces the per-boundary contract on what came back:








































CheckRaises if…AnchorTyperesult is not a PreprocessingResultpreprocessing/runner.py:152Image typeresult.image is not an np.ndarraypreprocessing/runner.py:158ShapeH/W differs from the input (img.shape[:2] != raw_input.shape[:2])preprocessing/runner.py:163Domaindeclared output_domain not in VALID_COLOR_DOMAINSpreprocessing/runner.py:169Dtypeactual dtype ≠ the domain’s expected dtype (_DOMAIN_DTYPE[declared])preprocessing/runner.py:174Finitenessany NaN/Inf in the outputpreprocessing/runner.py:179
_DOMAIN_DTYPE (preprocessing/runner.py:60) is the canonical dtype-per-domain map: srgb_u8 → uint8, the three *_f32 domains → float32. Every failure carries the offending operator’s name.
After validation the runner records one PreprocessingTraceStep (preprocessing/runner.py:256) with the operator’s name, input/output domains, cache_hit=False, and a copy of its metrics; then it merges the operator’s debug_maps into the accumulator (preprocessing/runner.py:265). Finally current and current_domain advance to the operator’s output (preprocessing/runner.py:287–288).

Note: PreprocessingTraceStep.cache_hit is hard-wired False here (preprocessing/runner.py:262); the runner itself does not cache operator outputs.

5. Preview emission — view-only
When a snapshot_publisher is supplied (preprocessing/runner.py:273), the runner canonicalizes the operator’s output to srgb_u8 via _to_srgb_u8_for_preview (preprocessing/runner.py:274) and publishes it under stage key preprocess/<module_name> (preprocessing/runner.py:281–283). This is view-only: the raster handed forward to the next operator stays in the declared domain (preprocessing/runner.py:287 advances current to result.image, not the previewed copy).
If the operator is palette-aware — "palette_metadata" in its required_context and the context actually carries metadata — the preview’s cache key folds in palette_metadata.request_fingerprint (preprocessing/runner.py:277–280) so the same module name under a different palette does not collide in browser cache. request_fingerprint is a real field on PaletteMetadata (palette_metadata.py:157).
The four color domains
The slot speaks exactly four color domains, defined as a Literal type (types.py:26) and enumerated in VALID_COLOR_DOMAINS (types.py:29):






























Domaindtype / rangeMeaningsrgb_u8uint8 [0, 255]sRGB primaries (Rec.709), D65, IEC 61966-2-1 transfer (types.py:5)srgb_f32float32 [0, 1]Same encoding as srgb_u8, normalized (types.py:7)linear_rgb_f32float32, nominally [0, 1]Same primaries + D65, linear light (no transfer); may exceed [0,1] for HDR-style ops (types.py:8)oklab_f32float32Ottosson OKLab, D65; L in [0,1], a/b in ~[−0.5, 0.5] (types.py:10)
Each operator declares an input_domain and output_domain from this set on the PreprocessingModule base class (pipeline/base.py:91–92, both default "srgb_u8"). The runner’s job is to bridge any mismatch between an operator’s output_domain and the next operator’s input_domain.
Per-boundary conversion
_convert (preprocessing/runner.py:70) is the boundary bridge. It is a no-op when src == dst (preprocessing/runner.py:76), routes the six adjacent pairs directly (preprocessing/runner.py:79–90), and two-hops every other pair through srgb_f32 (preprocessing/runner.py:92). So srgb_f32 is the single conversion hub; e.g. linear_rgb_f32 → oklab_f32 goes linear → srgb_f32 → oklab.
The conversion math lives in color_convert.py, and the runner imports exactly six helpers (preprocessing/runner.py:34–41):








































HelperDirectionNotessrgb_u8_to_srgb_f32u8 → f32divide by 255 (color_convert.py:22)srgb_f32_to_srgb_u8f32 → u8clamp [0,1], ×255, round half-to-even (color_convert.py:27)srgb_f32_to_linear_rgb_f32sRGB → linearIEC 61966-2-1 piecewise, sign-preserving, no clamp (color_convert.py:45)linear_rgb_f32_to_srgb_f32linear → sRGBpiecewise inverse, sign-preserving, no clamp (color_convert.py:62)srgb_f32_to_oklab_f32sRGB → OKLabtwo-hop via linear (color_convert.py:92)oklab_f32_to_srgb_f32OKLab → sRGBtwo-hop via linear (color_convert.py:97)
Two precision-relevant choices in color_convert.py:

It uses the true IEC 61966-2-1 piecewise transfer, not the **GAMMA approximation in model.py (color_convert.py:8), because round-trips through linear light must not bleed shadow precision near the project’s T_floor=0.003 noise floor (color_convert.py:11).
The sRGB↔linear helpers are sign-preserving and unclamped (color_convert.py:54, color_convert.py:70): HDR-style operators may temporarily exceed [0,1], and only the final emit to srgb_u8 clamps (color_convert.py:35). The OKLab conversions delegate to lib.transmission.linear_to_oklab / oklab_to_linear (color_convert.py:17), tying the slot’s color math to lib.transmission.

The runner inserts at most one converter per boundary, and operators never call these helpers directly except in tests (color_convert.py:5).
Read-only context handed to each operator
Every apply() receives a frozen PreprocessingContext (types.py:50). The runner builds it once per solve at pipeline/runner.py:1009 with:

config — the PipelineConfig (types.py:59)
image_fingerprint — from _fingerprint_preprocessing_image(image) (pipeline/runner.py:996)
source_path — None on the solve path (types.py:61)
source_image — the pre-slot raster (pipeline/runner.py:1013)
palette_metadata — the F2 service result, or None (types.py:63)

An operator only sees palette_metadata populated if it opts in via required_context (pipeline/base.py:94) — otherwise it stays None. palette_metadata is resolved exactly once per solve and only when at least one operator requests it (pipeline/runner.py:997, resolve_palette_metadata_for_chain). This service is documented on Palette metadata and protect masking. A concrete consumer: c2_soft_gamut_compress declares required_context = frozenset({"palette_metadata"}) (operators/c2_soft_gamut_compress.py:328).
The slot’s public types
All in preprocessing/types.py:

PreprocessingContractError (types.py:37) — the single exception type for every contract violation (wrong type/shape/dtype, non-finite output, illegal end-of-chain domain, ingress-dtype mismatch).
PreprocessingContext (types.py:50) — frozen, read-only, handed to every apply().
PreprocessingResult (types.py:67) — an operator’s return value: image, output_domain, optional debug_maps, optional metrics (types.py:74–77). Mutable (not frozen).
PreprocessingTraceStep (types.py:81) — one frozen audit row per executed operator; the list lives on PipelineState.

How to drive it (users)
You do not call the runner directly — you enable/order operators through the generator’s module management UI, which writes the live module state that _resolve_preprocessing_from_state reads (facade.py:438). Practical consequences of the contract above:

Order matters and is explicit. Operators run in order order, not enable order. If two operators tie, the class-name tiebreaker decides — see the Wing bands above.
A disabled chain is free. With no operators enabled, the whole F1 block is skipped (pipeline/runner.py:991) and the image passes through untouched.
The last operator must end in sRGB. If you build a custom chain whose final operator emits linear_rgb_f32 or oklab_f32, the solve aborts at chain-build time with a clear message (preprocessing/runner.py:137) — add a tail converter or reorder so an sRGB-emitting operator is last.
Previews are per-operator. Each enabled operator publishes a preprocess/<name> snapshot you can inspect; the previews are color-canonicalized to srgb_u8 for display but do not affect the data flowing downstream.

Related

Preprocessing operators — the actual operators (Wings A–D) and what each one does
Palette metadata and protect masking — the F2 palette-metadata service consumed via required_context
The solve target cloud — what consumes the post-preprocess raster
generator.pipeline.runner — the staged-backend runner that drives the slot
lib.transmission — OKLab conversion math the slot’s converters delegate to

prisma-lithophane-generator/technical-re.title: Palette metadata and protect masking
prisma-lithophane-generator/technical-re.content:
Palette metadata

In one sentence: F2 palette metadata samples what colors the chosen filament stack can actually reach — an achievable-color envelope (darkest/lightest points plus a per-hue, per-lightness chroma ceiling) — and hands it to the conditioning operators that compress tone and chroma toward what the print can reproduce.


Note — protect masking was removed. This page previously also documented an F3 protect-subject masking service (preprocessing/protect_mask.py, preprocessing/protect_blend.py, the rembg saliency provider, and brush/raster overrides). That whole subsystem has been deleted: those modules are gone, PreprocessingContext no longer carries a protect mask (preprocessing/types.py:63 holds only palette_metadata), and no operator consumes one. Only F2 survives, and it is what the rest of this page covers.

F2 runs in the generator.pipeline.runner preprocessing slot, before the image is turned into a solve target and before the The staged backend (Stage 0-5) does the actual layer solve. It is an input that conditioning operators (C1, C2) consume — it does not itself edit the image. It is resolved once per solve and passed down through PreprocessingContext.

F2 = “what colors can this palette make?” → fed to operators that compress toward the gamut or remap tone.

See also: Preprocessing operators · generator.preprocessing.palette_metadata

How it wires into a solve
F2 is resolved from pipeline/runner.py inside run_pipeline, which the webapp/facade uses. Preprocessing happens in the if config.preprocessors: block (pipeline/runner.py:991) — F2 resolves and the chain runs before the staged backend ever sees the raster.

























StepCall siteWhat happensF2 resolvepipeline/runner.py:997resolve_palette_metadata_for_chain(...) → PaletteMetadata | NoneHand to chainpipeline/runner.py:1009-1014stuffed into PreprocessingContext(palette_metadata=...)Chain runspipeline/runner.py:1016run_preprocessing_pipeline(...) runs each operator with that context
PreprocessingContext (preprocessing/types.py:50) now carries exactly one service field, palette_metadata (preprocessing/types.py:63); its ContextKey literal is "palette_metadata" (preprocessing/types.py:26).

What it produces (achievable-color envelope)

Source: preprocessing/palette_metadata.py.

resolve_palette_metadata returns a frozen PaletteMetadata (palette_metadata.py:143) with six pinned arrays plus a fingerprint:













































FieldShapeMeaningachievable_black_oklab(3,) float32The darkest OKLab point the stack can reach (lowest L among sampled stacks) — palette_metadata.py:151, palette_metadata.py:556achievable_white_oklab(3,) float32The lightest reachable OKLab point (highest L) — palette_metadata.py:152, palette_metadata.py:557max_chroma_by_hue(n_bins,) float32Per-hue-bin maximum reachable chroma — palette_metadata.py:153hue_degrees(n_bins,) float32Hue-bin centers those chroma caps belong to — palette_metadata.py:154l_bin_centers(n_l,) float32Lightness-bin centers for the 2D chroma ceiling — palette_metadata.py:155max_chroma_by_hue_l(n_bins, n_l) float32Per-(hue, lightness) chroma ceiling — palette_metadata.py:156request_fingerprintstr32-hex digest of the producing request — palette_metadata.py:157
The black/white anchors are C1’s input; the chroma envelopes are C2’s input. Binning uses _HUE_BINS_DEFAULT = 12 (30°-wide) and _L_BINS_DEFAULT = 8 (palette_metadata.py:162-163).
How the envelope is sampled
_candidate_oklab_points (palette_metadata.py:268) builds a cloud of OKLab points by composing transmission stacks within the print budget and projecting each to OKLab via compose + linear_to_oklab from lib/transmission.py (imported palette_metadata.py:50). It is explicitly an envelope sampler, not a full polytope enumeration (palette_metadata.py:287-289).
The coverage strategy (palette_metadata.py:277-282):

White sandwich alone — white base + white cap, across the d_wc samples (min / midpoint / max; _d_wc_samples, palette_metadata.py:193-204).
Single-filament stacks — each palette color at coarse thickness samples.
Pairs (k=2) — every 2-combination, when k_max >= 2.
Triples (k=3) — every 3-combination, when k_max >= 3.

Each stack must fit the color budget t_max - d_wb - d_wc (palette_metadata.py:300). The per-layer thickness-sample count is chosen adaptively (_adaptive_samples_per_layer, palette_metadata.py:254-265): the largest value in [_THICKNESS_SAMPLES_MIN=4, _THICKNESS_SAMPLES_MAX=8] (palette_metadata.py:171-172) whose combinatorial candidate count stays within _MAX_CANDIDATE_STACKS = 40_000 (palette_metadata.py:173, counted by _count_candidate_stacks, palette_metadata.py:207). Denser sampling raises each cell’s sampled max toward the true reachable max; the budget cap keeps resolve time bounded.
From that point cloud (resolve_palette_metadata, palette_metadata.py:518):

black/white = argmin/argmax of L (palette_metadata.py:555-557).
1D chroma envelope = _chroma_envelope (palette_metadata.py:372) bins points by hue and takes the max chroma per bin, empty bins set to 0 (palette_metadata.py:388-392).
2D hue×lightness ceiling = _chroma_envelope_by_hue_l (palette_metadata.py:486), with empty L-cells interpolated (_fill_chroma_envelope_l_holes, palette_metadata.py:424) and an L-only max dilation applied so queries near a cusp read the peak rather than an averaged-down value (_dilate_l_max_ceiling, palette_metadata.py:455).

If sampling somehow yields no points, the resolver falls back to the bare white-cap point for both anchors and all-zero chroma rather than failing (palette_metadata.py:531-553).
When it runs (opt-in) and how it is keyed
F2 is skipped unless some operator opts in. _chain_needs_palette_metadata (palette_metadata.py:582) returns True only if an operator declares "palette_metadata" in its required_context; otherwise resolve_palette_metadata_for_chain (palette_metadata.py:595) returns None and the chain sees context.palette_metadata = None (palette_metadata.py:608-609). The two opting-in operators are C1 (operators/c1_achievable_tonemap.py:217) and C2 (operators/c2_soft_gamut_compress.py:328) — both frozenset({"palette_metadata"}).
The request is the envelope-relevant slice of PipelineConfig, built by PaletteMetadataRequest.from_config (palette_metadata.py:91). It deliberately includes only fields that move the achievable envelope — palette (sorted, treated as an unordered set; palette_metadata.py:100), the white sandwich identities and thicknesses, t_max, k_max, layer_height, and corrections. It deliberately excludes solver weights like de_threshold / gamut_mode / chroma_weight, image resolution, and preprocessing params (palette_metadata.py:68-72). fingerprint() (palette_metadata.py:113) is a 32-char truncated SHA-256 over the rounded fields (palette_metadata.py:123-138); identical envelopes hash identically. This fingerprint is the palette-change invalidation key.
How C1 and C2 consume it




















OperatorUsesBehavior on missing / degenerateC1 achievable tonemapachievable_black_oklab / achievable_white_oklab L-endpoints to remap tone (c1_achievable_tonemap.py:311-312)raises if metadata is None (c1_achievable_tonemap.py:301-303)C2 soft gamut compresshue_degrees + max_chroma_by_hue + l_bin_centers + max_chroma_by_hue_l as the per-hue/per-lightness chroma ceiling (c2_soft_gamut_compress.py:391-406)raises if metadata is None (c2_soft_gamut_compress.py:386-388); returns an identity result if the envelope is empty / all-zero
C2 interpolates a per-pixel chroma bound around the hue circle via _query_chroma_bound (c2_soft_gamut_compress.py:28) and soft-knee-compresses chroma toward it. See The Transmission Model for the compose math the envelope sampler builds on and How a Solve Works for where preprocessing sits in the full solve.

Driving it (user-facing)

Reach a wider gamut fit / tone fit: enable C1 (achievable tonemap) and/or C2 (soft gamut compress). They self-resolve the F2 envelope; you do not configure F2 directly. Envelope width is determined by your palette, white sandwich, t_max, k_max, layer height, and corrections — those are the only knobs that move it (palette_metadata.py:68-72).


Liveness summary

F2 (resolve_palette_metadata_for_chain) — LIVE. Called pipeline/runner.py:997; opted into by C1 (c1_achievable_tonemap.py:217) and C2 (c2_soft_gamut_compress.py:328). Skipped (returns None) when no operator declares palette_metadata.
F3 protect masking — REMOVED. The service, blend, rembg provider, and overrides no longer exist; PreprocessingContext carries no protect mask.
