prisma-lithophane-generator/technical-re.title: Automatic palette suggestion
prisma-lithophane-generator/technical-re.content:
In one sentence: given your source image and a library of calibrated filaments, palette suggestion answers “which N color filaments should I load to print this picture?” — it summarizes the image as a handful of weighted OKLab colors, builds the color cloud each filament (and each pair of filaments) can physically reach when backlit, and picks the subset whose reachable cloud sits closest to the image’s colors.

This page covers the concept and the gamut machinery — how the image is reduced to a color signature, how filament gamut clouds are computed, and how a palette is scored by distance-to-nearest-gamut. The search, ranking, and swap-tier sweep that turn those scores into a ranked list live on Palette suggestion search and ranking. Backend node: generator.palette.suggest.

Trust the code, not the header. The module docstring at palette/suggest.py:8 still describes a 6-step “greedy → pairwise → local search → top-K” pipeline, and suggest_palettes still defaults search_mode="fast" (palette/suggest.py:1342). The web app no longer uses that path: the endpoint forces search_mode="thorough" (server.py:3875) and the “quality” mode raises if requested (palette/suggest.py:1412). Everything below is read from the live code.

How to drive it
Suggestion is a web-app feature on the conditioning side of the generator. POST /api/palette/suggest starts a background thread and returns {"status": "started", "job_id": "..."} immediately. GET /api/palette/suggest/status returns that same job id, progress, the eventual result, and whether cancellation has been requested. POST /api/palette/suggest/cancel?job_id=... atomically records the request; delayed worker entry cannot erase it, stale job ids are rejected, and the UI continues polling until the job reports a terminal state.
The request body is PaletteSuggestPayload (server.py:3511), which forbids unknown fields — stale clients that still send the removed search_mode/quality_weights get a loud 422 (server.py:3515):


















































FieldDefaultMeaningimage_pathrequiredimage under the generator’s images dir (server.py:3517)n_filaments7target palette size, color filaments only (server.py:3518)top_k5how many candidate palettes to return (server.py:3519)filament_idsNonerestrict the pool; None = all profiled filaments (server.py:3520)max_swapsNoneif set, run the AMS swap-tier sweep instead of a single suggest (server.py:3521)palette_mode"standard""standard" or "luminance_detail" (server.py:3522)improvement_thresholdNoneswap-tier early-stop gain % (server.py:3523)force_all_tiersNoneswap-tier: evaluate every tier regardless of gain (server.py:3524)
palette_mode is normalized before validation (server.py:3526): "source"/"source_color"/"source_color" all fold to "standard"; "luminance"/"detail"/"luminance-detail" fold to "luminance_detail"; anything else is rejected.
Two guardrails run before any work starts. The configured white base/cap are fixed inputs the suggester cannot drop, so if either is flagged exclude_from_model the endpoint refuses up front with a 400 (server.py:3766–3774). And color candidates flagged exclude_from_model are stripped from the pool via excluded_filament_ids(...) (server.py:3886) so an excluded filament never appears in a suggestion.
The three-part idea

Color signature — reduce the image to K weighted OKLab centroids (k-means). Each centroid is a representative color; its weight is how much of the image is that color.
Filament gamut clouds — for every filament, enumerate every printable (color-thickness × cap-thickness) stack and convert the predicted backlit RGB into OKLab. That point cloud is everything that filament can reproduce. Pairs of filaments get their own sampled cloud to capture mixed colors (a green from cyan + yellow).
Score = distance to nearest gamut — for a candidate palette, every signature centroid looks up its nearest point across the union of the palette’s single and pair clouds. The weighted mean of those nearest-distances (plus, in robust mode, the tail) is the palette’s error.

Steps 1 and 2 are this page. Step 3’s search and ranking are on Palette suggestion search and ranking.
Step 1 — the image color signature
The signature is a ColorSignature (palette/suggest.py:95): centroids (K×3 OKLab), weights (K, summing to 1), n_pixels, and a domain tag (default MODEL_OKLAB_DOMAIN, i.e. "model_oklab").
The web app does not cluster raw image pixels. It first runs the image through the same target-cloud path the solve runner uses, so the colors being matched are the colors a solve would actually try to hit. solve_target_oklab_for_signature (palette/suggest.py:323) calls compute_solve_target_cloud (pipeline/target_cloud.py:64) and returns its solve_oklab cloud, optionally applying the gamut-white rescale (palette/suggest.py:341). That cloud is then clustered by extract_color_signature_from_oklab (palette/suggest.py:286), which runs k-means and turns per-cluster pixel counts into normalized weights (palette/suggest.py:307).

Why the solve-equivalent cloud, not raw pixels? The signature’s domain must match the gamut clouds’ domain, or scoring is meaningless. The endpoint asserts this — _assert_signature_gamut_domain_match (palette/suggest.py:467) raises if sig.domain != gamut_backend.domain (called from palette/suggest.py:1404). Routing the image through the solve target cloud guarantees both sides live in model OKLab.

The k-means itself (_kmeans_oklab, palette/suggest.py:589) is a hand-rolled implementation: k-means++ seeding via a running-minimum distance (palette/suggest.py:599), then up to 30 Lloyd iterations using a scipy.spatial.KDTree for the assignment step and np.bincount for vectorised centroid updates (palette/suggest.py:617–632). Fixed seed 42 (palette/suggest.py:593), so a given image yields a stable signature. The web app asks for 100 clusters in standard mode (server.py:3842).

Saturated-corner caveat (from the code). Both solve_target_oklab_for_signature (palette/suggest.py:330) and extract_color_signature (palette/suggest.py:383) carry a docstring note: deeply saturated source pixels map to inverse-LUT corners that are extrapolated beyond measured swatch evidence and can shift between Camera Transform generations. Suggestion deliberately mirrors solve ingress for those pixels rather than promising stable precision — it leaves downstream gamut handling to the normal solve machinery. See Gamut mapping and Model-domain ingress.

Luminance-detail mode
When palette_mode == "luminance_detail", the endpoint swaps in extract_luminance_residual_signature (palette/suggest.py:482) with 120 clusters (server.py:3827). The premise (its docstring, palette/suggest.py:491): a luminance-detail solve lets the white cap carry most of the source’s lightness structure, so palette suggestion should chase chroma reach instead of fitting full source luminance as if the color stacks carried all the detail.
It does two things differently:

L is down-weighted for clustering. _scale_oklab_l (palette/suggest.py:454) multiplies the OKLab L axis by a small luminance_weight (0.15, server.py:3822) before k-means, so clusters split on chroma, not lightness (palette/suggest.py:529).
Centroids are chroma-weighted. Each cluster’s centroid is a chroma-importance-weighted average of its members (palette/suggest.py:556), and a cluster’s weight is the sum of its members’ chroma importance (palette/suggest.py:561), where chroma importance is the member’s chroma normalized against the 90th-percentile chroma and clipped to [0,1] (palette/suggest.py:519–521). Low-chroma grays contribute little weight; vivid colors dominate.

There is a companion metric knob, gamut_luminance_weight, derived from the session’s chroma_weight as 1.0 / chroma_weight in standard mode and detail_l_weight / chroma_weight in luminance-detail mode (server.py:3820, 3823). This scales the L axis again at scoring time (see “How a palette is scored” below). It is distinct from the clustering luminance_weight above.

extract_color_signature (palette/suggest.py:359) and extract_appearance_color_signature (palette/suggest.py:434, a deprecated alias with no remaining callers) are convenience wrappers that load + downsample + cluster in one call. extract_color_signature is exercised by the dev CLI (main, palette/suggest.py:1926) and tests, not the web endpoint, which assembles the signature step-by-step. Confirmed by grepping server.py: the endpoint imports extract_color_signature_from_oklab / extract_luminance_residual_signature (server.py:3788–3789), never the wrapper.

Step 2 — filament gamut clouds
A filament’s gamut is the set of OKLab colors it can produce when backlit, across every printable stack. Two providers exist for these clouds, chosen by which color model is active.
Which provider you get
_build_palette_suggestion_model (server.py:3656) resolves the backend from the session’s appearance_model_provider:




















Active color modelGamut sourceranking_modehistorical_spline (“Color Model v1”)the spline-profile functions in this module (server.py:3667)"mean" (server.py:3673)photo_stack_bundle (“Color Model v2”, default)PhotoStackPaletteGamutBackend (server.py:3696)"robust" (server.py:3722)
When the spline path is used gamut_backend is None, and suggest_palettes falls back to the in-module gamut functions. When the photo-stack model is active (the default) the backend object is passed through and used instead — same scoring contract, different color predictions. (Both report domain "model_oklab".) The photo-stack branch requires a calibration-fit bundle and 400s if none exists (server.py:3686).
Single-filament gamut
For the spline path, _compute_single_filament_gamut (palette/suggest.py:639) enumerates a 2-D grid: every color-layer count 0..max_layers × every sampled cap thickness from d_wc_min up to d_wc_max (sampling every 4th cap step for speed — cap_step=4, palette/suggest.py:648). It batch-evaluates the white-base, white-cap and color transmissions, multiplies them per the transmission model
T_total = T_wb · T_wc · T_color (palette/suggest.py:684),
masks out any stack whose cap + color height exceeds the budget t_max (palette/suggest.py:689), clips, and converts to OKLab (palette/suggest.py:697). The result is a few-hundred-point cloud per filament.
For the photo-stack path, PhotoStackPaletteGamutBackend.single_gamut (palette/suggest.py:227) does the same enumeration but predicts RGB through a _PhotoStackGridEvaluator (palette/suggest.py:158, 247) instead of multiplying spline transmissions, then converts to OKLab via _gamut_oklab_from_model_rgb (palette/suggest.py:214). Single clouds are cached per filament (palette/suggest.py:229).
Pair gamut — capturing mixed colors
Two filaments stacked produce colors neither can reach alone (the canonical example in the code: green from cyan + yellow, palette/suggest.py:15). _compute_pair_gamut (palette/suggest.py:700) samples n_samples=10 evenly-spaced thicknesses per filament (palette/suggest.py:732) across a coarser cap grid (cap_step=8, palette/suggest.py:711), builds the full T_wb · T_wc · T_a · T_b product over the 3-D meshgrid (palette/suggest.py:741), budget-masks, and converts to OKLab. The photo-stack equivalent is PhotoStackPaletteGamutBackend.pair_gamut (palette/suggest.py:253), cached per unordered pair.
Pairs are on by default (include_pairs=True, palette/suggest.py:1353). Pair clouds are precomputed for all C(N,2) filament pairs in _precompute_centroid_distances (palette/suggest.py:833–855), which is the dominant cost and the source of the “Computing pair gamuts i/N” progress messages (palette/suggest.py:839).
Whites are not color candidates
The photo-stack backend’s supports(fid) (palette/suggest.py:187) returns False for any white filament (is_white(text), palette/suggest.py:193) and for filaments absent from the model’s curves. The white base and white cap are fixed parameters of every gamut (the T_wb/T_wc factors), never selectable members of the palette.
How a palette is scored (the bridge to ranking)
The gamut clouds feed scoring through one precomputation. _precompute_centroid_distances (palette/suggest.py:795) builds, for each filament and each pair, a per-centroid nearest-neighbor distance array: it scales both the gamut points and the signature centroids’ L axis by gamut_luminance_weight (palette/suggest.py:820, 827), builds a KDTree over the scaled gamut, and queries each centroid (palette/suggest.py:828). The result is dist_single[fid] and dist_pair[(a,b)], each a (K,) vector.
Given a candidate palette, _palette_distance_vector (palette/suggest.py:859) takes the element-wise minimum across the palette’s single distances and all its pair distances (palette/suggest.py:868–874) — for each signature centroid, the distance to the nearest reachable color in the whole palette. From that vector _score_palette_metrics (palette/suggest.py:878) produces four numbers: weighted mean dE, max dE, % of image weight above the JND threshold, and weighted p90 dE (palette/suggest.py:892–895). The in-gamut threshold is SUGGESTION_COVERAGE_DE_THRESHOLD = 0.02 OKLab (~1 JND) (palette/suggest.py:61).
These four metrics collapse into one rank score by _palette_rank_score (palette/suggest.py:913):

mean mode (spline path): score = mean_de (palette/suggest.py:923).
robust mode (photo-stack path): score = mean_de + 0.35·p90_de + 0.15·max_de + 0.03·(pct_above/100) (palette/suggest.py:924–929) — penalises visible holes in coverage, not just the average.

The actual greedy/exhaustive/multi-start search over palettes, the top-k assembly, the swap-tier sweep, and the response shape are all on Palette suggestion search and ranking.
What comes back
The endpoint formats either a candidate list (single suggest, _format_candidate_response at server.py:3590) or a tier list (swap-aware, _format_tier_response at server.py:3620), each candidate carrying filament_ids, mean_de, max_de, and coverage (server.py:3600, 3632). Alongside the candidates it returns signature_stats (clustering + ingress provenance, server.py:3846) and model_metadata (gamut backend, domain, provider fingerprint, ranking mode, server.py:3855). Both palette_mode and metric_luminance_weight are echoed so the UI can label the scoring space honestly.
Related

Palette suggestion search and ranking — the search algorithm, top-k assembly, AMS swap-tier sweep, and HTTP response shape
generator.palette.suggest — module Architecture node
OKLab, Gamut mapping, Model-domain ingress — color-space and domain concepts the signature/gamut depend on
The Transmission Model — the T_wb · T_wc · T_color product the spline gamuts use
The photo-stack v2 model — the alternative color model behind PhotoStackPaletteGamutBackend
Appearance provider — the swappable color model the photo-stack gamut backend wraps

prisma-lithophane-generator/technical-re.title: Command-line entry points and filament availability
prisma-lithophane-generator/technical-re.content:
In one sentence: the generator ships two command-line scripts — a legacy batch solver (pipeline_cli.py, not the web-app path) and a preprocessing A/B harness (preprocessing_eval_cli.py) — and one of pipeline_cli.py’s files quietly hosts the image-loader and palette-validator that the live server still imports, gated by an exclude_from_model generation-availability policy.

This page serves two readers: the user who wants to drive a CLI, and the developer who has forgotten which parts of pipeline_cli.py are dead and which are load-bearing. The short version: the CLI’s run() solve engine is legacy and unused by the product, but several helper functions defined in the same file are imported by the live server.
Related: How a Solve Works · The Joint LUT and Staged Solve · generator.facade · generator.filament_policy · generator.evaluation.preprocessing_harness

The two scripts at a glance























Scriptprog nameWhat it doesLive as a CLI?generator/pipeline_cli.pylith_pipelineLegacy batch solve → diagnostic PNGs (no mesh)Runs, but legacy — not the product solve pathgenerator/preprocessing_eval_cli.pypreprocessing_eval_cliSolve two images under one config, print A/B metricsYes — dev/evaluation harness
A third entry point lives in palette/suggest.py (main() at palette/suggest.py:2461, prog="lith_palette" at palette/suggest.py:2466) — the palette-suggestion dev CLI — but it is outside this page’s scope.

pipeline_cli.py — legacy batch solver
Driving it
python pipeline_cli.py photo.jpg bambu-basic-cyan bambu-basic-magenta bambu-basic-yellow --out Prisma/output/lithophanes
python pipeline_cli.py photo.jpg --palette-file palette.json --out my_print
python pipeline_cli.py --list-filaments
main() (pipeline_cli.py:894) parses args, resolves the palette (positional IDs or --palette-file JSON, pipeline_cli.py:911-918), auto-loads pair corrections from data/filaments/pair_corrections.json unless --no-corrections (pipeline_cli.py:920-934), calls run(...) (pipeline_cli.py:936), then prints a per-filament usage table via print_summary() (pipeline_cli.py:969). --list-filaments (pipeline_cli.py:889-906) just lists every spline profile on disk with its registry display name and exits.

Header warning. The module docstring (pipeline_cli.py:1) calls the file lith_pipeline.py and shows from lith_pipeline import run — that filename no longer exists. Trust the line anchors below, not the header.

run() is legacy and unwired
run() (pipeline_cli.py:413) is a self-contained “6-step” solve engine: validate palette → load image → load spline profiles → build joint LUTs → solve (per-pixel or SLIC-superpixel) → save diagnostic PNGs (de_map.png, predicted.png, source.png, cap_height.png, etc.). It explicitly does not export a mesh — the final step prints “Mesh export is handled by the post-solve exporter” (pipeline_cli.py:765).
This engine is not the web app. The product solve runs the staged backend — run_staged_backend_path (pipeline/staged_runner.py:11163), invoked from pipeline/runner.py:1222-1225. Grep confirms no product module imports run: it is reachable only from pipeline_cli.main(). The in-repo legacy audit reaches the same verdict — “pipeline_cli.run(...) is not part of the live webapp solve path” (generator/docs/legacy_audit/03_LEGACY_PIPELINE_CLI_SOLVE_PATH.md:106), classing both run(...) and its segment_image(...) helper as dead_or_legacy_cli_only (lines 164-165). See generator.pipeline.staged_runner for the path that is live.
Silently-ignored legacy parameters
run()’s signature carries four deprecated parameters kept only for call-site compatibility (pipeline_cli.py:413-451):






























ParameterCLI flagBehaviordark_filament--dark-filament (argparse.SUPPRESS)Ignored; prints a one-line deprecation note when verbose (pipeline_cli.py:504-505) — “joint LUT handles luminance”tone_map--no-tone-map (argparse.SUPPRESS)Accepted, never readtone_map_gamma--gamma (argparse.SUPPRESS)Accepted, never readpixel_size_mm—Aliased onto image_sample_pitch_mm when the pitch is still default (pipeline_cli.py:507-508); otherwise inert
The three suppressed flags are hidden from --help (pipeline_cli.py:854-860). Of the four, only dark_filament produces visible output, and only as a warning.
What in this file the live server actually uses
The same pipeline_cli.py file hosts a handful of helpers that the product imports — this is the trap. They live in a CLI file but are not legacy. server.py:65 imports exactly two of them:
from pipeline_cli import (
    load_image,
    apply_adjustments,
)



































HelperDefinedLive caller(s)Roleload_imagepipeline_cli.py:61server.py:795 (in _load_run_source_image), palette/suggest.py:470sRGB load + EXIF transpose + frame crop/rotate/flip + resize to print resolutionapply_adjustmentspipeline_cli.py:199server.py:802 (only call site)non-destructive exposure/contrast/saturation/tint/highlight/shadow/temperature on the loaded rastervalidate_palettepipeline_cli.py:338pipeline/runner.py:34 import and :853 call, and run() itself (pipeline_cli.py:520)profile-present + not-excluded gate for a new solveload_filament_registrypipeline_cli.py:330pipeline_cli.py palette helpers and main(); no separate production caller foundread data/filaments/registry.json (→ {} if absent)
So in the product: server.py’s shared loader _load_run_source_image (server.py:792) calls load_image then apply_adjustments, and the live solve calls validate_palette from pipeline/runner.py:853 (the staged path’s Load step). The legacy audit confirms the shared loader/validation boundary (generator/docs/legacy_audit/03_LEGACY_PIPELINE_CLI_SOLVE_PATH.md:159-163); their eventual rehoming out of a CLI file is a noted cleanup, not done yet.

For developers: do not assume “it’s in pipeline_cli.py, so it’s dead.” run()/segment_image()/main() and load_filament_registry() are CLI-side/legacy helpers; load_image/apply_adjustments/validate_palette are the helpers confirmed on the live product path. See Pipeline Map for where they sit.


preprocessing_eval_cli.py — the A/B harness
Driving it
python preprocessing_eval_cli.py \
    --case-id my_case \
    --baseline baseline.png \
    --candidate candidate.png \
    --profiles Prisma/data/filaments/profiles \
    --palette bambu-basic-cyan bambu-basic-yellow \
    --white-base panchroma-matte-cotton-white \
    --out-dir /tmp/eval_out
This is a thin wrapper (main(), preprocessing_eval_cli.py:97). It loads two images, builds one shared SolveConfig from --palette / --white-base / --profiles (preprocessing_eval_cli.py:89), calls evaluate_pair (preprocessing_eval_cli.py:114), and prints the metric bundle as JSON. Artifact writes (predicted PNGs, delta-dE heatmap, report.json) are opt-in via --out-dir (preprocessing_eval_cli.py:72). --solver-preset accepts only "full" (preprocessing_eval_cli.py:49, :75-80) and is not used to select another path.
How it works (and why it’s not the legacy engine)
The CLI delegates to evaluate_pair (evaluation/preprocessing_harness.py:105), part of generator.evaluation.preprocessing_harness. Because it builds a real SolveConfig, each arm solves through the live facade/staged path, not pipeline_cli.run() — so the two scripts share a name space (“CLI”) but exercise different engines. evaluate_pair is live and tested (tests/generator/test_preprocessing_evaluation_harness.py) and is also driven by scripts/evaluate_preprocessing_first_bakeoff.py:315. The CLI module itself is a leaf — nothing imports preprocessing_eval_cli (only the harness it wraps is imported elsewhere).

Note the metrics reported are A4 primitives — dE, out-of-gamut, small-component, cap total-variation — per the CLI’s own description (preprocessing_eval_cli.py:58). Its own header cites a planning doc (F4_PHASE.md) — verify behavior against the line anchors, not the prose.


Filament generation-availability policy (exclude_from_model)
Both the CLIs and the web app share one gate on which filaments may enter new work, defined in generator.filament_policy (filament_policy.py).
The rule
A filament flagged exclude_from_model: true in data/filaments/registry.json is treated as unavailable for new generation (filament_policy.py:1). The flag is originally a calibration model-fit policy field, but the generator reuses it as a stop-gap until a dedicated generation_availability field exists. The contract: an excluded filament must not silently enter a new solve, palette validation, or palette suggestion just because a stale profile file still sits on disk — but existing saved palettes/runs are preserved; only NEW work is gated (filament_policy.py:9).
The three functions and who calls them





























FunctionDefinedReturnsLive callersis_generation_available(fid, registry)filament_policy.py:35False iff flaggedbase predicate for the other twounavailable_for_generation(ids, registry)filament_policy.py:48excluded subset, ordered + de-dupedpipeline_cli.validate_palette (pipeline_cli.py:360), server.py:3524 (palette pre-check), server.py:3818 (suggestion white-base/cap refusal)excluded_filament_ids(registry)filament_policy.py:40set of all excluded idsserver.py:3843 and :3937 + palette/suggest.py:2464 (passed as exclude_filament_ids to the suggester so candidates are filtered up front)
Where the gate fires

Palette pre-check (UI): POST /api/palette/validate (server.py:3516-3535) returns missing (no profile on disk) and unavailable (excluded) separately. This is advisory; the solve re-validates.
Solve / suggestion validation: validate_palette (pipeline_cli.py:338) raises plain ValueError for a missing profile, and raises FilamentUnavailableError (filament_policy.py:18) for an excluded one. That error subclasses ValueError so existing except ValueError handlers still catch it, while callers that care can distinguish a policy refusal from a missing-profile error (pipeline_cli.py:342-362, filament_policy.py:18-22).
Suggestion: an excluded white base/cap is a hard 400 up front (server.py:3815-3826), because the suggester cannot drop a fixed white the way it drops color candidates; excluded color candidates are filtered via excluded_filament_ids before search (server.py:3843, :3934-3937).

See Model-domain ingress and generator.model for why a profile’s existence on disk is not sufficient to trust it.
Disambiguation — two different excluded_filament_ids
There are two unrelated functions with this name; do not confuse them:

























GeneratorCalibration / fittingModulegenerator/filament_policy.py:40calibration/fitting/filament_exclusions.py:19Inputa registry dicta store object (calls store.list_filaments())Purposegate new generation workdrop a filament from every production fit
Both read the same underlying exclude_from_model field, but they operate on different inputs and serve different halves of the product (generation vs. model fitting). When working in the generator, the registry-dict version is the relevant one.

Quick reference — file/line anchors





















































ClaimAnchorLegacy solve enginepipeline_cli.py:413 (run)run() does no mesh exportpipeline_cli.py:765Silently-ignored legacy paramspipeline_cli.py:413-451Suppressed legacy flagspipeline_cli.py:854-860Live solve path (not this CLI)pipeline/staged_runner.py:11163, pipeline/runner.py:1222-1225Server imports from this fileserver.py:65 (only load_image, apply_adjustments)Shared loader uses bothserver.py:792 (_load_run_source_image)validate_palette live callpipeline/runner.py:853A/B harness CLIpreprocessing_eval_cli.py:97 (main)Policy contractfilament_policy.py:1, :35, :48, :40Policy error typefilament_policy.py:18 (FilamentUnavailableError)

prisma-lithophane-generator/technical-re.title: Driving the Generator
prisma-lithophane-generator/technical-re.content:
In one sentence: the generator web app (port 8010) is a four-step wizard backed by a FastAPI server that runs every long job — solve, palette suggest, palette compare, export — in a background thread on a single module-level session dict, which the browser drives by start-then-poll and which makes the whole app strictly single-user, one-job-at-a-time.

This page serves two readers: the user who wants to drive the app end to end (pick an image, build a palette, solve, review, compare, export), and the developer who has forgotten the backend’s job model — how a click becomes a background thread, how progress reaches the screen, and why two browser tabs will fight each other. It stays at endpoint-contract altitude; for what happens inside a solve see How a Solve Works and The Joint LUT and Staged Solve.
Related: How a Solve Works · Pipeline Map · Exporting Print Files · Settings, resolution, and the config contract · Command-line entry points and filament availability · generator.facade · generator.filament_policy

Starting the app
In a packaged Generator-only release, double-click Prisma.exe. In the shared Suite, double-click Prisma Generator.exe. The launcher creates the portable folder layout, selects and validates the active immutable model library, starts the local server on port 8010, and opens the browser. Keep the console window open while using Prisma; closing it stops the server. See Launching Prisma for the user-facing procedure.
server.py builds one FastAPI instance (server.py:333) titled “Prisma — Lithophane Generator API”, wide-open CORS for development (server.py:340), and — as the last mount so it doesn’t shadow the API — serves the single-page app from generator/app/ with html=True so / resolves to index.html (server.py:6276). All JSON routes live under /api/...; everything else is the static frontend (app.js, style.css, data.js).
Developers running from source may still invoke Uvicorn directly, but that is not the distribution path and the Generator’s data-path contract expects the launcher-provided environment. The stale command in the server.py module header is not end-user guidance.

The wizard at a glance
The frontend is a four-step bar (index.html:64-77): 1 Image → 2 Palette → 3 Preview → 4 Export. The steps map to backend route families like this:






























Step (UI label)What you doPrimary endpoint(s)1 ImagePick / upload a source imageGET /api/images, POST /api/images/upload2 PaletteAuto-suggest, compare, or hand-build a palettePOST /api/palette/suggest, POST /api/palette/compare, POST /api/gamut-preview, POST /api/palette/validate3 PreviewKick off the full solve and review the resultPOST /api/solve/start, GET /api/solve/status4 ExportGenerate STL/3MF print files + AMS swap planPOST /api/export/files/start, GET /api/export/swap-instructions
A persistent Palette Deck, Model Library, Active Filaments, and Printer configuration area lives in the left rail and is separate from the linear workflow. Use Model Library → Manage to manage complete published model libraries; that remains separate from choosing which filaments appear in palette tools.

The job model (read this if you are the developer)
One global session, one process
All mutable app state is a single module-level dict, session (server.py:474), created once at import. It holds the live config, the current solve slot, an in-RAM solve_cache keyed by card_id, and one slot each for compare, suggest, and export. Each long-running slot is a small state machine on a status string: idle | running | complete | error | cancelled (e.g. server.py:477).
Because this state is process-global and not keyed by user or browser session, the app is single-user by construction. Two tabs share the same session; a solve started in one tab is visible (and cancellable) from the other, and GET /api/session (server.py:2634) returns the same config and solve status to everyone.
Start, then poll
No endpoint blocks for the duration of a long job. The pattern is always: a POST .../start validates inputs, sets the slot’s status to "running" synchronously before returning (so an immediately-following request sees the job as active), spawns a daemon threading.Thread, and returns {"job_id": ..., "status": "running"}. The browser then polls a matching GET .../status on an interval until status leaves "running".








































JobStartStatus pollCancelBrowser poll cadenceSolvePOST /api/solve/start (server.py:4653)GET /api/solve/status (server.py:5383)POST /api/solve/cancel (server.py:5397)500 ms (app.js:10153)SuggestPOST /api/palette/suggest (server.py:3746)GET /api/palette/suggest/status (server.py:3942)POST /api/palette/suggest/cancel (server.py:3956)1000 ms (app.js:4031)ComparePOST /api/palette/compare (server.py:4044)GET /api/palette/compare/status (server.py:4382)(none — cooperative cancel flag only)500 ms (app.js:3601)ExportPOST /api/export/files/start (server.py:5666)GET /api/export/files/status (server.py:5745)POST /api/export/files/cancel (server.py:5764)500 ms (app.js:10493)
Each /status route reads the slot and returns status, a progress string (the current stage_label), a richer progress_detail dict, elapsed_s, and — once finished — the result payload (e.g. server.py:5383-5394). The status endpoint is a pure read; it never advances the job.
One job at a time
Each start endpoint refuses to run on top of itself with HTTP 409: solve guards on if session["solve"]["status"] == "running" (server.py:4656), and suggest/compare/export do the same on their own slots (server.py:3758, :4058, :5670). There is no global “only one of any kind” lock at start time, but the cache-management and run-load endpoints call _assert_no_active_job() (server.py:5926), which raises 409 if any of solve/export/compare is running — so you cannot, for example, clear the cache or load a saved run mid-solve.
Internally each background worker grabs a module-level lock (_solve_lock, _compare_lock, _suggest_lock, server.py:521-523) for the body of its run, so the heavy numeric work is serialized even if the 409 guard were bypassed.
Cancellation is cooperative
Cancel endpoints don’t kill the thread — they set a cancel_requested flag on the slot (server.py:5403). The worker’s progress callback checks that flag and raises a sentinel (SolveCancelled / ExportCancelled) on the next progress tick, which the worker catches and turns into status = "cancelled" (e.g. server.py:5364). So a cancel only lands at the next progress checkpoint, not instantly. Compare has a cancel_requested flag honored in its progress callback (server.py:4086) but, as of this code, no dedicated cancel route.

Step 1 — Picking an image
GET /api/images (server.py:2554) lists files in the images dir filtered to a fixed extension allow-list — .png .jpg .jpeg .tif .tiff .bmp .webp (server.py:2551). POST /api/images/upload (server.py:2566) accepts a multipart upload, rejects unsupported suffixes with 400, sanitises the filename to its basename (path-traversal guard), auto-suffixes _1, _2, … to avoid overwriting, then re-opens the saved file with Pillow to confirm it is a real image (deleting it and returning 400 if not). GET /api/images/preview/{filename} (server.py:2610) streams an EXIF-transposed, max-800px JPEG thumbnail for the gallery.
Selecting an image writes image_path into the session config (via the config endpoints — see Settings, resolution, and the config contract); the solve later resolves it against the images dir and 404s if it has gone missing (server.py:4666-4668).

Step 2 — Building a palette
There are three ways to arrive at a palette, plus a cheap validity pre-check. All of them respect the exclude_from_model generation-availability gate documented in Command-line entry points and filament availability and generator.filament_policy.
Validate (instant, advisory)
POST /api/palette/validate (server.py:3487) is a synchronous pre-check: it returns missing (no spline profile on disk) and unavailable (flagged exclude_from_model) as separate lists, plus a combined valid boolean (server.py:3502). It is advisory only — the solve path re-validates regardless.
Gamut preview (synchronous, one palette)
POST /api/gamut-preview (server.py:3972) is the one palette operation that runs inline rather than as a background job. It accepts an optional palette override so the UI can probe a non-active deck palette without mutating the session (server.py:3972-3979), runs a preview-quality solve, and returns coverage %, out-of-gamut count, mean/max dE, and URLs to freshly-baked preview PNGs (dE map, gamut overlay, source, predicted) with a cache-busting ?t= suffix (server.py:4013-4027).
Auto-suggest (background job)
POST /api/palette/suggest (server.py:3746) launches the suggester in a thread. Suggestion is always thorough now — the old fast/quality switch was removed, and unknown legacy fields are rejected loudly with 422 (server.py:3511-3515). Two modes:

Plain top-K (max_swaps unset): returns the best top_k palettes of n_filaments colors.
Swap-aware tiers (max_swaps set): sweeps AMS swap tiers honoring ams_slots, n_ams_units, and reserved white_slots from config (server.py:3891-3908).

Before any model loads, the endpoint hard-rejects (400) if the configured white base/cap is itself excluded from generation, because the suggester can drop color candidates but not the fixed whites (server.py:3766-3774). Excluded color candidates are filtered up front via excluded_filament_ids (server.py:3886). The start response supplies a job id used by status polling and cancellation. Cancel is a durable request for that active job: the UI stays attached and keeps polling until the worker reports cancelled, complete, or error.
Compare (background job, N palettes side by side)
POST /api/palette/compare (server.py:4044) takes a list of palettes and solves each at preview quality via solve_compare (server.py:4094, defined facade.py:992), then writes per-palette diagnostic PNGs (compare_<idx>_predicted.png, cap maps, surface maps) into the shared run-cache dir. A palette that errors comes back as an {"error": ...} entry rather than failing the whole batch (facade.py:1031). Poll GET /api/palette/compare/status (500 ms). This is how you A/B several candidate palettes before committing one to the full solve.

Preview ≠ full. Suggest and compare use the COMPARE_PRESET / preview path; the Step-3 solve uses the FULL_PRESET path. Numbers from compare are directional, not the final solve’s metrics.


Step 3 — Solving
Kicking it off
POST /api/solve/start (server.py:4653) validates that an image and a palette exist (the palette can be overridden in the body, else it comes from config; server.py:4662), snapshots the config so mid-solve setting changes can’t perturb the running thread (server.py:4671), mints an 8-char job_id, sets solve.status = "running" synchronously, and spawns the worker. The body may carry a card_id (for per-run caching), a profile_ref / recipe_snapshot (provenance recorded into the run metadata), and a palette override (SolveStartPayload, server.py:4398).
What the worker actually runs
The worker (_run_solve, server.py:4688) resets the solve slot, loads the source image through the shared loader, then calls solve_full(...) (server.py:4740, defined facade.py:967).

The product solve is the staged backend, not the CLI engine. solve_full → run_pipeline (facade.py:988) → run_staged_backend_path (pipeline/runner.py:846, defined pipeline/staged_runner.py:10310). It does not use pipeline_cli.run()’s legacy “6-step” engine — that engine is unwired from the product (see Command-line entry points and filament availability and Pipeline Map).

Progress detail
Inside the worker, a _progress(msg) closure (server.py:4732) both checks the cancel flag and writes the latest stage into solve["progress"] — accepting either a bare string or a dict carrying stage_label/stage_pct. That dict is exactly what GET /api/solve/status surfaces as progress_detail, so the UI’s progress bar is driven by whatever the staged backend reports. On completion the worker logs a one-line SOLVE_PHASE_TIMINGS JSON of coarse phase durations (server.py:5352).
What lands when it finishes
On success the worker writes a large pile of diagnostic artifacts into the run-cache dir (predicted/source/reference PNGs, dE maps, per-filament thickness maps, white-cap and color-ceiling/total-surface maps, contour blobs, recipe-breakdown artifacts), then assembles a JSON-safe solve["result"] dict of metrics plus /api/run-cache/files/... URLs (built from server.py:5148). The headline metrics include mean_de, source_rms_de, max_de, coverage_pct, out-of-gamut count, image dimensions, and max_height. Every URL carries a cache-bust query (?run=<card>&t=<epoch>, server.py:5007) so the browser fetches fresh images for each run. The worker also records a solve_owned_fingerprint (server.py:5344) — a hash of the solve-coupled settings — which export later checks for staleness.
Reviewing the result
The frontend reads solve["result"] from the status poll and renders the predicted render, the dE heatmaps, the per-filament thickness maps, the color-ceiling / total-surface views, and the recipe breakdown (which colors compose which regions — the Color Ceiling / Recipe Viewer sub-tab). The blocky look of the predicted render is intentional: it honors the true solve resolution and never fakes smoothness the print won’t have. Binary .bin blobs of the thickness/surface fields are served alongside the PNGs for the interactive viewers.
Auto-archiving
If the solve carried a card_id, on completion the worker writes a completed-solve cache entry and then _maybe_write_auto_run(...) (server.py:5357, defined :6059) silently packs the run into the auto-runs archive tier (labeled Auto <timestamp>). This is best-effort — failures are logged and swallowed, never failing the solve.

Step 4 — Exporting print files
The full mesh + serialization details live in Exporting Print Files; this is the driver’s view.
Two export entry points
POST /api/export/files (server.py:5651) runs the export synchronously and is retained for direct API callers and tests. The UI uses the background variant POST /api/export/files/start (server.py:5666), which threads the same _perform_export_files worker with a progress callback, then polled via GET /api/export/files/status (500 ms) and cancellable via POST /api/export/files/cancel.
What export needs from the solve
_perform_export_files (server.py:5432) refuses with 400 if there is no complete solve to export, and — when exporting the current solve (no explicit card_id) — refuses with 409 if the solve is stale: it recomputes _solve_owned_fingerprint(cfg) and rejects if it differs from the fingerprint captured at solve time, telling you to re-solve first (server.py:5443-5450). Export options come from ExportFilesPayload (server.py:742): geometry_source (default field_derived), field_scale (one of 2/4/8/16, default 4), and output_format (stls or 3mf, default 3mf).
Swap instructions and downloading
GET /api/export/swap-instructions (server.py:5774) returns the AMS swap plan — grouped filament bands with z-ranges and slot assignments, human-readable instructions, and OrcaSlicer pause G-code (server.py:5848). It reads the currently selected AMS capacity (ams_slots/white_slots) rather than whatever was active at solve time, since AMS capacity is export-time printer state (server.py:5797-5802). Generated files are downloaded as a zip via GET /api/export/files-zip (server.py:5855), or served individually under GET /api/export/files/{path} (server.py:5897). Run-cache diagnostics are served by GET /api/run-cache/files/{path} (server.py:5912); both use _safe_path to reject traversal.

Saving, loading, and comparing runs
Beyond the per-job state there is a small archive layer (Stage 9b) for keeping runs around:













































ActionEndpointNotesSave current runPOST /api/runs/save (server.py:6073)packs the cached solve into the user-curated saved tierList runsGET /api/runs/saved (server.py:6086)merges saved + auto tiers, newest first, each tagged tierDownloadGET /api/runs/saved/{id}/download, .../auto/{id}/download (server.py:6095, :6106)streams the run zipPromote auto → savedPOST /api/runs/auto/{id}/promote (server.py:6117)guarded by _assert_no_active_job()Rename / deletePOST .../rename, DELETE .../{id} (server.py:6127, :6135)delete returns 409 if the file is lockedLoad by idPOST /api/runs/load (server.py:6242)tier is "saved" or "auto"; both rehydrate via the same pathLoad from uploadPOST /api/runs/load-upload (server.py:6256)multipart zip, size-capped before the full read
Loading rehydrates the archive into a fresh card_id, restores the whole run-cache subtree to disk, rewrites every ?run= URL to the new card, and installs a complete entry into session["solve_cache"] (_rehydrate_loaded_archive, server.py:6176) — so a loaded run behaves like a just-finished solve for review and re-export. Both load routes are gated by _assert_no_active_job() so you cannot load over a running job.
Caches you can clear
POST /api/cache/clear-runs (server.py:5933) sweeps the run-cache and auto-run archives plus the in-RAM solve_cache, keeping LUTs, output, and user-curated saved runs. POST /api/cache/clear-all (server.py:5950) additionally drops the LUT cache. Both first call _assert_no_active_job().

Single-user caveats (what will bite you)

Two browser tabs share one backend. The session dict is process-global (server.py:474); there is no per-client isolation. A second tab sees and can cancel the first tab’s solve.
One job per kind at a time. Starting solve/suggest/compare/export over a running one of the same kind returns 409 (server.py:4656, :3758, :4058, :5670). Cache-clear and run-load return 409 if any of solve/export/compare is running (server.py:5926).
Cancellation is deferred, landing only at the next progress checkpoint (server.py:4733-4734).
Mid-solve setting changes are ignored for the running solve — config is snapshotted at start (server.py:4671) — but they will make the result stale, and export/swap-instructions will 409 until you re-solve (server.py:5443).
Local desktop server, not a hosted multi-user service. Single process, daemon threads, and in-RAM state are lost when the packaged launcher restarts the server (saved-run archives on disk survive). The launcher binds locally and opens the browser; it is not intended for network hosting.


Quick reference — file/line anchors

























































































ClaimAnchorFastAPI app + wide CORSserver.py:333, :340SPA served last from app/server.py:6276Global session dict + status enumserver.py:474, :477Per-kind background locksserver.py:521-523Solve start (snapshot, 409, thread)server.py:4653, :4656, :4671Solve worker → solve_full → staged backendserver.py:4740, facade.py:988, pipeline/runner.py:846Solve result payload assemblyserver.py:5148Solve status / cancelserver.py:5383, :5397Suggest (always thorough)server.py:3746, :3758Compare (preview, per-palette PNGs)server.py:4044, :4094Gamut preview (synchronous)server.py:3972Palette validate (advisory)server.py:3487Export start / status / cancelserver.py:5666, :5745, :5764Export staleness 409server.py:5443Swap instructionsserver.py:5774_assert_no_active_jobserver.py:5926Auto-run archive on completionserver.py:5357, :6059Run load rehydrationserver.py:6242, :6176Browser poll cadencesapp.js:10153, :4031, :3601, :10493Wizard step barindex.html:64-77

prisma-lithophane-generator/technical-re.title: Exporting Print Files
prisma-lithophane-generator/technical-re.content:
In one sentence: export turns a completed solve’s per-pixel layer thicknesses into printable 3D geometry — a white base, one object per color filament, and a white cap — written as STL or 3MF for your slicer, with a separate AMS swap plan telling you when to change filament.

What export produces
A finished export folder contains, per object, a watertight mesh (one STL each, or all of them bundled into a single .3mf), plus an export_manifest.json describing every object, its material, the coordinate frame, and a quality/build report. The objects are always: a white base plate, one z-slab object per color filament, and the white cap (possibly split into several bodies). Each object is tagged with the material it prints in (build_export_manifest, post_solve_export.py:1820; per-object record at post_solve_export.py:1875).
The contract lives in generator.mesh.post_solve_export (Prisma/generator/mesh/post_solve_export.py), deliberately kept clear of any FastAPI/UI concern. The webapp calls into it through one entry point, export_solve_bundle (post_solve_export.py:2549).
How you drive it (the webapp)
Export runs in the background so the UI can poll progress. The flow is:



































HTTP routeWhat it doesCodePOST /api/export/files/startkicks off a background export job, returns a job_idserver.py:6086GET /api/export/files/statuspolls stage/progress and, when done, the resultserver.py:6165POST /api/export/files/cancelrequests cancellation of a running exportserver.py:6184GET /api/export/swap-instructionsreturns the AMS swap plan + M600 G-codeserver.py:6397POST /api/export/filessynchronous variant retained for direct API/test callersserver.py:6070
Both variants use the same all-or-nothing publication boundary. Prisma builds the entire requested export in a hidden sibling staging directory, checks and finalizes its manifest and optional swap instructions, then renames that directory into its permanent {export_id} location. Cancellation or failure before publication removes the stage, so the output browser never sees a half-written export. A last-moment destination collision fails without replacing the directory that appeared. Requests to download a nonexistent export return 404 without creating an empty output folder.
The request body (ExportFilesPayload, server.py:742) has four export knobs, plus an optional card_id target selector (covered below):

geometry_source — "field_derived" (default) or "exact_raster" (server.py:743).
field_scale — must be one of 2, 4, 8, 16; default 4 (server.py:744, server.py:754). Only affects the field-derived white cap.
output_format — "3mf" (default) or "stls" (server.py:745, server.py:761).
validate_written_meshes — re-load each written mesh and re-check topology after writing (off by default; server.py:746).

Staleness guard: re-solve before exporting
If a solve-owned setting changed since the last solve, export refuses with HTTP 409 and the message “Solve is stale … Re-solve before exporting.” The check compares the current solve-owned fingerprint against the one captured at solve time (server.py:5443–5450). The swap-instructions endpoint enforces the same guard (server.py:5781–5788). This only fires for the live current target — exporting a saved card by card_id skips it.
The two geometry sources
Export can build the geometry two ways (GeometrySource, post_solve_export.py:55). Field-derived is the default; exact-raster is the faithful-to-the-solve alternative.























SourceColor stacks + baseWhite capEntry pointfield_derived (default)exact rectilinear solve-grid objectsreconstructed as a smoother field, optionally on a finer grid (field_scale)build_field_derived_mesh_bundle_mixed_resolution, post_solve_export.py:1634exact_rasterexact rectilinear solve-grid objectsone rectilinear cell per solve pixel — matches the solve exactlybuild_exact_raster_mesh_bundle, post_solve_export.py:1407
A key fact that holds for both sources: the color stacks and white base are always exact solve-grid geometry. They are built the same way regardless of geometry_source (_base_and_color_objects, post_solve_export.py:1291, called from both builders at post_solve_export.py:1423 and post_solve_export.py:1706). The geometry source only changes how the white cap is built.
Because the color layers are exact, the color part of the print is blocky at the solve resolution — by design. This is the same fidelity rule the preview honors: the geometry never fakes detail the solve didn’t produce. See Thickness map and the white base / cap budget in How a Solve Works.
Why field-derived is the default
In the field-derived path, the combined color-top “witness” surface is nearest-neighbor upsampled to the field grid (_nearest_upsample_map, post_solve_export.py:2067; lifted at post_solve_export.py:1721), and the reconstructed white cap is meshed on that finer grid via the hybrid white-cap builder. The result is a cap that can carry sub-pixel luminance detail and a smoother top surface than a per-pixel staircase, without disturbing the exact color layers underneath. field_scale (2/4/8/16) sets how much finer the cap grid is than the solve grid.
The exact-raster path skips reconstruction entirely: it meshes the cap as one rectilinear interval on top of the color floor (post_solve_export.py:1434), then falls through topology-safety strategies (below) only if that single body would weld badly.
The post-solve export contract
export_solve_bundle (post_solve_export.py:2549) is the single integration point. It is fed a materialized solve bundle — not the live session — and walks ten named stages (DEFAULT_EXPORT_STAGES, post_solve_export.py:199), each surfaced as an ExportProgressEvent the UI polls. The stages include loading the bundle, detecting solve mode, preparing maps, building geometry and cap meshes, auditing swap-banded geometry, serializing outputs, optionally reloading written meshes, and writing the manifest.
What the solve owns vs. what export adds
Export reads, never re-derives, the solve’s geometry. Before the bundle is built, the server materializes the solve’s Thickness maps through _prepare_export_materialization (server.py:835) → prepare_export_material_maps. That step also pins mandatory product safety settings on the config (_force_mandatory_product_settings, server.py:847): the minimum white-cap thickness is snapped up to a whole number of layers, printability enforcement and cap-continuity cleanup are forced on, etc. These guarantee every viewer-facing surface keeps at least one white skin layer — a hard print constraint.
From the materialized bundle, export_solve_bundle reads three settings out of the solve’s own metadata (it raises rather than guessing if they’re missing — _first_config_float, post_solve_export.py:1952):

























SettingLookup keysMeaningpitch_mmpitch_mm, evaluation_pitch_mm, solver_fine_pitch_mm, solve_grid_pitch_mmsolve-grid XY pitchlayer_height_mmlayer_height_mm, layer_heightprint layer height (typically 0.08 mm)d_wb_mmd_wb_mm, d_wb, white_base_thickness_mmwhite base thickness (typically 0.20 mm)
These flow into a RectilinearExportConfig (post_solve_export.py:200) and a GeometryExportPolicy (generator.mesh.geometry_policy) that all builders share. The defaults that originally shaped these come from PipelineConfig (pipeline/state.py:58): layer height 0.08 mm, white base 0.20 mm (d_wb), total height budget ~3 mm (t_max), cap variable for luminance.
Solve mode is auto-detected, not a toggle
Standard vs. luminance behavior is detected from run/bundle metadata (detect_solve_mode_from_metadata, post_solve_export.py:253) — preferring the luminance_mode flag, with an array-presence fallback for old bundles. The webapp deliberately does not expose solve mode as an export option.
Optional border frame
If the solve was configured with a border, export wraps the content in a white frame and shifts all content objects inward by the border width (_with_export_border, post_solve_export.py:1178). The border prints in the white-cap material and is reported as a separate __border__ object. Border dimensions are read from solve metadata unless overridden (post_solve_export.py:2191–2226).
How the white cap is built (mesh internals → see linked page)
The cap is the most involved object and the only one whose construction differs by geometry source. The short version:

Field-derived: the reconstructed cap field is meshed by the hybrid builder (generator.mesh.hybrid_white_cap) on the finer grid; reconstruction itself lives in generator.mesh.field_white_reconstruction.
Exact-raster: the cap is a single rectilinear interval if it welds cleanly; otherwise export tries, in order, a topology-risk quarantine split, then an adaptive Z-partition, then per-level slabs — each a same-material body that keeps the geometry exact while avoiding non-manifold pinches after STL vertex welding (post_solve_export.py:1454–1509; topology_risk_column_mask from generator.mesh.rectilinear_interval).

Color stacks get the same quarantine/slab fallbacks if a single color body would weld badly (_build_color_quarantine_parts / _build_color_z_slab_parts, post_solve_export.py:1102, post_solve_export.py:985).
The full per-cell meshing, the rectilinear interval mesher, and the cap reconstruction math are out of scope here — they live in From solve to mesh the export pipeline.
Quality gates and the manifest
Every built mesh is topology-checked (_quality_for, post_solve_export.py:324; check_mesh_quality from generator.mesh.quality). A part “passes” only if it is watertight with zero open edges and zero pinch edges (_quality_passes, post_solve_export.py:328), and color/cap parts additionally re-check quality after a strict STL-style re-weld (_strict_processed_quality, post_solve_export.py:336). Parts that still fail are quarantined into their own bodies rather than silently shipped.
The manifest’s top-level status is "ready" only if no object has open edges, pinch edges, or a watertight failure; otherwise "mesh_quality_failed" (post_solve_export.py:1833–1844). With validate_written_meshes=true, export additionally re-loads each written file from disk and re-checks it (_reload_quality_for_path, post_solve_export.py:2096).
STL vs 3MF

STL (output_format="stls"): each object becomes one .stl under …/stls/ (write_export_mesh_bundle_as_stls, export_serializers.py:90). The manifest names every file and its material so you can assign filaments in the slicer by hand.
3MF (output_format="3mf", the default): all objects are packaged into a single {export_id}.3mf with package-local filament assignments and registry display names (server.py:5929–5941), so OrcaSlicer can open it with materials mapped. These package slot numbers are separate from the active AMS slot table used by swap instructions.

Both formats are handled symmetrically by generator.mesh.export_serializers.
AMS swap instructions (M600)
A multi-color lithophane usually needs more color filaments than your AMS has slots. The solver groups colors into swap groups that each fit, stacked by Z height, so you load one group, print up to its top, pause, swap to the next group, and continue. White base and white cap stay in fixed slots the whole print.
GET /api/export/swap-instructions (server.py:6397) returns this plan. It is computed from the persisted solved swap_grouping block, while AMS capacity is read from the current printer profile (ams_slots, white_slots — server.py:6298–6310). The server validates that each persisted band fits the active color-slot capacity and assigns current slot tables, but it does not regroup or change band boundaries after solving; an incompatible plan returns HTTP 409.
The response carries two artifacts, both built in generator.swap:

Human-readable instructions (generate_swap_instructions, swap.py:16) — a text block with print dimensions, total height, per-group AMS slot assignments, the exact remove/load actions at each pause, and the white-cap section.
Pause G-code (generate_orcaslicer_pause_gcode, swap.py:49) — one M600 ; pause for filament change per swap (swap.py:189–205).

How M600 maps to your print
For each boundary between consecutive groups, the swap height is the previous group’s z_end, and the layer is round(z_end / layer_height) (swap.py:402–403, swap.py:633). You add an OrcaSlicer pause (which emits M600) at that layer; when the printer pauses, you make the listed slot changes and resume. N groups means N-1 mid-print swaps. If everything fits in one AMS load, there are zero swaps and the G-code is just a ; No filament swaps needed comment (swap.py:628).

Note on AMS capacity: the live webapp reads the selected printer profile’s ams_slots and white_slots at export time (server.py:6298–6310), so a changed printer profile can make an existing persisted plan incompatible. The webapp reports that incompatibility; it does not recompute the solved bands.

See also

How a Solve Works — produces the thickness maps export consumes.
From solve to mesh the export pipeline — the per-cell meshing internals routed out of this page.
Thickness map — the exact structure export reads.
generator.mesh.post_solve_export · generator.swap · generator.mesh.export_serializers · generator.mesh.hybrid_white_cap · generator.mesh.rectilinear_interval · generator.mesh.geometry_policy · generator.server

prisma-lithophane-generator/technical-re.title: Settings, resolution, and the config contract
prisma-lithophane-generator/technical-re.content:
In one sentence: the generator stores a flat dict of solve settings per session, validates resolution fields against a canonical schema that rejects legacy aliases and enforces a solve-coupled pitch pair, force-enables the mandatory printability settings the UI cannot turn off, and then translates that dict into the typed SolveConfig / PipelineConfig dataclasses whose __post_init__ re-runs the resolution backstop as a last line of defence.

This page is for two readers: the user driving the Settings panel who wants to know what each knob does and which ones they are not allowed to disable, and the developer who has forgotten how a flat session dict becomes the typed config the solver consumes. See also Pipeline Map, generator.facade, and generator.config.resolution_schema.
The two-layer config model
There are two distinct config representations and you should never confuse them:























LayerTypeWhereRoleSession configplain dictsession["config"] in server.pyMutable per-session settings the frontend PATCHes. Canonical-only.Typed solve configSolveConfig dataclassfacade.py:46Built fresh from the session dict at each solve via _build_solve_config (server.py:976). Immutable snapshot the solve consumes.
A third type, PipelineConfig (pipeline/state.py:53), is what the runner actually receives. The facade translates SolveConfig → PipelineConfig field-by-field in _to_pipeline_config (facade.py:497). Both dataclasses re-validate resolution in their __post_init__ (covered below).
The flow at solve time:
session dict
  → _apply_luminance_mode_preset       (server.py:899)   expand luminance_mode → backend flags
  → _force_mandatory_product_settings  (server.py:817)   force printability ON, etc.
  → _build_solve_config                (server.py:976)   dict → SolveConfig (validates in __post_init__)
  → _to_pipeline_config                (facade.py:497)   SolveConfig → PipelineConfig (validates again)
  → run_pipeline                       (runner.py:587)   → run_staged_backend_path (staged backend)


Note for developers: the webapp solve runs the staged backend. run_pipeline delegates to run_staged_backend_path (pipeline/runner.py:736, handoff at :1222-1225; implementation pipeline/staged_runner.py:11163). The “6-step” engine in solve.py is the legacy CLI engine and is NOT on the webapp path. Diagnostics (__de__, __gamut_mask__) for staged results live in PipelineState.diagnostics, not in thickness_maps (pipeline/state.py:262-269).

Resolution: three canonical fields, one coupled pair
All resolution is expressed through exactly three canonical fields (config/resolution_schema.py:17):

























FieldDefaultMeaningimage_sample_pitch_mm0.20mm per sampled source pixel — the observation grid the image is read onto.solver_fine_pitch_mm0.20mm per solver cell — the solve grid the thickness maps are computed on.color_region_target_mm0.60target width for color regions — independent of the pitch pair.
The defaults are _PITCH_FAMILY_DEFAULT = 0.20 and _COLOR_FAMILY_DEFAULT = 0.60 (config/resolution_schema.py:149-150).
The solve-coupled pitch invariant
image_sample_pitch_mm and solver_fine_pitch_mm are a coupled pair: when both are present they must agree (within rel_tol=1e-9, abs_tol=1e-6 per _agree, config/resolution_schema.py:95), and supplying one without the other is an error. The normalizer (normalize_resolution_schema, config/resolution_schema.py:99) enforces this three ways:

image set but solver missing → conflict error (:119)
solver set but image missing → conflict error (:123)
both set but disagree → conflict error (:127)

When valid, the normalizer collapses the pair: it writes the single accepted pitch into both fields (config/resolution_schema.py:132-134), so downstream code can read either. The color-region target is validated independently and never coupled (:139).

Practical consequence for users: there is no way to set the image sampling pitch different from the solver pitch. They are one number wearing two names. The color-region size is the only resolution knob you can move independently.

Rejected legacy aliases
Three retired field names are hard-rejected at ingress (LEGACY_RESOLUTION_REPLACEMENTS, config/resolution_schema.py:23):





















Legacy aliasReplaced bypixel_size_mmimage_sample_pitch_mm and solver_fine_pitch_mmmesh_xy_pitch_mmimage_sample_pitch_mm and solver_fine_pitch_mmcolor_pixel_mmcolor_region_target_mm
If any of these appears with a non-None value, the normalizer raises ResolutionSchemaLegacyFieldError (config/resolution_schema.py:111-112), whose message names the canonical replacement(s). A legacy key present but set to None is silently dropped, not rejected (:113).
ConfigPayload is declared with model_config = ConfigDict(extra="allow") (server.py:547) specifically so stale aliases land in model_extra and can be inspected and rejected loudly — _payload_model_fields (server.py:2758) scans the extras for legacy aliases (:2773-2777) and for a frozen set of _RETIRED_CONFIG_FIELDS (server.py:2681, e.g. smooth_stl, solver_backend, the retired guided_surface_* / hybrid_* cap-shaping fields, tv_weight, the v2_translucent_underfill_* family) and raises HTTP 422 rather than silently swallowing them. Unknown non-retired extras keep the old behavior and are ignored (:2761-2763).
On egress, _with_canonical_pitch_egress (server.py:1937) defensively pops pixel_size_mm, color_pixel_mm, and mesh_xy_pitch_mm from any dict before it is returned to the client, so the live session never serializes a legacy alias.
Where the schema runs (ingress vs. backstop)
There are two enforcement points and they have different jobs:


Ingress normalizer — normalize_resolution_schema(...) operates on external dict payloads. It rejects legacy aliases and validates the pitch pair before anything is stored. It runs at every external write surface:

POST /api/session/config (server.py:2797) — merges incoming over current session, then normalizes the merge
POST /api/settings-profiles create (server.py:3386)
PUT /api/settings-profiles/{id} update (server.py:3431)
loading a saved settings-profile record (server.py:3140)



Runtime dataclass backstop — _apply_resolution_backstop(cfg) (config/resolution_schema.py:153) runs inside __post_init__ of both typed configs: SolveConfig (facade.py:130-132) and PipelineConfig (pipeline/state.py:151-153). Because the runtime dataclasses use canonical fields only and never see external dicts, the backstop does not check for legacy aliases. It only:

applies the family defaults when both pitch fields are absent (config/resolution_schema.py:167-169)
re-enforces the coupled pitch invariant — missing-one or disagreeing values still raise ResolutionSchemaConflictError (:170-181)
defaults color_region_target_mm to 0.60 when absent, else coerces to float (:187-190)



So even a SolveConfig constructed directly in a test or a future code path cannot smuggle in a mismatched pitch pair: construction itself raises.
Typed errors → HTTP
Both schema errors subclass ValueError:

ResolutionSchemaConflictError (config/resolution_schema.py:39) carries field_a, value_a, field_b, value_b.
ResolutionSchemaLegacyFieldError (config/resolution_schema.py:63) carries field and replacements.

_translate_resolution_schema_error (server.py:2648) maps them to HTTP 422 with structured detail:




















Errordetail.errorExtra fieldsLegacy aliaslegacy_resolution_fieldfield, replacementsPitch conflictresolution_schema_conflictfield_a, value_a, field_b, value_b
Retired non-resolution fields map to retired_config_field (also 422) via _retired_config_field_error (server.py:2744). The session-config and settings-profile endpoints all wrap their normalize_resolution_schema calls in try/except (ResolutionSchemaConflictError, ResolutionSchemaLegacyFieldError) and re-raise the translated HTTPException (e.g. server.py:2814-2817, :3396-3398, :3443-3445).
Mandatory product settings the UI cannot disable
_force_mandatory_product_settings (server.py:817) is the safety gate. It is called on every config merge (server.py:2830), on egress (server.py:1939), and again inside _build_solve_config (server.py:982) — so even a hand-edited saved profile cannot ship with printability off. It forces:























































SettingForced toEffectenforce_printabilityTruePrintability enforcement is always on.cap_continuity_cleanupTrueSingle-pixel cap pinholes are always filled.color_region_target_from_printabilityTrueColor-region width is derived from the printability floor.stage2_final_printability_gate_fine_overrideTrueFinal Stage-2 printability gate always runs.stage2_printability_gate_fine_overrideTrueStage-2 printability gate always runs.stage2_printability_repair_fine_overrideTrueStage-2 printability repair always runs.stage4_printability_gate_detailTrueStage-4 detail printability gate always runs.model_domain_ingressTrueCamera Transform model-domain ingress is always applied; the legacy gamma-2.2 path is unreachable.detail_cap_enabledTrueThe detail cap is always built; ConfigPayload rejects a False value (server.py:688-692).
It also quantizes d_wc_min up to a whole number of layers (server.py:822-825) — the minimum white cap is rounded to ceil(d_wc_min / layer_height) layers — and force-enables model_domain_ingress (server.py:826) and detail_cap_enabled (server.py:830), neither of which the UI exposes as a toggle any more.
Inside _build_solve_config these same flags are hard-wired again — enforce_printability, emit_blueprint_printability, the three stage-2 gates, stage4_printability_gate_detail, and color_region_target_from_printability are all passed as literal True / _enforce (server.py:1033-1045), regardless of what the session dict said. The defaults in ConfigPayload (server.py:575-580) and _DEFAULT_CONFIG (server.py:385-391) agree: these ship True.

User-facing summary: printability is not a toggle. You can change how aggressive the printer feature-size floor is (via the active printer’s nozzle config, threaded in at server.py:998-1003), and you can set allow_print_despite_hazards to acknowledge a hazardous result, but you cannot turn the gates off.

Research-only knobs
A few flags are deliberately not exposed for normal webapp solves and stay off unless a CLI/API caller sets them:

emit_pressure_diagnostics and emit_geometry_attribution — heavier attribution artifacts, defaulted False and only honored from the raw session value (server.py:1027-1031). The comments around server.py:994-998 mark them CLI/API-only.
emit_blueprint_printability stays on for normal solves (forced True at server.py:1033).

Solve-cache invalidation
