prisma-lithophane-generator/technical-re.title: Color Solver settings
prisma-lithophane-generator/technical-re.content:
The Color Solver section governs the core of a solve: the color model, how target colors are prepared and matched to filament recipes, and how the image is partitioned into color regions. Two closely related controls — Solve Pitch (resolution) and Solve Mode — sit at the top of the Essentials section in the app but are documented here, since they set the solve’s resolution and cap strategy. For the mechanism behind these stages, see The Solve.
Solver core
Solve Pitch — default 0.20 mm; recommendation follows the active nozzle. The physical resolution of the solve grid: the spacing of the points the solver decides a recipe for. Smaller values preserve more detail but increase solve and export cost roughly with the square of the resolution. The recommended value shown is advisory and tracks the nozzle size; it is not enforced.
Solve Mode — Color (default) or Luminance. It changes how the white cap is built and — indirectly — the color recipes. In Color, the cap realizes the brightness the color solve already chose. In Luminance, the cap is reconstructed from the image’s own luminance and carries the photo’s tone and fine detail as white relief; because that reserves part of the height budget for the cap, the recipe table is built over a narrower range of cap thicknesses, so the solver can pick different per-filament recipes than in Color mode. Solve Mode is a preset: selecting Luminance reconfigures several White Cap fields at once — it reveals Shading balance and forces the boundary cap to its smooth form. See Solve Modes and White Cap settings.
Appearance Model — Color Model v1 or Color Model v2 (default). The forward color model used to predict stacks, build the recipe table, render previews, and score accuracy. Color Model v1 is the multiply-based transmission model and is always available; Color Model v2 is the interaction-aware photo-stack model and requires a published calibration bundle. See Appearance provider.
Recipe Search
This subsection controls how target colors are prepared and matched to filament recipes. Most fields are advanced.
Out-of-gamut handling (advanced) — Nearest reachable color (default) or Reduce saturation. How target colors the palette cannot reproduce are moved onto reachable ones before recipe lookup. Nearest reachable color projects to the closest printable color; Reduce saturation keeps brightness and hue and only pulls vividness in. See Gamut mapping.
White-point rescale (advanced) — default off. Rescales every target so the source’s white maps to the print’s actual paper white (the thinnest white stack), keeping pale tints in gamut instead of clipping them to white. Predicted previews read slightly darker and warmer when it is on.
Color corrections — default on. Applies calibrated correction data while the recipe table is built — pair corrections for Color Model v1, the correction layer for Color Model v2. For Color Model v1 it only takes effect when Max colors per region is at least 2.
Max colors per region — 1–7 (enforced), default 3. The most distinct colored filaments a single region’s recipe may stack. Higher values can match colors more closely but multiply the recipe search; the effective cap is the smaller of this and the palette size.
Color mismatch tolerance (advanced) — default 0.01, in OKLab color difference. The threshold above which a target is considered out of gamut and remapped — it sets when to remap, while Out-of-gamut handling sets how. Lower is stricter. The 0.01–0.20 shown is a guide, not an enforced limit.
Chroma weight (advanced) — default 1.0. Weights chroma against lightness when matching recipes: above 1 favors hue and saturation over brightness, below 1 favors brightness. It changes which recipe is chosen, not the reported color error, which is always measured in plain OKLab. The 0.1–5.0 shown is a guide, not an enforced limit.
Region Construction
This subsection controls how the image is divided into color-planning regions and how those regions are refined. Every field except Color region target is advanced.
Region method (advanced) — Image regions (default), Superpixels, or Fixed grid. How the image is partitioned into initial color regions before recipes are chosen. The image-aware modes follow image structure; Fixed grid uses uniform square cells.
Region planning scale (advanced) — 1–4×, default 1. Plans the regions on a grid coarsened by this factor. Higher values make broader, simpler regions that solve faster but follow fine edges less closely. Experimental.
Color region target — default 0.60 mm. The target physical width of the initial regions: smaller follows image structure more closely, larger makes broader, simpler regions. Note that this value is raised to a printability-derived minimum, so entering a value below that minimum has no further effect. This is the only always-visible field in the subsection.
Local recipe corrections (advanced) — default on. Lets individual grid cells inside a broader region adopt a better-matching recipe when the color improvement is strong enough. This preserves fine detail at the cost of more small recipe patches.
Boundary mutation (advanced) — default on in the current product configuration. Lets the solver redraw recipe boundaries between neighbors when borrowing a neighbor’s recipe lowers local color error. Turning it off disables that refinement. When enabled, the UI reveals three tuning fields:

Mutation current-dE percentile — empty by default (the placeholder 80 is not a default). When set, only pixels whose current color error is at or above this percentile are eligible to change; empty considers every candidate.
Mutation min gain — empty by default, which means automatic (about 0.010 color difference). The minimum color-error improvement required to accept a change, judged per pixel.
Mutation min contact — empty by default, meaning the implementation’s minimum contact requirement is used. When set, it is converted from millimeters to solve-grid pixels and requires the accepted patch to share at least that much boundary contact with the donor region.

The older Mutation grouping control is not present in the current UI or config contract. Boundary mutation already evaluates connected patch components and records its component/edge-run diagnostics internally.
The result of this section is the per-cell recipe map that the white cap, grouping, and export stages build on.

prisma-lithophane-generator/technical-re.title: Geometry settings
prisma-lithophane-generator/technical-re.content:
The Essentials section holds the print’s physical envelope — total height budget, layer grid, base plate, and the white base/cap filament — together with the two headline solver controls, Solve Mode and Solve Pitch (covered in Color Solver settings). This page documents the geometry controls. They are read by every later stage: they define how much room the color layers and white cap have, and the layer grid everything is quantized to. None are advanced; all are always visible. A cross-section diagram in the panel shows how they relate — base at the bottom (light enters here), color layers above, white cap on top, all within the maximum total thickness.
Stack Geometry
Max Total Thickness — default 3.0 mm, range 1.0–5.0 mm. The hard ceiling on the finished object’s height, counting base, color layers, and cap together. Everything else is fitted underneath it: the white cap is clamped so base + color + cap never exceeds this value, and the color-layer budget is whatever remains after the base and the minimum cap are reserved. Raising it gives the solver more layers to work with; lowering it forces thinner stacks.
Layer Height — default 0.08 mm; range follows the active nozzle (0.04–0.20 mm when none is loaded). The thickness of one printed layer, and the quantization step for the whole stack: color layers, the white cap, and detail relief are all rounded to whole multiples of it. It must match the layer height set in your slicer exactly. The model reasons in millimeters, but the printer lays down whole layers of this height, so a mismatch produces physically wrong thicknesses. A value outside the active nozzle’s supported range is flagged.
White Base/Cap Filament — the white filament used for both the solid base plate (the surface light enters through) and the viewing-side cap. As the base it is the first layer in every stack, so its transmission underlies all the color above it; the same filament forms the white cap over the top. Only filaments with a fitted profile appear in the list.
Base Thickness — default 0.20 mm, range 0.08–1.0 mm. The thickness of the base plate. It is subtracted from the total height budget before color and cap are sized, so a thicker base leaves fewer layers for color.
The read-out below the table reports the resulting color-layer budget — how many layers remain for color at the current settings — and warns when that budget is not a whole number of layers, or when the layer height falls outside the nozzle’s range.
For how the base layer enters the optical model, see The Transmission Model; for how the cap consumes the remaining budget, see White Cap.

prisma-lithophane-generator/technical-re.title: Grouping settings
prisma-lithophane-generator/technical-re.content:
There is no user-selectable grouping method in the current generator. When a full solve’s color palette fits within the available AMS color slots, no swap grouping is created. When it does not fit, the pipeline automatically runs a bounded scout and deterministic swap-band planner; the resulting plan is exposed in the solve result and used by export and swap-instruction endpoints.
The old Greedy Optimize and Group Budget settings described here previously belonged to the deleted pluggable grouping subsystem. They are not current UI controls or production solver paths.
When automatic grouping runs
The live trigger is:
FULL_PRESET
and no nested swap-banding scout run
and len(palette) > color_slots()
color_slots() is the total AMS slot count minus the effective white-slot count. The check is made by _swap_banding_requested (pipeline/runner.py:50-55), before the normal LUT build. The server uses the same palette-versus-slot condition when reporting solve progress (server.py:4854-4857). Preview and compare presets do not enter this full-solve swap-banding route.
Planning contract
The first pass is a bounded, unbanded scout. Its long side is limited to 384 pixels (pipeline/runner.py:47, _downsample_swap_scout_image), so the scout can estimate material usage without changing the main solve raster. The planner then calls choose_band_plan (grouping/band_plan.py:149) with the canonical palette, scout thickness maps, color-slot capacity, layer height, and available color-layer budget.
choose_band_plan:

refuses palettes larger than ten colors (MAX_EXHAUSTIVE_FILAMENTS = 10, grouping/band_plan.py:12-14, :165-168);
enumerates constrained partitions in canonical order, with at most color_slots colors per band (:40-71, :181-184);
estimates each band’s height from the 99th percentile of its scout usage (BAND_HEIGHT_QUANTILE = 0.99, :12, :83-87);
chooses the candidate with the smallest total raw band layers, then lowest predicted white-fill volume, then canonical partition order (:190-223); and
clamps the selected band layers to the available color-layer budget when necessary (:224-225, _clamp_band_layers).

The resulting swap_grouping is an immutable plan containing the canonical palette, groups, band-layer budgets, usage statistics, and whether clamping occurred. The live runner records it on PipelineState.swap_grouping and in diagnostics; the facade transfers it to SolveResult.swap_grouping (facade.py:714-816). The normal solve then uses the corresponding banded LUT route and white-fill calculations.
White fill and export
Each band’s color stack is assigned an exact whole-layer height. band_fill_thicknesses and band_fill_maps derive the white fill as:
assigned band layers × layer height − color thickness
Negative fill is rejected (grouping/band_plan.py:99-140). The white fill is therefore a derived carrier for exact band height; it is not a user-selected grouping setting and does not represent an independent color recipe.
The export path validates the persisted plan rather than inferring groups from final maps. It writes fixed-slot band metadata, generates swap instructions, and inserts M600 pauses where required. The plan is also used by preview reconstruction and solve summaries. If the plan is absent, the ordinary single-load export path is used.
What remains user-controlled
Users control the inputs that determine whether grouping is needed:

the palette size and order;
the active printer’s AMS slot count and reserved white slots; and
palette suggestion settings such as Max colors and Extra color loads.

Those controls do not select a grouping algorithm. A palette exceeding the available color slots may require swaps; the solve and export paths decide the deterministic grouping plan.
Related

AMS grouping and swap planning — the full scout, partition, export, and instruction lifecycle.
Pipeline Map — where the swap-banding expansion enters the five-phase spine.
The staged backend (Stage 0-5) — the solver stages that consume the banded plan.

prisma-lithophane-generator/technical-re.title: Pre-processing settings
prisma-lithophane-generator/technical-re.content:
Pre-processing conditions the source image before the color solver sees it. It has two parts: how the image is resampled onto the solve grid, and an ordered chain of optional modules that clean or reshape it. For the mechanism behind these operations, see Preprocessing.
Source Sampling
Resample kernel (advanced) — default Lanczos. The filter used when the source image is scaled down to the solve resolution. Lanczos is sharper and preserves detail but can ring at hard edges; Area integrates over each destination pixel for a softer, more anti-aliased result, better suited to coarse print-scale solves. It acts only when the source is larger than the solve grid — the image is never upscaled — so on a small source it does nothing. The current setting is source_resample_kernel (server.py:459-461).
Pre-processing Modules
The modules run on the image just before solving, in a fixed order: Noise Reduction → Print-Scale Smoothing → Flat-Area Smoothing → Palette Tone Fit → Palette Saturation Fit. Each is toggled independently. Every operator class defaults to disabled when no persisted state exists, but the current checked-in Prisma/generator/app/modules.json explicitly enables Palette Saturation Fit (c2_soft_gamut_compress: true); the other four are false. The persisted module state therefore matters more than the class default when documenting the current checkout. Discovery, normalization, and execution are documented in Preprocessing operators.
Each module is set with a named preset (strength levels plus Off and Custom); choosing Custom exposes the individual fields listed below. The first three clean and simplify the image so color regions come out less fragmented; the last two reshape the image toward what the selected palette can reproduce, and do nothing until a palette is built.
Noise Reduction
Off by default. An edge-preserving (bilateral) blur that softens small noise so it does not splinter the image into many tiny color regions, while keeping edges intact.

Filter radius (1–8) — the blur window size; larger covers more area.
Color similarity (0.005–0.25) — how different two colors can be and still be averaged together; higher blurs across stronger color differences.
Spatial reach (0.5–10) — how far, in pixels, the blur extends.

Print-Scale Smoothing
Off by default. A bilateral blur tuned to the scale the printer can actually resolve, producing simpler, larger color regions. Its physical reach is derived from the nozzle diameter and the solve pitch, so changing either changes its strength.

Feature scale (0.5–2.0) — multiplies the print-feature blur radius; below 1 keeps more detail, above 1 flattens more.
Color similarity (0.005–0.25) — the color-difference threshold for blurring, as above.
Passes (1–3) — how many times the blur is applied.

Flat-Area Smoothing
Off by default. A total-variation flatten that collapses gradual texture into broad flat areas, giving a more painted or graphic look at higher strengths.

Flattening strength (0.005–0.40) — how aggressively texture is flattened.
Scale strength to print width (on/off) — ties the effective strength to the print-feature scale (nozzle size) so it tracks the printable resolution.
Flattening mode — which color axes are flattened: Lightness only, Lightness and chroma, or RGB channels.
Iteration limit (20–500) — caps the number of iterations used to compute the flatten.

Palette Tone Fit
Off by default. Requires a palette. Remaps the image’s tonal range, in perceptual lightness, toward the darkest and lightest the selected palette can physically print, so shadows and highlights land where the filaments can reach. It anchors on source shadow and highlight percentiles and blends the result in by a chosen amount.

Tone fit strength (0–1) — how strongly the remap is applied (0 = none, 1 = full).
Shadow anchor (0–10) — the source lightness percentile treated as black.
Highlight anchor (90–100) — the source lightness percentile treated as white; must sit above the shadow anchor.
Midtone curve (0.5–2.0) — bends the curve between the anchors toward lighter or darker midtones.

Palette Saturation Fit
Off by default. Requires a palette. Softly pulls colors more saturated than the palette can reproduce back toward its per-hue limit, preserving hue and lightness, using a smooth knee rather than a hard clip.

Compression start (0.50–1.00) — the fraction of the palette’s hue-local saturation limit at which compression begins; lower starts earlier and affects more pixels.
Compression softness (0.05–1.50) — how gradual the knee is.

prisma-lithophane-generator/technical-re.title: White Cap settings
prisma-lithophane-generator/technical-re.content:
The White Cap section governs the white layer built over the color stack — the surface the print is viewed through. It sets the cap’s minimum thickness, how the boundary cap (the closed white surface) is constructed, and the detail relief above it. The white filament itself is the shared White Base/Cap Filament, chosen in the Essentials section. For the mechanism, see White Cap.
The Solve Mode setting (in Color Solver settings) strongly affects this section. In Luminance mode the boundary cap follows source luminance: the Boundary cap selector is hidden and forced to its smooth form, and the Luminance-only Shading balance field appears. See Solve Modes.
Min Cap Layers — default 1. The minimum number of white layers in the cap, counted in printed layers (its millimeter thickness is this count times the layer height). The cap is never thinner than this anywhere.
Boundary
The boundary cap is the closed white surface that covers the color stack; its thickness sets how bright each region reads.
Boundary cap (advanced) — Detail Aware (default) or Smooth. Smooth shapes the boundary cap into one continuous outer surface that carries the tonal relief directly. Detail Aware keeps the boundary cap structural — holding its predicted appearance close to the raw optical cap — and pushes the remaining tonal relief up into the detail cap instead. Hidden and forced to Smooth in Luminance mode.
Appearance budget (advanced) — default 0.008 dE, range 0–0.05. (Detail Aware boundary cap only.) The most extra predicted color error, in the color model’s space, allowed as the smoothed boundary cap departs from the raw optical cap. Lower values preserve the solved appearance more aggressively, at the cost of a busier surface.
Smoothing radius — default 1.0 mm, range 0–20 mm. The physical radius over which the boundary cap’s top surface is smoothed. Lower values keep more tonal relief in the surface; higher values produce a cleaner, more contiguous cap. The smoothing is edge-aware — pulled back near strong color edges — and the underside still fits the color stack exactly. This field stays active in both modes.
Shading balance — default 75. Shown only in Luminance mode. A 0–100 slider (from Detail to Smooth) setting whether the broad luminance shading is carried more by the smooth boundary cap or by fine detail-cap relief. Higher values put more shading in the smooth cap; lower values reserve more for fine detail. The Suggest button proposes a value from the selected image.
Detail
The detail cap adds fine white relief above the boundary cap. It is always on — in both Color and Luminance modes — and adds whole white layers only where they measurably improve the predicted result, up to a layer ceiling.
Detail depth — default 5. The maximum number of whole white detail layers allowed above the boundary cap. It permits height but does not force the cap to use every layer; it applies in both modes.

prisma-lithophane-generator/technical-re.title: Settings
prisma-lithophane-generator/technical-re.content:
The settings page configures how a solve runs — print geometry, image conditioning, the color solver, the white cap, and material grouping. These are the parameters that rarely change between runs; per-image choices (the source photo, palette, image adjustments, export format) live on the workflow tabs, not here.
Settings are organized into four editable sections, in pipeline order:

Essentials — the print’s physical envelope (total thickness, layer height, base thickness) and the white base/cap filament, plus the two headline solver controls, Solve Mode and Solve Pitch (detailed under Color Solver).
Pre-processing — how the source image is conditioned before solving: resampling onto the solve grid, plus optional smoothing and palette-fit modules.
Color Solver — the color model, the recipe search, and how the image is partitioned into color regions. (Solve Mode and resolution now live in Essentials.)
White Cap — the white layer over the colors: minimum thickness, the boundary cap, and the detail relief. (The white filament is shared with the base, set in Essentials.)

AMS swap grouping is not an editable settings section in the current build. It is created automatically during a full solve only when the palette exceeds the available AMS color slots; see Grouping settings and AMS grouping and swap planning.
Settings profiles
A settings profile is a saved, named bundle of the editable settings values, including preprocessing module state and parameters. The bar at the top shows the loaded profile and its state: Save updates it, Save As… captures the current values as a new profile, and Profiles… lists, loads, sets a startup default, or deletes them. The built-in profile is Basic — the system default. It cannot be overwritten, renamed, or deleted; saving over it instead creates a new named profile, and it can always be restored to factory values. A modified marker appears whenever the current values differ from the loaded profile.
Showing advanced settings
Many fields are hidden by default as advanced. The Show advanced settings checkbox reveals them across every section. It changes only what is displayed — nothing about the solve — and is not stored with a profile, so it resets each time the app loads. Throughout this reference, fields noted as advanced are the ones this toggle controls.

prisma-lithophane-generator/index.title: Prisma Lithophane Generator
prisma-lithophane-generator/index.content:
Turn a photo into a backlit color lithophane you print on a multi-color 3D printer. The app decomposes an image into a stack of filament layers whose transmitted colors reproduce the picture when it is lit from behind, then exports print files and an AMS swap plan.
How the documentation is organized
The same app is documented at four depths. Each section answers a different kind of question, from “how do I start?” to “what exactly does the code do?” — start shallow and go deeper only when a question demands it.

Getting Started — your first session. What you need, how to launch the app, and a walkthrough that takes one photo all the way to print files.
How To Use — the user guide. Plain-language instructions for every screen and control, explained by what they do to the print — what to reach for, when, and why.
How It Works — the mechanism. Why the app behaves the way it does: the physics of light passing through stacked filament and the math that turns an image into layer choices. No controls, no code — concepts.
Technical Reference — the implementation. Code-level documentation with real identifiers and file:line citations, for verifying exactly what the software does and finding your way around the source.

See also the Prisma Calibration app, which measures filaments and fits the color models this app prints from.

readme.title: README
readme.content:
This folder is an Obsidian vault and the source of the published docs site. To read it locally: Open folder as vault in Obsidian → choose this Documentation/ folder → start at Prisma Lithophane Generator or Prisma Calibration. On the website, the landing page at / covers the same ground.
Prisma has two Windows distribution shapes. Generator-only is the small
user path for making lithophanes from a published model library. Suite
adds Calibration, which owns the private sample database and working model
fits. Calibration can publish a complete immutable library for Generator, but
Generator never reads Calibration’s live Workspace. The user-facing install,
launcher, folder, and backup guidance lives in each app’s Getting Started
section.
Everything here uses built-in Obsidian features only (wikilinks, tags, graph view, backlinks, search) — no community plugins — so the same vault publishes as a static Quartz website without rework.
Structure
Two top-level sections, one per app, each with four tiers:

Getting Started — orientation and a first run.
How It Works — the phenomena and the math, textbook register, no code identifiers.
How To Use — a plain, task-focused user guide.
Technical Reference — the code-level map, including the dual-audience usage overviews (Using/) and the auto-generated Architecture/ module nodes.

The one rule these docs follow
Every claim is traced to the actual code, not to prior notes or memory. Technical Reference pages cite source file and line (e.g. Prisma/generator/pipeline/runner.py:587) so any reader can verify them directly. If a page and the code ever disagree, the code wins — fix the page.
Authoring rules (for maintainers and agents)

Never hard-wrap a wikilink or inline-code span across a line break — Obsidian won’t parse it. Don’t hard-wrap body prose at all.
Page basenames must be unique vault-wide (Quartz resolves wikilinks by shortest path; duplicate basenames across sections make links ambiguous). Don’t title a page a case-variant of another page either — slugs collide.
Landing/overview diagrams are generated by scripts/gen_landing_diagrams.py and injected between LANDING-DIAGRAM markers; per-page nav diagrams by scripts/gen_local_nav_diagrams.py; Architecture nodes by scripts/gen_docs_module_graph*.py. Edit the script tables and re-run — never hand-edit the generated blocks.
Screenshot placeholders use the form > [!note] 📸 Screenshot to capture (one shared convention across both apps).
Check links with scripts/check_docs_wikilinks.py (the vault should stay at 0 dangling links).

Publishing
scripts/sync_docs_to_quartz.py mirrors the vault into the local Quartz clone’s content/ (stripping title-duplicate leading H1s and rewriting folder-index wikilinks on the copy). scripts/publish_docs.py additionally builds and pushes the live site — only run it when the site should actually update.

index.title: Prisma Documentation
index.content:
Prisma is a color lithophane generator: photograph 3D-printed filament swatches to characterize how each filament transmits light, then decompose an image into a stack of filament layers that reproduces its colors when backlit. Both halves of the system are documented here, built from their source code — every technical claim traces to a file:line.
The two apps

Prisma Lithophane Generator — turn a photo into a backlit color lithophane and export print files for a multi-color 3D printer. The Generator-only Windows package includes a published Standard Model Library.
Prisma Calibration — measure how filaments transmit light on a lightbox, fit personal working models, and publish an immutable model library for the Generator. Calibration is included in the Windows Suite.

The apps deliberately do not share live data. Calibration owns its database, evidence, and current working models. Generator owns its installed published libraries and uses one complete library at a time. Publishing copies Calibration’s exact current models and public filament catalog across that boundary; later Calibration changes cannot alter a library already installed in Generator. A locally fitted generation becomes Generator-usable only through this same publish step (to the Suite’s Generator folder or as an exported library package).
Each app is organized into four tiers:

Getting Started — orientation and a first run.
How It Works — the phenomena and the math.
How To Use — a plain, task-focused user guide (the calibration app’s is still being rebuilt).
Technical Reference — the code-level map, including the usage overviews (Using) and an auto-generated module-import graph under Architecture/.
